metadata.title: How a Hacker Turned Nvidia's $2,500 Mining Card Into a $20,000 A100
metadata.author: LOCKBREAK
metadata.shortDescription:
In 2021, Nvidia sold the CMP 170HX, a $4,299 crypto-mining card with just 8GB of usable memory. Underneath, it was the same GA100 silicon as the Nvidia A100, the data-center AI chip that can cost $20,000 or more, with about 80GB of HBM2e memory physically sitting on the package. On November 10th, 2026, a hardware researcher who goes by Kate posted one line on her blog: she had converted her CMP 170HX into what is effectively an A100-80G.

Software had already gone part of the way. Jon Pry's research at Arizona State University found a flaw in the security processor inside the GPU, and Amogh Munikote's free tool cmpunlocker exposed 64GB of memory and doubled the link speed. But the real limits lived in a grid of 16,384 electronic fuses that, by design, nothing could rewrite. Kate used voltage fault injection, an $8 microcontroller and precisely timed power dips to make the fuse controller misread its own security setting, then wrote new fuse records that switched the memory and the spare SMs back on. Nine of her ten cards got all 80GB back, and in one OpenCL FP16 benchmark the unlocked mining card beat a retail A100.

In this documentary investigation, we break down how Nvidia's fuses decide what a chip is allowed to be, how the voltage glitch works, the fine print behind the benchmark claim, why no driver update can undo a burned fuse, and why memory, not compute, is the scarcest part of AI hardware in 2026.

TIMESTAMPS:
00:00 - Intro
01:07 - One Die, Two Price Tags
03:05 - The First Cracks
04:05 - Attacking the Electricity
05:25 - 80 Gigabytes and 126 Cores
06:33 - The Flaw No Driver Can Reach
07:40 - The Real Catch
08:40 - The Hardware You Actually Paid For

Topics covered in this video:
Nvidia CMP 170HX unlock, CMP 170HX 80GB, CMP 170HX 64GB cmpunlocker, CMP 170HX for local AI and LLMs, Nvidia A100 80GB, GA100 die, Nvidia GPU unlock, voltage glitching and fault injection attacks, Nvidia eFuses, HBM2e memory, Jon Pry "A Canary in the Crypto Mine", Reddit LocalLLaMA Raspberry Pi Pico replication, OpenCL FP16 TFLOPS benchmark, why AI GPUs are so expensive in 2026, SK Hynix memory shortage.

Sources:
- Kate's blog, November 10, 2026
- Tom's Hardware: CMP 170HX turned into a full A100 80GB with voltage glitching
- TechRadar: the CMP 170HX fuse unlock and its limits
- Hardware Busters: CMP 170HX unlocked SM count
- Jon Pry (Arizona State University): "A Canary in the Crypto Mine", June 26
- Wccftech: cmpunlocker and CMP 170HX prices
- Reddit r/LocalLLaMA: user replication report (unconfirmed)
- Nvidia: A100 product page, CMP page, Ampere architecture in-depth
- Thumbnail photo of Jensen Huang: Anders Eidesvik / CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

metadata.title: everything i learned building 100 GPU servers
metadata.author: Alec Glover
metadata.shortDescription:
https://youtu.be/iuLuDflfEE4?si=lAot8-Lb3mDnCVRf

In this first episode of my 6-part series, I, Alec Glover, break down how I scaled a GPU cloud from zero to 1,000 GPUs. I take you inside the chassis to show you exactly how we hand-built high-performance servers in a warehouse setting, the technical trade-offs between consumer (RTX 5090) and enterprise (B200/H200) hardware, and the secrets to maintaining stability at scale.

What you’ll learn in this video:

GPU Selection: Why the newest generation (B200/5090) offers the best depreciation and rental longevity.

Signal Integrity: Why we moved away from cheap PCIe risers to ASRock motherboards with native SlimSAS and MCIO ports.

Power Delivery: How to manage 6kW+ per server using Power Delivery Boards (PDB) and redundant 1600W PSUs.

Data Center Strategy: Scaling from 20kW racks to high-density pods with hot-aisle containment.

The Business Case: How to use the 100% tax write-off for IT infrastructure to fund your cluster.

00:00 - Introduction: Scaling from 0 to 1,000 GPUs
01:05 - GPU Selection: Business vs. Technical Needs

39:07 - Rack Scale: Designing 20kW-40kW Racks

metadata.title: I Built My Own GPU Cloud (and you can too)
metadata.author: Alec Glover
metadata.shortDescription:
https://youtu.be/ItT4pJoHWCk

What does it actually take to build and scale a GPU cloud? In this video, I break down the real lessons from scaling an AI infrastructure operation from 0 GPUs to nearly 1,000 GPUs inside a warehouse facility. If you’re thinking about starting a GPU rental business, building your own AI data center, or optimizing cloud operations, this guide gives you a practical overview of what works — and what can cost you serious money.

We cover the full stack behind an efficient GPU cloud operation: from choosing between DIY GPU server builds vs enterprise hardware vendors, to designing network redundancy, selecting the right data center strategy, and deploying automated OS provisioning systems. You’ll also learn why marketplace platforms can be a powerful starting point for GPU rentals, how reseller contracts differ from direct customers, and what financiers actually look for when funding AI infrastructure today.

This video is part of a larger upcoming series that will go deeper into topics like GPU server assembly, colocation economics, cooling strategies, and cloud software tooling. If you’re an operator, founder, engineer, or investor looking to understand the real business mechanics behind AI compute infrastructure, this is your high-level roadmap.

Chapters:
00:00 – Scaling a GPU Cloud From 0 → 1,000 GPUs (Biggest Mistakes)
01:21 – SlimSAS Motherboards Explained (How Multi-GPU Servers Actually Work)
03:31 – Enterprise vs Budget Hardware Vendors (Real Tradeoffs)
05:22 – Building a Warehouse Data Center vs Renting Colocation
06:41 – Power, Cooling, UPS & Certifications That Actually Matter
08:03 – Dedicated Internet + BGP Redundancy Setup
08:35 – Simple Network Architecture for GPU Clouds
10:06 – MC-LAG & Hardware Redundancy (Avoiding Total Outages)
11:42 – Automating OS Deployment with PXE & DCIM Tools
13:39 – Cloud Platforms Like OpenStack vs Internal Tooling
14:59 – GPU Rental Marketplaces (Vast, RunPod) vs Doing Sales Yourself
16:50 – Reseller Contracts vs Direct Customers (Revenue Differences)
17:59 – Financing GPU Infrastructure & What Investors Want

videos.full_text: I scaled a GPU cloud in a warehouse from zero GPUs to about a thousand of them by the time that we closed down. And along the way I made every mistake in the book. Running that many GPUs or just that many servers in general is very difficult. And I think a ton of people that come into this business, they just look at okay, what are the costs of the GPUs or the servers? What are the hourly rates that I'm seeing online? And they just divide that totally evenly, right? Cloud computing is so much more than just the hardware. And I think we learned a lot of lessons the hard way. So I want to make a guide so that if anyone's considering, you know, doing something like this or is already doing something like this, maybe we can give you a bit of a three year head start here. So the plan is is I'm actually going to make six videos that cover all of these topics in way more detail. But for the purposes of today, I'm going to give, you know, an overview or just a very light guide on how to build an efficient cloud operation for a GPU business. And this this is holds true for if you're running GPUs for your own company or if you're running GPUs and selling them out into the market. The goal of this is to help you avoid the mistakes that, you know, we made that ended up costing us a ton of money in the long run. So hopefully this gives you, you know, a place where you can kind of hit the ground running. The first thing we're going to talk about is building and buying GPU servers. So that motherboard that I have behind me there, that is a SlimSAS based motherboard. It's different from a normal motherboard where you've got PCI slots on it, right? Like if anyone's ever built a gaming PC before, you take GPU, put it in a PCI slot, and that connects it to the CPU. In a SlimSAS based motherboard, all of the PCI connectivity runs through SlimSAS ports, and then you're using SlimSAS cables to, you know, fan the connectivity up, right? You can imagine if you take eight 4090s or eight 5090s, you need a lot of space to spread those out around a chassis or if you're doing open air, you need to, you know, put them on different racks and stuff like that. So SlimSAS is the way to go. There's really one motherboard. Put the name of it somewhere right here. If you're doing dual or if you're doing single socket, there's a different one that I will now put the name right here. These are these are both ASRock boards. I think there's some other manufacturers that make them. I think there's some knockoffs of these ASRock boards. But I would just say we wasted so much time trying to avoid going this route, and it was it was for the worst. If if you're going to do it yourself, that is the way to go. And, you know, you've got more flexibility I think if your plan is to do, you know, standard GPU form factors. Like if we're talking about like actual enterprise cards, but then at that point I would just say, you know, unless you have a ton of experience with this, like buying the GPU servers might only cost you, you know, a 10 15% margin over building it yourself, and you lose or you introduce a ton of risk in doing yourself. So like if we're talking about building hundred thousand dollar servers, I would just, you know, pay the extra 10 grand and get a, you know, a manufactured one with a warranty from a vendor over trying to build it yourself. I think the the advantage of building your own comes if you're going to do the consumer GPU thing. So that's like 4090s, 5090s, and sort of everything in between. Buying GPU servers, there is >> [sighs and gasps] >> I think the part that everybody has to understand is there's different tiers of vendors, and you know, good reason why some of them cost more than others. So like tier one, think of like Dell, Lenovo, Cisco, HPE. They are servicing the enterprise IT market, right? So like they have services that in all these countries like across the world where they can have parts on site in four hours, and they've got 24/7 you know, support line set up to orchestrate all this. Massive supply chains, so they can, you know, get things when things are are scarce, and they charge premium because that service is very valuable to large enterprise. So if you're thinking of buying, you know, hardware to run yourself and you want to, you know, maintain things yourself, they are going to look more expensive than if you were to go and buy something from like a Supermicro who's going to just, you know, give you like a basic parts warranty on the hardware, and, you know, if something breaks, you typically have to ship it back to them, they'll fix it, and they'll send it back to you. So it's it's sort of like, you know, different levels there. And then there's sort of a third tier underneath all that where you've got like lesser known just simple hardware manufacturers like like Gigabyte, ASUS, ASRock. There's one called Avariz that makes like a good H200 B200 node. These are these are just equipment manufacturers that can assemble a very reliable server. They have good warranty. They have support engineers, but they're not they're not going above and beyond. They don't have multi-decade track records of providing like that that top tier service. So that's why they're cheaper, but I think that actually is an advantage in a lot of cases for people who are DIYing this stuff cuz you can save a lot of money up front. So that's the hardware. I want to talk about the data centers next. So you can either you can either build your own data center. So that's that's kind of what we did. We rented a warehouse that had a lot of power in it. We basically fanned that power out through the warehouse, and then connected that directly to machines. Your other option is obviously renting colocation space where, you know, you're in a a certified facility. metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to run a 125b model for free on Kaggle using the QEN 3.8 Flash Next architecture. We analyze if this hardware setup handles high-parameter inference efficiently.

Running large-scale models on restricted hardware is a significant challenge, yet recent tests show surprising performance gains on older systems. This breakdown examines the optimization techniques that allow users to bypass typical memory constraints and achieve usable speeds on free cloud instances. We evaluate how the QEN 3.8 Flash Next model manages resource allocation compared to standard deployments to help you determine if your current environment can handle these heavy requirements.

By assessing the throughput of these limited machines, we provide a clear picture of whether you need a dedicated workstation or if these free cloud resources are sufficient for your local ai needs. Understanding these operational differences ensures you are not paying for capacity that your specific coding tasks do not actually require. We also review the efficiency of running large language models on restricted hardware to see if the latency trade-offs align with your project goals.

00:00 – Running a 180B AI Model Completely Free
00:43 – Qwen 3.8 Flash Next: What Exactly Is It?
01:21 – Understanding the 125B vs 180B Parameter Count
02:40 – Mixture of Experts and How the Model Works
04:10 – Free Kaggle GPU Setup and Hardware Requirements
06:00 – Running the Model on Two Tesla T4 GPUs
09:56 – RAM, VRAM and Memory Optimization Explained

metadata.shortDescription:
Hey guys, in this video I unbox a “new to me” Octominer server I bought from Custom Computing here in Canada for about $600 CAD (~$450 USD) to expand my AI GPU rental setup.

The goal was simple: add another enterprise-grade server to my rack and rent out GPUs on AI workloads (similar to my 3090 and 3060 rigs that are already earning daily with low power usage). But things did NOT go as planned…

After powering it on, the server wouldn’t boot, no VGA signal, flashing motherboard LEDs, and hours of troubleshooting including:

Reseating RAM (256GB DDR4)

Resetting CMOS

Removing expansion board

Swapping CPUs (Xeon E5 v3)

Testing different RAM configs

Checking NVMe drive

Inspecting motherboard & power connections

I even pulled the CPUs and noticed heavy thermal paste and possible wear, which raises the question: is the motherboard dead? Power issue? Or shipping damage?

Now I’m at a crossroads:
Should I attempt a full motherboard swap… or troubleshoot further in a future video?

Also — once this server is working — I need your help deciding the GPU setup:
Option 1: RTX 3070s (better compatibility, 8GB VRAM)
Option 2: CMP 170HX (HBM2E, compute focused, possible driver issues)

My current AI rigs (3090 & 3060) are mostly rented while barely being utilized, which makes AI rentals far more power-efficient than traditional crypto mining right now.

metadata.author: GPU Battle
metadata.shortDescription:
Today, we are going to be looking at why Vast.ai is the best value for renting consumer GPUs and budget H100s - and the mistakes that waste your money there, whether you rent by hand or let an AI agent like Claude rent for you with your API key. These come straight from benchmarking GPUs for GPU Battle: power-capped cards (a 5090 running at 450 of its 575 watts), cheap cards sitting on old mining rigs with a fraction of the CPU cores, cards with almost no healthy hosts, cheap hourly rates that cost more per job, and stopped machines that keep billing for disk.

Paste this into your AI agent before it rents for you:
1. Search by quality, not price
2. Reliability 99%+, 16+ CPU cores, 800+ Mbps
3. Prefer datacenter hosts
4. Price the whole job, not the hour
5. In the first 2 minutes, check the power limit, CPU and download speed
6. If anything is off, destroy it. If it stalls, move to the next host
7. Always destroy, never stop
8. Keep my API key on my machine, never in chat

Check power limit: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=power.limit,power.default_limit --format=csv

metadata.title: 2x24GB GPUs Are NOT One 48GB GPU: RunPod vs Vast.ai
metadata.author: HostingCompared with Natalie
metadata.shortDescription:
Two 24 GB GPUs do not automatically behave like one transparent 48 GB GPU. This guide explains when data parallelism, device mapping and tensor parallelism actually help, why the interconnect matters, and which RunPod or Vast.ai fields to inspect before renting.

Compare current offers:
RunPod: https://filedesign.com/go/runpod?ref=yt-b0fXfKwASvI
Vast.ai: https://filedesign.com/go/vastai?ref=yt-b0fXfKwASvI

If you use a provider link, HostingCompared may earn a commission at no extra cost to you.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
- Two cards do not create one transparent VRAM pool for unchanged software.
- Data parallelism improves throughput, but each full model replica still needs to fit on one GPU.
- Device mapping can place whole layers on different GPUs, while tensor parallelism can shard supported layers across GPUs.
- Communication overhead and the interconnect can erase an apparent price advantage.
- Before renting, check whether the model fits on one GPU, whether your exact stack supports the split, and whether the total hourly bill still wins.

This is a documentation-based decision guide, not a paid hands-on benchmark. Availability, pricing, hardware topology and software support can change; verify the current provider listing and documentation before spending.

Official documentation checked 17 September 2026:
https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/03-advanced/multi-gpu-systems.html
https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.nn.DataParallel.html
https://huggingface.co/docs/accelerate/usage_guides/big_modeling
https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/tensor_parallelism
https://docs.runpod.io/sdks/graphql/manage-pods
https://docs.vast.ai/api-reference/search/search-offers

Production reference: HC-LF-MGVRAM-20260917-V6

metadata.title: LiteLLM Proxy Tutorial: Track Costs, Budgets, and Multi-Provider LLM Usage
metadata.author: Ready Tensor
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we walk through how to use LiteLLM as a unified proxy layer between your application and multiple LLM providers, allowing you to track token usage, control spending, and enforce budgets in real time.

You’ll see how to connect OpenAI models, custom self-hosted models, and fine-tuned deployments under a single interface, while monitoring cost, latency, and usage through a built-in dashboard.

You’ll learn how to:

Use LiteLLM as a proxy between your app and multiple LLM providers

Route requests to OpenAI, Anthropic, and self-hosted models using a single interface

Configure custom pricing for self-hosted or fine-tuned models

Track token usage, latency, and total spend across all models

Enforce budget limits and automatically block requests when exceeded

Create virtual API keys with per-key budgets and alerts

Run LiteLLM locally using Docker Compose with Postgres

Receive Slack alerts when budget thresholds are reached

Timestamps:
0:00 - Why you need an LLM proxy for cost and usage tracking
1:00 - LiteLLM architecture and multi-provider routing
2:00 - Configuring models and API keys in LiteLLM
4:00 - Custom token pricing for self-hosted models
6:20 - Running LiteLLM locally with Docker Compose
7:40 - Using the LiteLLM UI for usage and logs
9:00 - Virtual API keys and budget enforcement
13:00 - Budget exceeded errors and Slack alerts

Watch this video if you’re building production LLM applications, working with multiple providers, deploying fine-tuned models, or need strict control over LLM costs and usage.

metadata.title: Cheapest Provider Was 2x SLOWER? WILD Hugging Face + OpenRouter Routing Results
metadata.author: Prompt Engineer 48
metadata.shortDescription:
Hugging Face + OpenRouter provider routing tested: default vs :cheapest vs :fastest across 3 open models (gpt-oss-120b, Qwen 3.8 27B, GLM 5.3 Flash), 20 identical prompts each. Latency, time to first token, tokens, failures, cost, and a fallback check.

Honest limits: this is an OpenRouter proxy test (the Hugging Face router returned HTTP 402 without credits), a single run, answer quality not graded, and the custom-key change is quoted from the Hugging Face blog, not reproduced.

0:22 What Hugging Face changed
0:45 Four ways to name a model

4:58 Results: Qwen and GLM
6:51 Patterns and cost

9:06 Billing and custom keys

metadata.title: LiteLLM Auto Router: Send Each Prompt to the Right Model
metadata.author: LiteLLM AI Gateway
metadata.shortDescription:
Most AI apps let you pick one model, and then every query goes to it. "What's the capital of France?" and "refactor the auth module" end up on the same frontier model, at the same price.

LiteLLM Auto Router picks the model per request. Simple prompts go to a cheap model and complex ones go to a frontier model, all behind one model name in your config.yaml.

In this walkthrough we build the config from scratch and test it against a running gateway:

- Four tiers (SIMPLE, MEDIUM, COMPLEX, REASONING) mapped to gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-terra, claude-sonnet-5 and claude-opus-5
- Keyword rules that send anything mentioning "security review" or "incident" straight to the complex tier
- An LLM classifier that runs after the heuristics, with a heuristic fallback and the last three turns as context
- A default model, an escalation keyword, and housekeeping calls like session renaming routed to the cheapest tier
- Four test prompts, reading the routed model and response cost from each one

You can start with the heuristics alone, then add keyword rules and the classifier when you need them.


Chapters
0:00 One model for every query
0:26 What Auto Router does
0:47 Auto Router as a model in LiteLLM
1:19 Start from the docs config.yaml
1:34 Model list and tiers
2:27 Keyword tier rules
2:47 LLM classifier
3:17 Default model, escalation and housekeeping
3:47 drop_params and the master key
4:07 Test prompts
4:33 Start the gateway
4:40 Simple prompt
4:56 Keyword prompt
5:13 Billing service prompt
5:43 Housekeeping prompt
5:50 Test with your own prompts

Questions? Leave a comment below.

## Tags

litellm, auto router, llm routing, model routing, ai gateway, llm proxy, llm cost, gpt-5.6, claude, config.yaml

segments.text: Have you ever wondered how AI-powered applications like chatbots, code assistants, and more can respond so quickly?
Or perhaps you've experienced the frustration of waiting for a large language model to provide you a response.
And you're wondering, hey, what's taking so long?
Well, behind the scenes, there's an open source project that's aimed at making inference or responses for models more efficient and fast.
So, VLLM, which is originally developed at UC Berkeley.
Was specifically designed to address the speed and memory challenges that come with running large AI models.
It supports quantization, tool calling, and a whole wide variety of popular LLM architectures from llama to Mistral to granite, you name it.
But let's learn why the project is gaining popularity and start off by talking about some of the challenges of running LLMs today.
Because language models, and for example, LLMs, are essentially predicting machines, like this crystal ball right here.
And serving one of these LLMs on a virtual machine or in Kubernetes requires an incredible amount of calculations to be performed
to generate each word of their response.
And this is unlike other traditional workloads and can often be expensive, slow, and memory intensive.
And for those wanting to run these LLMs in production, you might run into issues such as memory hoarding.
So, what happens here is with traditional LLM frameworks for serving a model,
they sometimes allocate GPU memory inefficiently.
So for example, this can waste expensive resources and force organizations
to purchase more hardware than needed just to serve one of these models.
At the same time, there's issues with latency from the model or the responses and the time it takes to get a response back.
Since more users interacting with the LLM means slower responses back from the model,
well, this is because of batch processing bottlenecks
and is also an issue with running these models.
At the same time, there's issues with scaling.
So in order to take a model and be able to provide it to a large organization,
you're going to exceed single GPU memory and flop capability,
and it requires complicated setups and distributed environments that introduce additional overhead and technical complexity.
So there's a need for LLM serving to be efficient and affordable.
And that's exactly where a research paper from UC Berkeley came out to introduce
an algorithm, and an open source project called VLLM.
And it aims to solve issues from memory fragmentation to batch execution and distributing inference.
And with the initial paper, there were some incredible benchmarks and results,
including 24 times throughput improvements compared to similar systems like hugging face transformers
and TGI or text generation inference.
Now the project continues to improve performance and GPU resource usage while reducing latency, but let's learn exactly how it does so.
Within the original paper, there was the introduction of an algorithm called paged attention.
And what does this algorithm do?
Well, essentially it's used by VLLM in order to help better manage attention keys and values that are used to generate next tokens,
often referred to as K.V. cache.
So instead of keeping everything loaded at once and contiguous memory spaces,
it divides the memory into manageable chunks like pages in a book.
And it only accesses what it needs when necessary, kind of like how your computer handles virtual memory.
In addition, instead of handling requests like an assembly line going one by one,
what VLLM does is bundles together a request with what's known as continuous batching.
And what this allows us to do is fill GPU slots immediately as soon as sequences are completed.
It also includes optimizations for serving models such as CUDA drivers in order to maximize performance on specific hardware.
Now, you're likely going to end up deploying a model on a Linux machine, whether it's a virtual machine or a Kubernetes cluster,
using VLLM as a runtime or perhaps a CLI tool.
So you can actually use the pip command to do a pip install and point to VLLM in order to use it on your terminal interface
and be able to download and serve models with an OpenAI API endpoint that's compatible with your existing apps and services.
But it's optimized for quantized or compressed models, and it helps you to save GPU resources while ensuring model accuracy.
Now, VLLM is among many tools for serving LLMs, but it's quickly been growing in popularity.
But if you have any questions or comments about models and inferencing, please let us know in the comments below.
And don't forget to like and subscribe for more in-depth content on AI and beyond.
Thanks for watching.

segments.text: In 2026, the primary financial strain
for AI companies is no longer training.
Companies are actively burning through
cash the moment a model goes live and
begins serving thousands of queries at
scale. For a long time, the technical
barrier was a process called static
batching. To handle a request, the
server would estimate the maximum
possible length of the answer and block
off a massive chunk of GPU memory for
it, regardless of how much it actually
needed. This diagram shows the
inefficiency of that model. Because the
rigid boundary is set for the worst-case
scenario, the majority of the memory
sits empty. Your GPU runs out of memory
and crashes even when it's functionally
idle.
When teams ignore this waste, they're
forced to rent premium GPU clusters just
to host empty space. This is how the
unit economics of an AI application fail
before the product even launches. To
solve this, the 2026 production
landscape has split into three dominant
frameworks: vLLM, NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM,
and Hugging Face TGI. Choosing between
them requires a radar chart weighing raw
efficiency against ecosystem flexibility
and execution complexity.
Notice how each framework stretches
towards a different corner. You cannot
maximize all three. Highest efficiency
requires enduring extreme setup
complexity and sacrificing hardware
choice. Deploying an engine based on a
vanity speed metric without checking how
it fits your team's engineering capacity
will cause the application to choke the
moment your traffic scales. For most
startups building high concurrency chat
applications, vLLM has become the
industry standard. It operates on a
specific architecture called paged
attention, which works alongside a
continuous batching scheduler to keep
the hardware utilized. Paged attention
functions like virtual memory in a
computer, reorganizing the key-value
cache into small reusable pages. This
eliminates memory fragmentation. Because
the server only allocates memory for
tokens as they are generated, it can
manage hundreds of simultaneous users on
a single card. There is a trade-off.
These memory lookups add a 10 to 20%
compute overhead. vLLM also struggles to
match its competitors when processing
massive 200,000 token documents. For the
majority of interactive use cases, vLLM
provides the best balance of reliable
concurrency and simple deployment. When
latency is the only priority, such as in
algorithmic trading or real-time voice,
the choice shifts to TensorRT-LLM
running on Triton Inference Server. This
framework is highly specialized. It is
engineered specifically for premium
NVIDIA environments like these HGX H100
superchips.
To achieve microsecond response times,
it abandons general flexibility to
compile models into hardware-specific
graphs. This allows the model to run in
native FP8 precision directly on the
chip. This performance comes with high
overhead. You are locked into NVIDIA
hardware, and you will need a team of
specialized ML ops engineers who often
command six-figure salaries to manage
the complex engine build process.
This level of operational complexity
only yields a return when you are
working at the scale of these Blackwell
server racks, where shaving milliseconds
saves more than the cost of the
engineering team.
TensorRT-LLM
trades away all ease of use to squeeze
every possible drop of speed out of the
most expensive hardware on the market.
If your application involves parsing
massive legal documents or requires
hardware flexibility, Hugging Face's
Text Generation Inference or TGI version
3 is the primary alternative. Because it
is native to the Hugging Face ecosystem,
it integrates directly with the
open-source model pipelines used by most
research teams. The core innovation in
version 3 is conversation caching. By
remembering previous context more
efficiently, it can process 200,000
token prompts up to 13 times faster than
vLLM.
TGI also prevents vendor lock-in. It
allows you to move your workload from
Nvidia to Intel, AWS, or AMD hardware
like this MI300 with minimal code
changes.
The trade-off is that TGI's memory
management is less optimized for short
high-speed interactions. If your product
is a rapid-fire chatbot, your total
throughput will be lower than with vLLM.
TGI sacrifices some chat concurrency to
dominate long context rag workflows and
maintain hardware choice.
Ollama represents the fastest path for
local testing and desktop development.
It bundles the model and the execution
runner into a single executable that
runs in seconds, making it the preferred
tool for initial prototyping.
However, it lacks the continuous
batching and multi-tenant routing found
in production engines. It cannot handle
traffic from multiple users
simultaneously. Ollama is essential for
proving an idea on a laptop, but it
should be replaced the moment you move
that idea to a cloud server. Finding the
right fit is a simple process of
elimination based on your most rigid
operational constraint. This logic map
starts with your environment. For local
development or a single machine
prototype, use Ollama. For production,
consider your resources. Need sub-100
millisecond latency, a cluster of H100s
and ML ops engineers? If so, deploy with
TensorRT-LLM.
If you need to summarize 100,000 token
documents or run on AMD or Intel
hardware, TGI version 3 is your best
option. If your goal is high concurrency
interactive chat and an OpenAI
compatible API without high engineering
overhead, the answer is vLLM. Matching
the software to the specific hardware
and traffic shape is the only way to
ensure your application remains
cost-effective as it scales.
Prioritizing a tokens per second
benchmark without considering the
complexity of the setup is a mistake
that often leads to wasted resources. A
single specialized ML op salary can
easily cost more per month than your
entire GPU bill. Often, the cost of
engineers required to optimize a complex
engine exceeds what you save by simply
using a slightly less efficient, easier
to manage framework. In 2026, an
engine's value is measured by its
alignment with your team's expertise,
your hardware budget, and the actual
shape of your user traffic.

metadata.title: llama.cpp vs vLLM vs SGLang: Which Is Fastest on One GPU?
metadata.author: Tensor Garage
metadata.shortDescription:
An RTX 4090 provides 24 GB of GDDR6X memory, 16,384 CUDA cores, and a 2.52 GHz boost clock. That still does not produce one universal winner between llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang: first-token latency, sustained decoding, request throughput, and goodput measure different work.

This video explains how to compare the three runtimes under identical model, quantization, cache, prompt, output, and concurrency settings. It covers streaming TTFT, time per output token, median and p99 latency, KV-cache behavior, VRAM use, prefix reuse, PagedAttention, RadixAttention, and the point where additional load stops improving usable throughput.

Topics covered:

• How to define “fastest” across TTFT, decode speed, throughput, and goodput
• A controlled benchmark setup with fixed model, quantization, prompt length, output length, and concurrency
• Streaming tests, warmup, cold-cache passes, and prefix-cache handling
• Median and p99 latency measurement under batch-one and concurrent loads
• PagedAttention in vLLM versus RadixAttention and prefix reuse in SGLang
• KV-cache growth, fragmentation, precision, and peak VRAM measurement
• Where llama.cpp fits as a tuned local and desktop-hardware baseline
• How shared prefixes, structured outputs, and request patterns change the result
• Why goodput can fall while raw throughput continues to rise

On a 24 GB RTX 4090, do you prioritize batch-one response time or aggregate throughput under concurrent requests? Share your model, quantization, context length, and concurrency.

Every number in this video comes from the sources linked below. Corrections and your own measurements are welcome in the comments.

Research and pricing were checked in November 2026. Hardware prices, availability and runtime support change quickly, so verify current details before purchasing.

Keep streaming enabled, because

sustained generation speed.

successful requests meeting every
configured objective.

keep rising or flatten while goodput peaks
and falls.

the most compliant requests, not the one
producing the largest unconstrained token

metadata.title: Understanding vLLM with a Hands On Demo
metadata.author: KodeKloud
metadata.shortDescription:
🧪 vLLMs Labs for FREE — https://kode.wiki/4toLSl7

Most people can use an LLM. Very few know how to serve one at scale.
This video breaks down vLLM, the inference engine transforming production AI deployments, and shows you exactly why it dominates when it comes to throughput, concurrency, and KV cache efficiency.

No fluff. No theory overload. Just clear, hands-on learning starting from why your LLM is slow, all the way to launching a production-ready API server with a live monitoring dashboard.

─────────────────────────────────────────
📌 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN IN THIS VIDEO
─────────────────────────────────────────
✅ What LLM inference is and why tokens per second varies across platforms like ChatGPT & Gemini
✅ Comparison of different inference engines
✅ The KV Cache problem 
✅ How PagedAttention works — inspired by OS virtual memory paging
✅ Demo - Build a monitoring dashboard to track throughput, latency & concurrency live

🧪 FREE HANDS-ON LABS INCLUDED — https://kode.wiki/4toLSl7
Practice everything in a real sandbox environment with no local setup, no credit card, no surprises.
GPU environment, model weights, and all dependencies are already configured and ready to go.

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS
00:00 – Overview of LLM Inference Engines
00:52 – What Makes vLLM Stand Out
01:48 – How PagedAttention Works
02:31 –  Other Inference Engine
03:44 – Lab Intro & Environment Setup

05:58 – Task 2 - vLLM Offline Interference
07:04 – Task 3 - The K Cache problem
07:52 – Task 4 - PageAttention
09:11 – Task 5 - Launch vLLM as an OpenAI-compatible API server
10:08 – Task 6 - Multi-user Throughput under load
11:29 – Task 7 - Tuning vLLM Parameters for Production
12:21 – Task 8 - Capstone (Building a Monitoring Dashboard)
13:54 – Key Takeaways & When to Use vLLM vs Other Engines

metadata.title: LLM Inference Optimization Explained: KV Cache, Flash Attention, vLLM & SGLang
metadata.author: Micro Learning
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to understand how modern AI systems serve Large Language Models at scale? This video dives deep into LLM Inference Optimization, covering the core techniques that make AI applications faster, cheaper, and more efficient in production environments.

From KV Cache and Flash Attention to Speculative Decoding, Continuous Batching, and Prompt Caching, we'll explore the hardware and software innovations that power today's high-performance AI systems. You'll also learn how serving frameworks like vLLM and SGLang maximize GPU utilization while reducing latency and infrastructure costs.

🚀 In this video you'll learn:

✅ What happens during LLM inference
✅ Prefill vs Decode phases explained
✅ KV Cache and why it's essential
✅ Flash Attention for faster generation
✅ Paged Attention and memory efficiency
✅ Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
✅ Speculative Decoding for higher throughput
✅ Continuous Batching techniques
✅ Prompt Caching and latency reduction
✅ Optimizing GPU memory utilization
✅ How vLLM works internally
✅ SGLang architecture and benefits
✅ Scaling AI applications in production
✅ Best practices for LLM serving

Whether you're an AI engineer, ML practitioner, LLMOps specialist, cloud architect, or developer building AI applications, this video provides a practical understanding of the technologies behind modern AI infrastructure.

#LLM #AIInference #vLLM #SGLang #KVCache #FlashAttention #PagedAttention #GQA #SpeculativeDecoding #ContinuousBatching #PromptCaching #ArtificialIntelligence #AI #MachineLearning #DeepLearning #GenerativeAI #LargeLanguageModels #LLMOps #AIInfrastructure #ModelServing #GPUOptimization #InferenceEngine #OpenSourceAI #AIEngineering #CloudComputing #AIDeployment #TechExplained #HighPerformanceAI #FutureOfAI #AIArchitecture

We're going to demystify the entire alphabet soup of large language model optimization. You know, all those intimidating terms like KV cache, paged attention, and continuous batching. Okay, let's dive into this. So, it all starts with a simple, but honestly deeply frustrating problem. Why is generating text in AI inherently slow in the first place? Well, large language models are at their core just massive prediction engines. But, here's the catch. They can only generate text one single token or word piece at a time. So, every single time the model wants to output a new word, traditionally it has to run through the entire sequence of all the previous words all over again. As you can probably guess, this creates a massive computing bottleneck that engineers absolutely had to fix just to make these tools usable for us. Here's our road map for today. One, the inference bottleneck. Two, prefill, decode, and cache. Three, solving the memory problem. Four, tricks for faster decoding. And five, scaling for real users. All right, section one, the inference bottleneck. Why LLMs are slow. To really understand this bottleneck, we have to look at two fundamental phases of inference, prefill and decode. I want you to imagine prefill as this heavy muscular lifting. The model is processing your entire prompt all at once just to understand the context. It's heavily compute-bound, meaning it demands massive amounts of raw mathematical processing power. But then we hit decode and man is it a different story. This is where the model drips out your answer, one single token at a time, kind of like a slow hourglass. Decode is heavily memory-bound. It's completely starving for memory bandwidth because it constantly has to shuffle massive amounts of data back and forth just to spit out a single word. Section two, prefill, decode, and cache. Let's move to and see how this builds. How do we actually stop this back and forth memory transfer from just crippling our speed? Enter the KV cache, where K stands for key and V stands for value. Think of this cache as the critical bridge between the prefill and decode phases. Instead of the model basically getting amnesia, forgetting what it just read, and recalculating the entire context every single time it generates new word, it stores the mathematical representations, those keys and values, of the past tokens in a cache. Okay, so we fixed the compute repetition. But, you know how system design is, right? Every solution just introduces a massive new problem. In this case, the KV cache eats up almost all of your incredibly expensive GPU memory. Traditionally, naive AI serving engines would just allocate a big continuous block of memory for this cache right at the start, essentially just guessing how much they might need for the final answer. But, if the answer ends up being shorter than expected, that memory is just locked up and completely wasted. To fix this, engineers invented paged attention. They basically looked at how your everyday computer operating system manages RAM using paging and creatively borrowed that exact idea. metadata.title: SGLang vs vLLM: Which LLM Inference Framework Should You Use?
metadata.author: Neural AI Flair
metadata.shortDescription:
Two frameworks dominate production LLM serving today — SGLang and vLLM. Same GPU. Same models. Wildly different results depending on your workload.

In this video, we break down:

The KV cache bottleneck both frameworks solve
vLLM's PagedAttention — virtual memory for the GPU
SGLang's RadixAttention — shared prefix caching as a radix tree
Structured output: logit masking vs compiled FSM
Throughput benchmarks across diverse and prefix-heavy workloads
Latency: TTFT, TBT, and P99 tail latency comparison
Multi-GPU scaling and production maturity
Ecosystem and integrations
The exact decision framework for choosing between them
The one question that decides everything: what percentage of your tokens are shared across requests?

Above 40% → SGLang. Below 40% → vLLM.

🔔 Follow @neural.ai.flair for more AI systems explainers.

This video is the theory foundation for my full hands-on series on local Vision-Language Model deployment. Before you touch chunking strategies, attention backends, or benchmark your setup — you need to understand what's actually happening inside vLLM's scheduler and GPU memory model. That's exactly what this 10-minute breakdown covers. I walk through how KV cache grows linearly with sequence length, why a 30,000-token video request gets silently rejected, and how chunked prefill (the vLLM V1 default) prevents massive latency spikes by giving decode requests scheduling priority over prefill.

✅ What You'll Learn:

Why KV cache fills your GPU linearly and how to control it
How max_model_len, max_num_batched_tokens, and max_num_seqs interact
Why a 30K token request gets rejected before inference even starts
What prefill vs decode phases are and why they have opposite resource profiles
How chunked prefill + decode-priority scheduling prevents latency spikes
How continuous batching reuses GPU slots without waiting for full batches
What scheduler preemption is and when vLLM triggers it
How to tune batch token budget for latency vs throughput tradeoffs

⏱️ Chapters:

0:00 — The 3 parameters that control everything
0:41 — KV Cache: why it fills GPU memory linearly
1:22 — max_model_len: per-request context limit
2:21 — Prefill vs decode phase (resource profiles explained)
3:39 — max_num_batched_tokens: per-scheduler-step budget
4:31 — max_num_seqs and continuous batching
5:44 — Scheduler policies: FCFS vs priority + preemption
7:14 — Real failure case: 30K token video rejected
8:07 — Chunked prefill: how V1 solves everything
9:42 — Tuning for inter-token latency vs time-to-first-token

Discover which LLM inference engine truly delivers the best performance! In this comprehensive benchmark, I put vLLM and SGLang head-to-head using real workloads to settle the debate once and for all.
Most engineers obsess over training costs, but 80-90% of your AI budget actually goes to INFERENCE. Choose the wrong engine and you're bleeding money every single day. I'm Łukasz, Lead AI Engineer specializing in inference optimization, and today I'm sharing real-world benchmarks that could save your company thousands.

🔥 What You'll Learn:
✅ Why inference costs more than training (and why nobody talks about it)
✅ How KV-cache actually works (with visual explanations)
✅ The difference between prefill and decode phases
✅ Memory fragmentation: the silent performance killer
✅ Real benchmark results: vLLM vs SGLang on 1,000 concurrent requests
✅ Which engine wins for YOUR use case
📊 Benchmark Results Revealed:


🔧 Test Setup:

Hardware: AMD EPYC 9374F, vGPU L40S 48GB
Model: Qwen Coder (FP8)
Load: 1000 concurrent requests (burst scenario)
Dataset: ShareGPT real-world prompts
Context: 10,000 max tokens

💡 Key Takeaways:
vLLM excels at: Dynamic batching, handling mixed request sizes, early decode start, concurrent diverse requests
SGLang dominates: Decode efficiency, long outputs, streaming smoothness, multi-turn conversations
Perfect for AI engineers, MLOps professionals, and anyone building production LLM applications who needs to optimize inference costs and performance.

metadata.title: SGLang vs. vLLM: The New Throughput King?
metadata.author: System Decisions
metadata.shortDescription:
🔥 Stop Wasting GPU Cycles on Conversational AI!
Serving Large Language Models (LLMs) for complex tasks like autonomous agents, multi-turn chat, and JSON generation—what we call "Language Model Programs" (LM Programs)—is expensive and inefficient with traditional inference engines.
Here’s the technical edge that saves startups major capital:
🧠 The Caching Revolution: RadixAttention
• The Problem: In multi-turn chat or agentic workflows, the model often re-computes the same conversation history or prompt prefix repeatedly.
• The Solution: SGLang introduces RadixAttention, a novel optimization that maintains the Key-Value (KV) cache in a specialized radix tree data structure.
• The Benefit: This architecture allows the system to automatically and systematically detect and reuse partial overlaps and dynamic tree structures in conversation context, unlike caching mechanisms optimized primarily for exact prefix matches in batch inference (like vLLM’s PagedAttention).
💰 Massive Cost Savings
For complex, structured tasks, this specialized efficiency translates directly into budget extension:
• Throughput Gains: SGLang achieves up to 6.4x higher throughput compared to state-of-the-art inference systems on workloads like agent control, logical reasoning, and multi-turn chat.
• Targeted Savings: For structured output tasks, this level of optimization can potentially cut H100 bills in half. In multi-turn conversational applications, benchmarks show that RadixAttention can provide a 10-20% performance improvement over vLLM when the cache is involved.
• The Choice: Choose SGLang for complex, multi-turn dialogue systems and required structured outputs (e.g., JSON schemas enforced by Compressed Finite State Machines). Reserve frameworks like vLLM for maximizing throughput on high-concurrency single-round tasks and predictable batch inference.
Deploying LLMs sustainably means choosing the engine that matches your workload complexity. Stop paying for redundant computation!

metadata.title: Journey of a token in vLLM and SGLang
metadata.author: Vizuara
metadata.shortDescription:
Journey of a token in vLLM and SGLang. Part 2 of a free live series by Dr. Sreedath Panat (Co-founder, Vizuara AI Labs; PhD, MIT).

Part 1 showed why vLLM and SGLang serve the same model about 6 times more cheaply. This lecture opens up both engines and follows one chat request, "What is the capital of France?", from the moment it arrives to the moment the answer streams back.

We start with the four parts every serving engine has and the loop that runs them, and why the CPU must plan the next step while the GPU runs the current one. Then we follow the request through vLLM V1: the API server and tokenizer, the scheduler, the KV cache manager and its 16-token blocks, prefix caching by hashing, one flat batch that mixes prefill and decode, how each token finds its own chat's keys and values, and sampling and detokenizing on the way back. The same request then goes through SGLang: its processes, the radix tree that stores shared prompt openings, and the cache-aware scheduler that runs the most-cached requests first. We finish by comparing the two side by side and with a simple chart for choosing which engine to try first.

metadata.title: Continuous Batching - How LLM Servers Keep the GPU Full
metadata.author: DataMListic
metadata.shortDescription:
Generating one token from a large language model means streaming every weight of the model out of memory, around 140 GB for a 70-billion-parameter model, just to pick the next word. The arithmetic is tiny next to all that reading, so a GPU serving one request at a time sits mostly idle. The fix is to batch requests so a single weight load produces many tokens at once. But requests don't finish together, and static batching locks the batch until the slowest one is done, leaving finished slots dead while the queue piles up.

Continuous batching is the scheduling idea that fixes it: instead of deciding the batch once, it re-decides at every decode step, evicting a finished sequence and admitting a queued one at the very next iteration. We walk through why decode is memory-bandwidth bound, why batching scales throughput almost for free, exactly how many slots static batching wastes on an unequal workload, and why mid-flight swaps are legal at all, namely that the rows of a batched decode step never interact, since each sequence reads only its own KV cache while sharing the same weights. This is how engines like vLLM keep the GPU essentially full and serve thousands of users on one chip.

metadata.title: How LLMs Actually Run on a GPU: vLLM, SGLang & Quantization Explained
metadata.author: AI WITH Rithesh
metadata.shortDescription:
What actually happens on a GPU when an LLM answers you? We follow one prompt through Qwen3.8-27B running on an NVIDIA H100, from first principles.
You'll see why every generated token streams about 54 GB of weights out of memory, and why the GPU spends most of each step waiting rather than computing.
We cover tokens, attention and Gated DeltaNet layers, prefill vs decode, the roofline model, the KV cache, batching, FlashAttention and CUDA graphs.
Then quantization: how FP8, 4-bit and NVFP4 weights actually run, plus AWQ, GPTQ, speculative decoding and tensor parallelism.
Finally, how vLLM (PagedAttention, prefix caching) and SGLang (RadixAttention, overlap scheduling) make it all fast, with every number traced to a source.

A random drop picks one. That token's ID goes back to the CPU, gets turned back into text, and shows up on your screen. And that's one token. What we just walked through is called prefill. The whole prompt goes through in one pass, so every weight matrix gets multiplied against all the prompt tokens at once. You load a weight one time and use it for every token. That's a lot of math per byte, and it's exactly what GPUs are good at. After the first token, things change. You generate one token at a time, and each new token still has to go through all 64 layers, so you read almost all 54 GB of weights just to multiply them by a single vector. Work it out. One token takes about two operations per parameter, so roughly 54 billion. At 989 teraflops, that's about 55 microseconds. Reading 54 GB at 3.35 TB a second takes about 16 milliseconds. The memory side takes almost 300 times longer. For most of every step, the Tensor Cores are just waiting. You can draw this as a roofline. On the left side, speed is capped by memory bandwidth, on the right by compute. The corner sits at 295 operations per byte. Prefill lands on the right. Decoding for a single user does about one operation per byte, way down on the left. So, for one user, the speed limit is just bandwidth divided by model size. That's around 60 tokens a second and a bit less in practice. There's a problem, though. During decode, attention still needs the keys and values of the whole conversation, and recomputing them for every new token would be hopelessly slow. So, each token's keys and values are computed once and kept in HBM. This is the KV cache. So, how big does it get? Keys plus values [music] times four heads times 256 numbers times two bytes. That's 4 KB per token for each attention layer. Across 16 attention layers, 64 KB per token. At the full context of 262,000 tokens, a single conversation needs 16 GB. If all 64 layers use full attention, it would need 64. The Delta net layers keep their own state. The model's config stores it in 32-bit floats, which comes to about 144 MB per conversation. It's the same size at the first token and the last. The cache gets read on every decode step, as well. In a long chat, each new token means streaming the weights and the whole cache. A bigger cache means slower tokens. Keeping the cache small for long context is a big part of why this model mixes in linear layers. So, if a single user leaves the Tensor Cores idle, how does anyone serve these models at a profit? You batch. Line up 32 users' tokens, and every weight you load now gets used 32 times. The step takes about as long, but you get 32 tokens out of it. Operations per byte grow with the batch size, so you can keep adding users until you get near that 295 corner or until their caches no longer fit in memory. Real traffic doesn't arrive in neat batches. Requests come in whenever and they finish at different lengths. Continuous batching decides the batch one step at a time. When a sequence finishes, a waiting request takes its place on the very next step, so no one waits for the whole batch to finish. On one card that looks like this, vLLM claims 90% of GPU memory by default, about 72 of those binary gigabytes. Take out 50 for weights and a few for working memory, and you're left with roughly 18 for cache. A user at 8,000 tokens needs half a gigabyte of attention cache plus 144 megabytes of Delta net state. So, the card fills up at around 28 users. Zoom into a single decode step. Each operation runs as its own kernel. Done naively, every kernel reads its input from HBM and writes its output back there. Kernel fusion merges neighboring kernels, so a norm, an activation, and an add can all happen while the data is still on chip. Flash attention does the same for attention. With a long prompt, the full grid of attention scores would be huge. Flash attention goes through the keys and values in tiles, keeps a running soft max in shared memory, and never writes that grid out to HBM. There's one more hidden cost. A decode step launches hundreds of small kernels, and each launch costs the CPU a few microseconds. Those gaps add up. With CUDA graphs, the engine records the whole step once and then replace it with a single launch. Decode speed is roughly bytes divided by bandwidth, so the biggest lever you have is fewer bytes per weight. That's quantization. Take a group of weights, say 128 of them, find the largest one, and pick a scale so the whole group fits into a small range of integers. With four bits, you get 16 levels from minus eight to 7. Each weight gets rounded to its nearest level. You store those 4-bit codes plus 1 16-bit scale for the group. The scale only adds an eighth of a bit per weight. So, our model goes from 54 GB in BFloat16 to about 27 in FP8 and roughly 14 at 4 bits. On an H100, the single user ceiling moves from around 60 tokens a second to about 120 and then close to 240, at least on paper. Every gigabyte you don't spend on weights also becomes room for KV cache, which means more users per card. But, an H100's Tensor Cores can't multiply 4-bit integers by 16-bit activations. So, how does a 4-bit model actually run? The most common way is weight only quantization, written W4A16. The weights stay packed at 4 bits in HBM. A kernel like Marlin, which both vLLM and SGLang use, loads a tile of packed weights into the SM, unpacks it, multiplies by the group scale, and hands normal 16-bit numbers to the Tensor Cores. The full-size weights only exist on chip for a moment and never go back to HBM. Unpacking and scaling is extra work for every weight, but in decode, the Tensor Cores were mostly idle anyway. What was slow was memory traffic and that just dropped by about four times. The Marlin authors measured close to that ideal four times speed up over 16 bit up to batches of around 16 to 32 tokens. With bigger batches, the math starts to matter again and the unpacking stops being free. The other way is to quantize the activations as well. H100 Tensor Cores can multiply FP8 numbers directly at about 1,979 teraflops, twice the BFloat16 rate. With FP8 weights and FP8 activations, the matrix multiply itself runs in 8 bits. The Tensor Core accumulates the result at higher precision and the scales are applied at the end. That speeds up prefill, which is compute bound, and decode, which now reads half the bytes. Newer Blackwell GPUs push further with a 4-bit float format called NVFP4. Every block of 16 values shares an FP8 scale plus one more scale for the whole tensor. That works out to about 4 and 1/2 bits per value, and the tensor cores compute on it directly. It's what VLLM's recipe uses to fit this model on a single Blackwell card. The KV cache can be quantized, too. Storing it in FP8 cuts the attention cache in half from 64 kilobytes per token to 32. Rounding 27 billion weights always something. Good methods choose where the error goes. AWQ runs sample text through the model, finds the small fraction of weight channels that see the largest activations, and scales them up so rounding hurts them less. GPTQ quantizes a layer one column at a time, and adjusts the columns it hasn't done yet to cancel out the error. Both need only a small calibration set and no retraining. This is also how a model this size gets onto a desk. An RTX 4090 has 24 gigabytes and about a terabyte a second of bandwidth. At 4 bits, the weights fit with room left for cache, and the single user ceiling works out to around 70 tokens a second. Speculative decoding puts those idle tensor cores to work. Qwen 3.8 ships with an extra multi-token prediction layer that cheaply drafts the next few tokens. The full model then checks all of them in a single pass. At small batch sizes, decode is memory-bound, so checking a few tokens costs about as much as generating one. Correct guesses come out almost free. At the first wrong guess, the main model's own token takes over, and the output follows the same distribution the model would have produced without drafting. When one card isn't enough for longer contexts or more users, you split the model. Tensor parallelism cuts each weight matrix across GPUs, so each card stores and reads only its own slice. Less to read per card means faster steps. The cost is communication. After each mixing block and each feed-forward block, the cards have to add up their partial results over NVLink. With 64 layers, that's 128 of these exchanges on every decode stepping. You don't have to write any of this yourself. Two open-source engines do most of it. vLLM came out of UC Berkeley. SGLang came from researchers at LM-Sys. They share a lot, but each was built around a different core idea. vLLM's is paged attention. Before vLLM, servers reserved one contiguous chunk of memory for each request, big enough for the longest possible output. The vLLM team found that existing systems wasted 60 to 80% of that memory to fragmentation and over-reservation. vLLM borrowed virtual memory from operating systems. The cache is split into blocks, 16 tokens each by default, and each request gets a block table pointing to wherever its blocks happen to be. Waste fell to under 4% and in the paged attention paper, throughput went up two to four times at the same latency. Its scheduler plans one step at a time with a budget of tokens per step. Requests that are already decoding get served first. Whatever budget remains goes to prompts. Long prompts get split into chunks, which is called chunked prefill, so one huge document can stall everyone else's streams. Prefix caching lets requests share work. vLLM hashes every full 16 token block, and each block's hash includes the hash of the block before it. So, when a new request starts with the same system prompt, its hashes match blocks already in memory, and that part of prefill is skipped. Hybrid models need one more piece. Attention layers want paged KV blocks, and DeltaNet layers want one fixed-size state per request. vLLM's hybrid allocator groups layers by type and serves both from one memory pool. It grows the attention block size until an attention page is the same size as a state page. In practice, it looks like this. This is vLLM's published recipe for the FP8 version of this model. It uses tensor parallelism across four GPUs, stores the KV cache in FP8, and turns on speculative decoding with the model's own prediction head drafting three tokens at a time. You've now seen what every one of those flags does. SGLang started from a different observation. Real workloads repeat themselves. Chat turns and agent loops keep resending the same prefixes. So, SGLang keeps the KV cache of finished requests in a radix tree indexed by tokens. They call it radix attention. A new request walks down the tree, matches the longest prefix it can find, and computes only the part that's new. When memory runs low, the least recently used branches get evicted first. The SGLang paper reported up to 6.4 times higher throughput on workloads with lots of shared prefixes. Its scheduler also hides the CPU's work. While the GPU runs one batch, the CPU prepares the next. The team's profiling showed no idle gaps on the GPU across consecutive decode steps. For structured output like JSON, the original paper added another trick. Where the grammar allows only one possible continuation, it emits several tokens in a single step instead of one at a time. Across many GPUs, SGLang's router keeps a rough copy of every worker's radix tree and sends each request to the worker most likely to have its prefix cached already. In their benchmark, the cache hit rate went from 20 to 75% and throughput rose by up to 1.9 times. >> [snorts] >> Beyond that, the two engines overlap a lot. Both use CUDA graphs, fused attention kernels, quantization, speculative decoding, and tensor parallelism. Both can also run prefill and decode on separate GPUs and ship the KV cache between them, so big prompts don't slow down tokens that are already streaming. So, that's the whole trip. You hit enter and your message becomes token IDs. Prefill runs all of them through 64 layers in one compute-heavy pass, fills the KV cache and the delta net state, and samples the first token. Then decode takes over one step per token. Each step streams the weights out of HBM, reads the cache, runs a chain of fused kernels through every layer, and samples. It repeats until the model emits an end token or hits its limit. Every optimization in this video, from batching and paging to quantization, speculative decoding, and even the hybrid layers, is a response to that 295 ratio. When you're serving one user, memory is the bottleneck. So, next time you download a model, open its config, look up your GPU's memory bandwidth, and divide. You'll know roughly how fast it'll run before you even start the server.

metadata.title: Qwen3.8 Flash: Over 7x Faster First Token | llama.cpp vs SGLang vs FreeToken. Benchmarked!
metadata.author: Lukasz Gawenda
metadata.shortDescription:
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 35.4 seconds to the first token in SGLang versus 258.4 in llama.cpp. A 7.3x gap on the same GPU in my full-window test. FreeToken took 80.4s; llama.cpp + MTP took 210.2s.

I tested all three engines on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell with 96GB VRAM and 96GB RAM. The full-window test uses ~261,500 input tokens and a 128-token answer inside the 262,144-token window. Prefill processes the prompt; decode generates the answer.

📌 Correction at 37:09: the “+14% prefill” result for PR 28136 is withdrawn. A renamed flag was ignored, so the intended direct-read mode was never exercised. See the report for details.

🔥 What You'll Learn:
✅ The 51B lookup table: small rows fetched by address, without matrix multiplication
✅ Memory placement: llama.cpp puts the table in RAM; SGLang reads from NVMe with io_uring; FreeToken uses disk-backed PLE
✅ Why the NVFP4 setup's 63.32 GiB of experts + 47.68 GiB table need more than one memory pool
✅ Expert caching, CPU offload, PCIe transfers and when double buffering helps
✅ FreeToken setup: --moe-backend offload + --ple-backend disk
✅ Separate context sweep, 2K → 259,584 input tokens: llama.cpp decode 101.9 → 20.2 tok/s; FreeToken 100.1 → 94.8; SGLang 182.7 → 191.5 with NEXTN. This sweep uses 2,048-token answers
✅ FreeToken prefill: behind llama.cpp at 2K, about 2.4x faster at 128K
✅ Matched-build llama.cpp MTP: 94.9 → 155.1 tok/s at 8K; 83.1 → 140.4 at 32K
✅ Full-window MTP configuration: 52.6 vs 20.3 tok/s; this 2.59x gap also involves a different build
✅ N-gram: +6.8% decode on tested code; no drafts on tested prose with the 24-token match setting
✅ Why forcing output length can inflate coding throughput with repeated filler
✅ Startup to first answer: llama.cpp 16s, SGLang 108s, FreeToken 126s; HTTP health is not serving readiness
✅ Accuracy: GSM8K 95.22–95.75%, MATH-500 92.20–93.00%; no significant pairwise differences detected, not proof of equal quality
✅ Loading modes, recall after server reuse, GPU temperatures, estimated energy and live cache resizing

🔧 Setup:
Ryzen 9 9950X · RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96GB · 96GB DDR5 · CUDA 13 · Ubuntu · Docker
Model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (125B main + 51B n-gram memory, 6B active)
Formats: UD-IQ4_XS GGUF (87.2 GiB) for llama.cpp; NVFP4 for SGLang/FreeToken; MTP head ~2.6GB
Builds: llama.cpp b10666 + qwen4exp/mtp fork; SGLang 2026-08-17 nightly + PRs 36567, 36556, 36749, 36750; FreeToken
Method: AIPerf, thinking off, one engine at a time, cooldowns and GPU telemetry. Main sweep: one request at a time. Quantization, KV cache, placement and speculation differ, so results compare the tested stacks on this workstation.

metadata.title: AWS FinOps Explained in 5 Minutes
metadata.author: AWS With A Beer
metadata.shortDescription:
💡 AWS FinOps Explained in 5 Minutes 💡
Struggling with your #aws  cloud bills? Wondering how to balance innovation with financial control? In this video, we break down AWS #finops  —a game-changing practice for managing and optimizing your cloud costs while ensuring your organization’s goals are met.

🎯 What you’ll learn:
• What AWS FinOps is and why it’s essential.
• Common challenges in cloud cost management (like zombie instances and complex pricing).
• Key AWS tools to help you master FinOps, including Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, Trusted Advisor, and more.
• How FinOps bridges the gap between finance, engineering, and leadership teams.

Whether you’re part of a startup or managing enterprise-scale cloud operations, this video is your ultimate guide to keeping costs under control without compromising on performance.

🔔 Don’t forget to like, subscribe, and share for more cloud insights and strategies to optimize your AWS experience!

👉 Got questions or tips? Drop them in the comments! Let's make the cloud work smarter for everyone.

#AWSFinOps #CloudCostManagement #FinOps #AWSOptimization #CloudBudgetTips

metadata.title: The State of Cloud & AI Cost Management in 2026 | FinOps Summer Camp Session 1
metadata.author: Vantage
metadata.shortDescription:
The state of cloud and AI cost management in 2026, backed by fresh 451 Research (S&P Global) survey data. Jean Atelsek and Vantage CEO Ben Schaechter break down four insights every FinOps team should know.

In this first session of FinOps Summer Camp, senior analyst Jean Atelsek of 451 Research, part of S&P Global, shares new data from IT decision-makers and FinOps practitioners on where cloud and AI cost management is heading. Vantage co-founder and CEO Ben Schaechter follows each finding with what Vantage sees across thousands of customers.

What you'll learn:
- Why native cloud cost tools still lead, and why multi-vendor platforms are gaining share
- How FinOps is spreading into asset management, service management, and observability
- Why GenAI is the top cause of budget overruns, and why mature teams now spend ~80% of their time on AI spend
- What Vantage's own provider data shows about the explosion of AI cost
- How teams are tackling token attribution, AI gateways, and anomaly detection

Chapters:
00:00 Welcome and speaker introductions
02:28 What this session covers
03:55 Insight 1: Native tools vs. multi-vendor cost platforms
09:02 Insight 2: FinOps expands across IT and observability
15:25 Insight 3: GenAI, the top cause of budget overruns
21:00 Insight 4: Vantage data on the AI provider explosion
29:17 Audience Q&A: token attribution, gateways, and anomaly detection
41:41 Closing and Session 2 preview

Speakers:
Jean Atelsek, Senior Research Analyst, 451 Research by S&P Global
Ben Schaechter, Co-Founder & CEO, Vantage

FinOps Summer Camp is a four-part series on AI cost observability. Session 2 features the Make.com platform team on how they instrument AI cost in production, Thursday, July 30 at 11am ET.

Learn more about Vantage: https://www.vantage.sh

#FinOps #AICost #CloudCostManagement #CostObservability #Vantage

metadata.title: AWS re:Invent 2025 - FinOps+: A New Era of Accelerating Value (COP211)
metadata.author: AWS Events
metadata.shortDescription:
FinOps is evolving and AI is accelerating the shift. As organizations face increasing complexity, traditional FinOps approaches are no longer enough. We are entering a new era of FinOps; one that requires automation, governance & scale.
FinOps+ introduces an AI-powered approach that unifies CloudOps, emphasizes automation and expands into holistic spend management within a single platform. This talk will show how AI-driven FinOps and proactive governance can transform the way teams manage technology, enabling smarter decisions, streamlined operations & accelerated value.
Whether you’re beginning your FinOps journey or looking to scale, you’ll leave with a clear vision for how to move beyond traditional practices into the future of FinOps. This presentation is brought to you by Kion, an AWS Partner.

Learn more:
More AWS events: https://go.aws/3kss9CP 

Subscribe:
More AWS videos: http://bit.ly/2O3zS75
More AWS events videos: http://bit.ly/316g9t4

ABOUT AWS:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) hosts events, both online and in-person, bringing the cloud computing community together to connect, collaborate, and learn from AWS experts.
 AWS is the world's most comprehensive and broadly adopted cloud platform, offering over 200 fully featured services from data centers globally. Millions of customers—including the fastest-growing startups, largest enterprises, and leading government agencies—are using AWS to lower costs, become more agile, and innovate faster.

#AWSreInvent #AWSreInvent2025 #AWS

segments.text: - Well good afternoon everyone.
I'm Tatum Tummins, senior project manager at Kion.
If you're not familiar with Kion,
we're a FinOps and CloudOps enablement tool
focusing on automation and governance.
Prior to coming over to the vendor side of the space,
I spent over 7 1/2 years
at a large healthcare company doing FinOps.
I like to say I grew up in the industry in a lot of ways,
and I like to share that
because I'm passionate about the subject,
I'm passionate about helping people
get better in their practice,
and that's ultimately why I'm here today,
to talk about FinOps+,
an effort that I think will help organizations
be more successful.
So what we look at what we're gonna do today,
we're gonna start with a quick level set of
what has the FinOps industry looked like over the last year.
That will lead us into the 30,000 foot macro view
of what FinOps+ is.
And then I'll spend a few slides
getting into more of the details
of what that looks like in action, some examples,
and then we'll end with some next steps and takeaways.
But to start, it's important we reflect on
what the last year has looked like in the industry.
And for those of you that are familiar
with the FinOps Foundation,
every year they do a state of the FinOps survey
where they ask folks like you all what are your challenges,
what are your priorities, et cetera.
And in that survey, at the beginning of this year,
folks came back and said,
"Hey, we got three main priorities right now.
It's reducing waste and optimizing spend,
it's allocation of that cloud spend,
and trying to get a little bit better at forecasting."
But what I found really interesting
is when folks were asked
well what are you gonna care about
over the next 12 months, two new things enter.
The first is FinOps governance and policy at scale,
and the third was managing costs beyond public cloud.
Those two things along with three developments,
those three developments,
the first being the introduction of scopes.
So the FinOps Foundation introduced this topic,
which is essentially outlining the different areas
of your technology investment
that you can and should practice FinOps on.
The second is the common billing schema of FOCUS.
The 1.2 was released,
and what we're seeing is that practitioners
and vendors alike are starting to adopt that schema
or at least start to explore what that would look like.
And the last piece,
and this should be obvious
if you've walked around anywhere this week, AI's everywhere.
And the FinOps industry is no different.
So when I looked at that survey data,
and then I started to have conversations
with prospects and customers,
I was starting to package what are the areas
that folks can start to focus on of where FinOps is headed?
And earlier this year, I met a gentleman,
he's actually sitting right back there,
Matt Cofran from Insulet.
And we met Matt, and Matt came to us and said,
"Hey, Insulet's looking for really two things.
We want to get better visibility
into all of our technology spend.
We have all of these SaaS tools
that we wanna start bringing in
to have a single pane of glass."
And Matt also said, "Hey, we need to bring more governance
and more policy to our FinOps practice."
And so I thought about the survey data,
and I thought about what Matt was saying,
and I started to put this together.
And what Matt ultimately said,
and you can scan that QR code for a full case study,
is he said we didn't just need FinOps,
we needed FinOps Plus.
And so like any good product manager,
I steal good ideas when I see them.
And I decided to call this framework FinOps+.
And ultimately it's three pillars.
It's automated governance, it's AI driven,
and it's beyond public cloud.
And in a few slides, we'll show some examples
of what these look like in practice,
but I wanna stay high level for a moment
and talk about what FinOps+ is and is not.
So it's a modern approach,
and it's really focused on doing three things:
solving challenges a little bit more proactively,
driving efficiency, and enabling smarter decisions.
And what it's really trying to do is take the things
that you all are doing today,
the same challenges and processes,
and it's trying to make those more successful right now.
But what it's really trying to do is set you all up
for success for where FinOps is going
over the next 12 to 18 months as it evolves.
When we think about what it's not,
it is by no means trying to redefine FinOps.
These three pillars are meant to apply
to the same processes that you're doing today.
It's also not trying to add more work to your plate.
If anything, it's trying to do the opposite
by leaning on automation,
leaning on AI in strategic ways.
It starts to give you more time back in your day.
And then lastly, it's not just for certain maturity levels.
There's gonna be some things in the next few slides
that for some of you may seem too mature or too farfetched,
but I promise and I'm confident
that there's gonna be something within at least one
of these pillars that you can start to apply
to your practice leaving today.
And so with that,
let's talk about what these pillars look like in action.
And so the first we're gonna talk about
is automated governance.
And I like to just start by defining that with three steps.
The first is policy.
Policy becomes automation and automation becomes guardrails.
And when I talk about what policy means,
I'll throw some examples up
that probably apply to all of you.
Policy looks like how you wanna define waste
or what an orphaned resource looks at your organization.
It looks like what is your retention policy
for snapshots or storage.
It can be what your lights off policy looks like
for your sandbox and dev environments.
What time do you shut those off?
Are they off on the weekends?

metadata.title: Managing AI Budgets in the Age of Tokenmaxxing | FinOps Summer Camp Session 3
metadata.author: Vantage
metadata.shortDescription:
Everyone spent the last year chasing token counts and spots on the leaderboards. Then the CFO got the bill and everything changed. In Session 3 of FinOps Summer Camp, Vantage's Rem Baumann and Augusto Leal show how to put real budgets on AI spend without slowing your developers down.

As AI adoption exploded, so did tokenmaxxing, the habit of treating raw token usage as a proxy for productivity. This session covers what comes next. Rem and Augusto walk through a four-step framework for governing AI cost, visibility, allocation, measuring value, and budgets, then show it live inside Vantage across providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, Cursor, and AWS Bedrock.

What you'll learn:

Why cost per token is a vanity metric, and what to measure instead
The four-step framework for governing AI spend: visibility, allocation, measure value, budgets and guardrails
How to attribute AI spend to teams, customers, and features using virtual tags
How to measure value per developer with metrics like cost per merged PR and cost per resolved ticket
How to set budgets that hold without blocking engineers from shipping
A live demo of AI cost visibility, per-user budgets, and telemetry-based cost allocation in Vantage

Chapters
