01:42 Meet the speakers: Rem Baumann and Augusto Leal 
03:15 Housekeeping 
04:12 What is tokenmaxxing?

12:06 Step 2: Allocation 
14:20 Step 3: Measure value 
17:22 Step 4: Budgets and guardrails 
19:10 Demo: AI cost visibility and per-user budgets 
23:13 Demo: Telemetry-based allocation and agent costs 
24:57 Demo: Measuring value per developer with MCP and Linear 
26:49 Live Q&A 
27:11 Q: Breaking out AI spend hidden in a bigger bill (Bedrock in AWS) 
28:38 Q: Optimization recommendations for AI spend 
31:12 Q: Are virtual tags a Vantage-only construct? 
33:14 Q: Getting engineers to care about cost 
34:26 Closing

About the speakers
Rem Baumann is Director of Product at Vantage and a certified FinOps practitioner who spent five years at AWS helping enterprises get their cloud spend under control. Augusto Leal is a Sales Engineer at Vantage who came up through both finance and engineering, from a J.P. Morgan analyst seat to software engineering to founding his own company.

About the series
FinOps Summer Camp is a Vantage webinar series on managing cloud and AI cost. Catch the earlier sessions and read the recaps on our blog, and keep an eye out for the next series this fall.

All sessions and recaps: https://www.vantage.sh/blog

Connect with Rem and Augusto on LinkedIn, or find the team in the Vantage community Slack and the FinOps Foundation Slack.

https://finopsfoundation.slack.com/

metadata.title: AWS reInvent 2025:  FinOps A New Era of Accelerating Value
metadata.author: Kion
metadata.shortDescription:
FinOps is evolving and AI is accelerating the shift. As organizations face increasing complexity, traditional FinOps approaches are no longer enough. We are entering a new era of FinOps; one that requires automation, governance & scale.

FinOps+ introduces an AI-powered approach that unifies CloudOps, emphasizes automation and expands into holistic spend management within a single platform. This talk shows how AI-driven FinOps and proactive governance can transform the way teams manage technology, enabling smarter decisions, streamlined operations & accelerated value. 

Whether you’re beginning your FinOps journey or looking to scale, you’ll leave with a clear vision for how to move beyond traditional practices into the future of FinOps.

#finops #cloudgovernance #cloud #awsreinvent #aws

metadata.title: AWS re:Invent 2025 - Amazon's finops: Cloud cost lessons from a global e-commerce giant (AMZ308)
metadata.author: AWS Events
metadata.shortDescription:
Get an insider's view of FinOps at Amazon from the AWS Cloud Economics team. Drawing from experience supporting thousands of internal teams, we'll share battle-tested strategies for building a cost-aware culture and scaling cloud financial management. Learn how Amazon approaches cost allocation, leverages AWS tools, and drives optimization across its complex enterprise. You'll leave with practical approaches and proven best practices that can be applied to organizations of any size.

Learn more:
More AWS events: https://go.aws/3kss9CP 

Subscribe:
More AWS videos: http://bit.ly/2O3zS75
More AWS events videos: http://bit.ly/316g9t4

ABOUT AWS:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) hosts events, both online and in-person, bringing the cloud computing community together to connect, collaborate, and learn from AWS experts.
 AWS is the world's most comprehensive and broadly adopted cloud platform, offering over 200 fully featured services from data centers globally. Millions of customers—including the fastest-growing startups, largest enterprises, and leading government agencies—are using AWS to lower costs, become more agile, and innovate faster.

#AWSreInvent #AWSreInvent2025 #AWS

The AWS Cost and Usage Report gives, I'm sorry, Cost Explorer puts analysis capabilities directly into our teams' hands, and Organizations lets us implement governance at massive scale, whether we're managing dozens, thousands, tens of thousands of accounts. But data alone is not enough. We learned that lesson the hard way. Real transformation for us happened when we connected business outcomes to our cloud cost. You know, think about it, knowing you spent a hundred thousand dollars on compute or storage, that's important. It's a helpful metric, but understanding that that $100,000 can be attributed to like a million dollars in revenue, that's something that's very actionable. So that's where the AWS Cost Intelligence Dashboards come in for us. They don't just show costs, they show team level value. Everybody's able to see the metrics that matter to them in their language, aligned with their goals. And so, what began as like an internal efficiency mechanism has evolved into features really that can be implemented by anyone today. And automation. Imagine moving from monthly cross reviews to daily optimization actions. We're not talking about just alerts, we're talking about intelligent systems that detect anomalies, recommend optimizations, and even implement improvement automatically. Teams that once spent hours analyzing spreadsheets now focus on strategic decisions while automation handles a lot of the routine. And this isn't just about saving time, it's about operating at scale. I wanna make this concrete. Three years ago, we were where so many AWS customers were or still are today. We were juggling multiple tools. We were wrestling with manual processes and we were really struggling to get clear cost of visibility. Today, we're integrating AWS Services and we're automating insights. Looking ahead to 2026 and into 2027, we're enabling AI-enhanced optimization, predictive actions, and we're automating capacity planning. The part that is the coolest to me is that this evolution is not years away for anybody that's trying to embrace it today, the capabilities are available right now. So, the acceleration path starts with three clear layers. First, laying your data foundation enable the Cost and Usage Report, implement a solid tag strategy, and get comfortable with tools like Cost Explorer and Cost Optimization Hub. This gives you the visibility that you need to move forward confidently. Next, build your integration layer. Deploy tools like Cost Intelligence Dashboards to connect your business metrics and enable automated recommendations. This helps turn data into business intelligence. And finally, activate your optimization layer. Implement efficiency recommendations. Enable controls for transparency and automate response actions. This is where FinOps practices become really scalable. So, remember how we started talking about the Dunning Kruger effect? When Amazon started our FinOps journey, we really thought that our expertise in building custom solutions and tools was our greatest asset, and it gave us a very like false sense of confidence in terms of how successful we were gonna be right out of the gate. What we learned, and what I hope you all take away from this, is that often the fastest path isn't necessarily the obvious one. It requires that we challenge our assumptions. And while Amazon's scale can seem daunting, it still does to me at times, the principles that we've learned work for organizations of any size. Start with AWS Billing and Cost Management Services, build mechanisms that matter to your business units, and automate intelligently. metadata.title: Build a FinOps Agent I The Keys to AWS Optimization | S16 E6
metadata.author: AWS Events
metadata.shortDescription:
Join us as we explore how to build a FinOps agent that automates cloud cost optimization and brings observability practices into your financial operations. We'll walk through the practical steps of creating an AI-powered agent that monitors your AWS spending, identifies optimization opportunities, and provides actionable recommendations to reduce costs while maintaining performance. This hands-on session demonstrates how to leverage AI to bridge the gap between FinOps and observability, enabling your team to proactively manage cloud costs rather than reactively responding to budget overruns. You'll see real console interactions as we build the agent, configure cost anomaly detection, set up automated alerts, and integrate financial metrics with operational observability data to create a comprehensive view of your cloud environment's efficiency.

What we'll cover:

Step-by-step guide to building a FinOps agent from scratch
Integrating cost data with observability metrics
Automating cost anomaly detection and alerting
Practical optimization recommendations powered by AI
Real-world use cases and implementation patterns
Best practices for FinOps automation at scale
Perfect for: FinOps practitioners, cloud architects, DevOps engineers, platform engineers, and anyone responsible for cloud cost management and optimization.

Don't forget to subscribe for more practical AI and cloud optimization content!

#FinOps #CloudCostOptimization #AWS #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #CloudComputing #CostManagement #DevOps #Observability #CloudFinOps #AIAgents #Automation #CloudArchitecture #AWSCost #TechTutorial

Welcome back to CloudExpert Solutions — your favorite YouTube channel for free, structured, exam-ready cloud education! 🚀 In this module of the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner bootcamp series, we take a complete deep dive into Cloud Economics and FinOps — one of the most practical and most misunderstood topics on the Cloud Practitioner exam. Understanding why cloud computing is economically superior to traditional on-premises infrastructure is not just an exam topic — it is the foundational business case that every cloud professional must be able to articulate clearly to stakeholders, managers, and decision makers. This module covers everything from the difference between Capital Expenditure and Operational Expenditure, through economies of scale, real cost savings of moving to the cloud, rightsizing strategies, and licensing options. By the end of this video, you will be able to explain the financial benefits of cloud adoption in plain business language and answer every Cloud Economics exam question with complete confidence.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

✅ Understand what Cloud Economics and FinOps mean in the context of AWS
✅ Clearly differentiate between CapEx and OpEx and why cloud shifts costs from one to the other
✅ Understand Fixed Cost vs Variable Cost and how cloud changes the cost model
✅ Learn how Economies of Scale make AWS cheaper than running your own data center
✅ Identify the real cost savings of moving workloads to the cloud
✅ Apply Rightsizing strategies to eliminate wasted cloud spend
✅ Understand Licensing Strategies — BYOL vs License Included — and when each applies
✅ Tackle a real exam-style question on Cloud Economics

Let's start with the module outline. We
will start with what cloud economics is,
CAPEX versus OPEX, fixed cost versus
variable cost, economics of scale,
right-sizing, licensing strategies, and
we'll review bring your own license,
BYOL, versus included license. And
before concluding the module, we'll
review an exam-style questions and key
takeaways for the certification.
In the official exam guide, these topics
are part of multiple exam domains. We
discuss these across different modules.
However, every concept from this module
will appear on your AWS certification
exam either as a direct question or as a
scenario where you need to identify the
right economic concept. With Cloud
Expert Solutions, you are learning AWS

Every topic, every domain, no guesswork.
Let's get started with cloud economic
concepts.
Before we dive into the concept, let me
tell you exactly how AWS exam test cloud
economics. The exam does not ask you to
calculate cost. It asks you to identify
concepts. You will see a scenario
describing a business situation, and you
need to match to it the right economic
concept. A company stops buying servers
and pays monthly instead. That is CAPEX
to OPEX. A company is running servers at
10% utilization, that is a right-sizing
problem. A company gets lower price
because AWS buys hardware for a millions
of customers, and that is economics of
scale. Six concepts, know the definition
and the scenario for each one. That is
the entire exam requirement for these
topics.
Starting with CapEx versus OpEx. This is
the most fundamental cloud economics
concept for the exam. Capital
expenditure or CapEx, this is the
traditional IT spending model. CapEx is
an upfront investment in physical assets
or money you spent before you get any
value from that asset. Some real-life
examples are buying physical servers,
building or leasing a data center,
purchasing network hardware, installing
cooling and power infrastructure, paying
for software licenses upfront. Now,
let's review the consequences from a
business point of view. Maybe year one,
you spend $2 million on server, and you
enjoy the servers for next 5 years.
And the servers sit in a room or inside
your data centers, and you own them. By
year three, traffic drops and server
will cost money to run. By year five,
servers are outdated and you need to buy
new ones. And the outcome is you carry
the full financial risk.
During the certification, if you see any
terms like upfront cost, physical
servers, own the hardware, on-premises
investment, or a data center build-out,
all are pointing towards CapEx or
capital expenditure. Next is OpEx or
operational expenditure. It is the
ongoing operating cost or money spent to
run the business with no large upfront
commitment. Some real-life examples are
monthly AWS bill you pay for what you
use, maybe SaaS subscription what you
pay monthly and you can cancel anytime,
cloud storage cost that you pay per GB
of storage, compute capacity what you
pay per hour the servers you run. There
is no asset ownership. AWS owns the
hardware. Now, let's review the business
consequences. Maybe at month one you use
10 servers and you pay for 10 servers.
At month two, your traffic spike and you
use 50 servers. You need to pay for 50
servers. But in month three, your
traffic drops and only five servers are
used. You pay for five servers.
The result of that, your cost matches
your actual uses. There is no waste or
zero waste.
Pay as you go, monthly cost, no upfront
payment, variable cost, or only pay for
what you use. These are indication of
opex or operational expenditure.
Next is fixed cost versus variable cost
and this concept is directly linked to
capex and opex. A fixed cost stays the
same regardless of how much you use. If
your data center lease is $50,000 a
month, then it does not matter whether
your servers are running at 10% capacity
or 100% capacity, you pay the same bill
every way. A variable cost changes based
on the actual uses. On AWS, you pay 10
cents per hour for EC2 servers.
When you use one server, you pay $72 a
month. If you use 10 servers, you need
to pay $720 a month. But if your uses
drops to zero server, you are paying
nothing. The business impact of this is
enormous. Think about a retail company,
their website gets 10 times the traffic
in December, maybe due to Christmas,
compared to other months. For December,
they need 10 times the regular capacity,
that means 10 times the servers they
normally use. Under fixed cost model,
they buy enough servers to handle
December peak. Those servers sit 90%
idle for 11 months of the year, and
throughout the year, they pay for
December capacity, which is a waste of
huge sum of money. Under the variable
cost model, they scale up in December
and scale back in January, and they only
pay for what they actually consumed, a
huge savings.
Now, let's review economics of scale.
This is one of the six AWS cloud value
propositions. The concept is simple, the
more you buy, the cheaper each unit
becomes.
AWS buys a scale no individual company
can match, and you get the benefit of
those lower prices. Let's review the
numbers behind that. Your company may
buy 100 servers at $10,000 each. Total
cost is 1 million.
When AWS buys, AWS buys servers for 1
million customers simultaneously.
For the AWS, the individual server cost
could be $1,000.
These deep discounts are because of that
volume. They negotiate prices and
efficiencies that no individual
companies can achieve. AWS builds custom
chips, maybe Graviton, to reduce the
compute cost. They design their own data
centers and buy in quantities that
brings cost per server down to a
fraction of what you would pay.
Then, they pass those savings on to you
through lower pricing. And AWS has
reduced its prices over 100 times since
it's launched in 2006. Every reduction
driven by the growing scale of their
operation.
Now, let's review what cost actually
disappear when a company moves to AWS.
Physical server or hardware, AWS owns
it. Data center facility cost, AWS pays
for the building. Power and cooling, AWS
covers it. Hardware maintenance and
refresh every 3 to 5 years, AWS handles
it continuously. Network hardware
management, AWS owns the network.
Physical security staff for the server
room, no longer needed. And perhaps the
biggest savings of all, over provision
capacity that nobody uses. On AWS, you
pay for exactly what you consume,
nothing more, nothing less.
The IT team impact is also significant.
On-premises engineers spend time to
racking servers, replacing failed
hardware, managing cables, and dealing
with procurement. On AWS, none of these
tasks exist. Your engineering team

metadata.title: Colocation Pricing Explained: Space, Power, Cross-Connects
metadata.author: IPTP Networks
metadata.shortDescription:
Two colocation quotes for the same number of rack units can differ by
thousands a month. The gap is rarely arbitrary - it comes down to six
cost areas.

Full breakdown, with the 10 questions to ask every provider in our article:
https://www.iptp.net/blog/colocation-pricing-breakdown/?utm_source=youtube

WHAT THIS VIDEO COVERS

Colocation pricing is set by six things, and only some of them show up as
line items on the quote:

1. Location and carrier ecosystem - never a line item, yet it decides what you can connect to and at what cost: how many ISPs are in the building, whether an internet exchange is on site, which cloud on-ramps are reachable by cross-connect.

2. Space - measured in rack units. 1U is 44.45 mm and a standard cabinet holds 42U. Top-tier facilities rarely sell less than a full rack.

3. Power - flat allocation versus metered billing, plus the 15-20% that
redundant power adds to the rate. A standard server draws under 0.5 kW, a GPU server 5-15 kW.

4. The facility - PUE of 1.2-1.4 in modern Tier III/IV buildings against
1.8-2.2 in older ones, and why SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS apply to the whole facility rather than to your rack.

5. Connectivity - where quotes diverge most. Every cross-connect carries an installation fee of $500-$1,500 and $100-$300 a month.

6. Installation and on-site support - setup, cabling, and remote hands at $150-$350 per hour with a one-hour minimum.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Same racks, different price
0:12 The six cost areas
0:35 1. Location and carrier ecosystem
0:54 2. Space: rack units and cabinets
1:17 3. Power: flat allocation or metered
1:41 4. The facility: PUE and certifications
2:23 5. Connectivity and cross-connect costs
2:48 6. Installation and on-site support
3:11 The 10 questions to ask every provider

WHO THIS IS FOR
Infrastructure and network engineers, CTOs and procurement teams comparing colocation providers, reading a data center quote, or moving between facilities.

ABOUT IPTP NETWORKS
IPTP Networks provides carrier-neutral colocation from full cabinets to
private cages, with connectivity, remote hands and IT logistics from one provider - across 65+ Tier III/IV locations and 240+ network PoPs,
including our own data centers in Amsterdam, Limassol and Lima.

Colocation services: https://www.iptp.net/datacenter-services/colocation/?utm_source=youtube

Global network map: https://www.iptp.net/network/?utm_source=youtube

More articles: https://www.iptp.net/category/blog/?utm_source=youtube

even if it's the same number of rack units?
The gap is rarely arbitrary.
In most cases, the difference comes down to six cost areas.
These are location and carrier ecosystem.
Required space.
Power capacity.
The facility itself.
Connectivity.
Installation and on-site support. Some costs appear as line items.
Others might be embedded in the rack rates,
or surface later in the contract.
First, location and carrier ecosystem.
It never appears in the rack rate,
yet it determines what you can connect to and at what cost.
That depends on the carrier and network infrastructure available at the
facility, from the number of ISPs and on-site internet exchanges
to the cloud on-ramps available through cross-connects.
Second, space.
It is measured in rack units.
1U is equal to 44.45 mm of vertical space,
and a standard cabinet holds 42U.
Top-tier facilities rarely sell less than a full rack.
1U and partial cabinets typically come
through a reseller or a managed hosting provider,
not the data center itself.
Third, power.
Usually being the largest variable, it can be billed as a flat allocation,
where the customer pays for reserved capacity, or by the meter,
where charges are based on actual consumption.
Redundant power adds roughly 15 to 20% to the cost,
which is always included in the rate.
A standard server draws under half a kilowatt,
while a GPU server draws 5 to 15.
Fourth, the facility itself.
PUE measures how much total power the building
uses to deliver one watt of power to the IT equipment.
Modern Tier III and Tier IV facilities typically run at 1.2 to 1.4,
while older buildings can range from 1.8 to 2.2.
It does not appear as a separate line item. It is reflected in the rate.
Certifications work much the same way.
SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS apply to the facility as a whole,
not to an individual rack.
Both the PUE and the relevant certifications
should be considered when comparing facilities.
Fifth, connectivity, where quotes often diverge the most.
Every connection to another provider or
partner requires its own cross-connect, and each one carries two costs.
An installation fee, typically $500 to $1,500,
followed by a monthly recurring charge of around $100 to $300.
Four cross-connects can therefore mean
$2,000 to $6,000 in upfront cost alone.
Sixth, installation and on-site support.
Setup and cabling are one-time costs that vary by deployment.
Remote hands refers to work performed by the
facility's engineers on behalf of the customer: reboots,
drive swaps, cable checks.
It is typically billed at $150 to $350 an hour,
usually with a one-hour minimum.
That covers all six cost areas.
The article has ten questions for every provider.
Relying on the same ten questions each time will make the
quotes directly comparable.

metadata.title: How to Build a Warehouse GPU Data Center: A Practical Guide
metadata.author: Alec Glover
metadata.shortDescription:
I ran 1,000 GPUs in a DIY warehouse data center for three years, saving millions of dollars compared to traditional tier 3 facilities. But was the trade-off worth it?

Building your own GPU facility can drop your costs from $150/kW to under $50/kW, but the technical debt can be staggering. In this guide, I break down the infrastructure components of a warehouse-scale build—from 3-phase power and BGP networking to "free cooling" and the risks of humidity. I share exactly where we "got away with it" and the critical mistakes that eventually made it difficult for us to scale.

Chapter:

0:00 - The Economics: Saving millions with DIY
1:27 - Why Colocation is so expensive (The 6kW circuit trap)
3:00 - Power Infrastructure: Transformers & 3-Phase power
4:04 - UPS Systems: The key to stability
4:54 - Networking: BGP Routers and Public IP management
7:21 - Redundancy: Understanding N+1 and N+2
9:01 - Cooling & Humidity: Avoiding the "Static Shock"
12:20 - Generators: Moving from "Warehouse" to "Data Center"
15:09 - Fire Suppression: Water vs. Gas

Data is the lifeblood of our digital
lives. But have you ever stopped to
think about where all that info actually
lives? Let's break it down and explore
the four main types of data centers
powering everything from your favorite
apps to the biggest businesses on the
planet. First up, enterprise data
centers. These are like private
fortresses built, owned, and operated by
one company. If you're picturing banks,
healthcare giants, or insurance titans,
you're on the right track. These
organizations have serious security and
uptime needs. So, they want total
control. That means handling everything.

security, all of it. The trade-off, you

with a big price tag and slower growth
if your needs change. Next, let's talk
collocation data centers or coloss.

rent space from a third party, but you
bring your own hardware. Think of it as
leasing an apartment for your servers.
The data center handles the power,
cooling, and physical security, but you
get to control your own rack. It's
flexible, scalable, and perfect for
companies that want control without the
cost of building from the ground up.

are on another level. We're talking
Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, the
cloud giants. These places are massive
with hundreds of thousands of servers

is automated, optimized, and built to
handle mind-blowing amounts of data. If
you use the cloud or any major streaming
service, your data probably lives here.

like the neighborhood coffee shops of
the data world. Small, local, and right
where you need them. Edge centers
process data close to where it's
created, which means less lag and super
fast response times. That's a gamecher
for things like smart cities, connected
cars, or anything running on 5G. Instead
of sending your data across the country,
it stays close, making everything faster
and more reliable. So to sum it up,
enterprise means private and custom.
Colo is shared space, your gear. Hypers
scale, big tech, big scale, and edge,
that's local and built for the future.
Each type is critical to the way we
connect, work, and live. And together,
they're shaping the next chapter of
tech. Want to learn more? Hit subscribe
and join data center resources as we
keep exploring the world of data
centers.

of AI data center that is going to pay
you a thousand dollars a month? Let's
actually talk about the details.
So, picture this, a normal house in a
quiet new neighborhood. And out in the
yard, next to the air conditioner, there
is a plain white box. It looks kind of
boring. It looks like another piece of
HVAC equipment. But inside that box sits
16 Nvidia Blackwell GPUs, four server
grade processors, and three terabytes of
memory. That is more than a quarter of a
million dollars of computing hardware
bolted to the side of someone's home.
And here is the part that makes people
stop scrolling. The homeowner is not
paying for it. The companies behind it
are paying the homeowner by covering
their electricity and internet bills.
This is real. It has a name, and Nvidia
is one of the names attached to it. A
California startup called Span just
announced a partnership with Nvidia and
one of the biggest home builders, Pulte
Group. The plan is to install miniature
AI data centers on the outside of
regular homes and small businesses. And
Span calls these units XFRA nodes. Each
one is a small, liquid cooled, and
quiet. And it mounts outside the house
like an air conditioning condenser. The
hardware is built by Dell and maintained
by Span. And the idea is that instead of
building one giant warehouse size data
center in a single town, you spread the
same computing power across thousands of
homes with little boxes on each one.
Span describes XFRA as a way to turn the
unused electricity capacity sitting
inside ordinary homes and small
businesses into one big distributed
cloud that AI companies can rent. It is
worth slowing down on the hardware
because it is not a toy. Each XFRA node
packs 16 Nvidia RTX 6000 Blackwell GPUs,
four AMD EPYC server processors, and
three terabytes of DDR5 memory. Those
GPU cards alone run somewhere between
nine and ten thousand dollars each.
Those processors run thousands of
dollars each. The memory by itself would
cost almost a hundred thousand dollars.
Add it all up and you have more than two
hundred and fifty thousand dollars of
computing equipment sitting outside a
family home. This is the same class of
chip the big AI companies are buying by
the thousands to train and run the AI
models. This is the kind of hardware
that normally lives behind locked doors
in a guard building. And Span wants to
put it on the wall of a house. Now, when
you think about this, the design is just
important as the chips. The thing is
liquid cooled and fanless on purpose.
The design is just important as the
chips. The whole thing is liquid cooled
and fanless on purpose. That matters
because one of the biggest complaints
about data centers is the constant
noise. And Span wants their box to
basically disappear into the background
of the yard. Span says the unit is about
the size of a HVAC condenser, the same
kind of metal box that millions of homes
already have on the outside. A typical
install does not just drop the box on
the wall, either. It usually comes with
a Span smart electrical panel inside the
house, the outdoor XRF node, and a
backup battery of around 16 kWh, and
sometimes a solar panels on the roof.
So, the homeowner is not just hosting a
computer, they're getting essentially a
small energy system built around it. To
understand why anyone would do this, you
have to understand the problem the AI
industry is facing right now. Every new
AI model needs more computing power, and
computing power needs electricity and
physical space. Companies are trying to
build huge data centers everywhere, but
they keep hitting two walls. The first
wall is the power grid. There is often
not enough spare electricity in one
place to run a massive facility, and
building new power lines and substations
can take years. The second wall is the
public. A lot of communities are pushing
back hard against giant data centers
being built near them, and that pushback
has gotten serious. Now, this part is
bigger than most people realize. Over
the past 2 years, an estimated $64
billion of data center projects in the
United States have been blocked or
delayed because of local opposition. One
tracker counted at least 142 activist
groups across 24 states organizing to
slow or stop these builds. And it's not
a partisan thing. One poll found that
62% of Republicans and 76% of Democrats
and 73% of independents think the cost
of AI data centers outweighs the
benefits. People complain about the
noise that never stops, the water used
for cooling, [music]
the strain on the local grid, the higher
electricity bills, and the falling
property values. Some neighbors living
next to these facilities describe the
constant low hum as shaking them to the
core. The kind of sound that you cannot
escape even with the windows closed.
Others worry about what running these
places does to the air and the water
table around them. Because so many of
these projects need new substations and
transmission lines, the cost of all of
that gets passed on, which means even
people who never wanted the data center
can end up paying more on their own
power bill. So, the AI industry has a
real problem. It needs to build faster
than ever and at the very same time, a
growing number of towns are organizing
specifically to make sure it cannot
build near them. This is where Span's
idea gets interesting. Span is a smart
electrical panel company. Their main
product is a panel that sits in your
home and watches how you use your power.
And they noticed something. The average
American home only uses about 40% of the
electricity capacity it actually has
available. The other 60% just sits there
unused most of the time. And Span's
argument is simple. That spare capacity
is already there, already connected to
the grid, already paid for in terms of
infrastructure. So, instead of waiting
years to build newer power lines for big
data centers, why not tap into the
unused power that millions of homes
already sitting on? The smart panel can
detect the headroom and safely route it
to the box outside without tripping your
breakers or leaving you in the dark.
Now for the question everyone wants
answered. What is in this for you, the
homeowner? And this is where I have to
be a little bit careful because there
are some big numbers floating around
online. The deal that Span has actually
described in public works like this. So,
Span will pay your electricity bill and
your internet bill directly and in
exchange, you pay Span one low flat fee
every month. The example Span has given
is around $150 a month, which is about
half of what the average American pays
for electricity and internet combined.
And in some cases, Span says there may
be no fee at all. So, the realistic
confirmed benefit is not a fact check in
your mailbox, it's a much smaller
utility bill plus a backup battery
[music] and sometimes solar panels
included in the setup. For a new home
buyer, all of that gets built in during
construction, so there's nothing else to
install later. [music]
Now, you may have seen claims online
that hosting one of these boxes could
put around $1,000 a month in your
pocket, and I want to flag that clearly.
That figure is an estimate floating
around social media, and it is not the
deal that Span has officially described.
What Span has actually committed to
publicly is paying your power and
internet and then charging you a low
flat fee, roughly half your normal bill.
Could the payout model change as this
scales up and as homeowners ask for a
bigger cut? Maybe, but right now, treat
the $1,000 number as an unconfirmed
guess and not a promise. The confirmed
win is a smaller bill and a free backup
power, not rent money. It is always
worth separating what a company has
actually signed up to from what people
online are predicting. So, why is this a
big deal beyond a few houses in a test
program? Because if this works, it will
change how AI infrastructure gets built.
Span claims it can deploy 8,000 of these
XFRA units to match the capacity of a
typical 100 MW data center and do it
about six times faster and at five times
lower the cost, somewhere around $3
million per MW. That is a huge claim.
The whole bottleneck in AI right now is
power and speed of buildout. If you can
skip the multi-year fight over a giant
facility and instead drop small boxes
onto homes that already have the spare
power, you potentially unlock a lot of
computing capacity very quickly. And you
dodge the zoning battles and the angry
town hall meetings at the same time. The
AI boom would literally move into the
suburbs, spread across thousands of
ordinary backyards instead of
concentrated into one massive building
that a whole town is trying to block.
Now, not everyone is convinced. A senior
A senior infrastructure analyst at the
Dell Oro Group pointed out some real
problems. AI chips work best when
they're packed together in tightly
connected clusters, not scattered as
single racks miles apart from each
other. Servicing a fleet of boxes spread
across thousands of homes is expensive
and complicated. The hardware changes
fast, so today's box could be outdated
in a couple of years, and the security
of a computer bolted to someone's
outside wall is very different from the
security of a locked, guarded,
professional data center. His take was
that this could work as a complement to
big AI campuses helping with certain
lighter tasks, but like running models
rather than training them, but probably
not as a full replacement for the giant
clusters that do the heavy lifting.
There are also open questions that
nobody has fully answered yet. Who is
liable if the box catches fire or fails
in the middle of the night? What happens
to your home's resale value with a
stranger's quarter of a million dollar
computer attached to it? And would a
future buyer even want that? What
happens if you want to sell the house or
move or decide you don't want it
anymore? And what stops someone from
physically tampering with a machine that
is sitting on the outside of a wall
instead of inside locked inside a
guarded building? These are all the
kinds of questions that sound small when
you're talking about one test home, but
they get a lot more serious when you are
talking about tens of thousands of
houses across the country. So, how real
is this right now? Well, it's still
early and Span says that within a year
it plans to launch a 100 home proof of
concept with Pulte Group and other home
builders, likely a southwestern state
like Nevada or Arizona. The first wave
focuses on brand new homes under
construction because it is easier to
install the smart panel, the box, the
battery, and sometimes [music] solar all
at once during the build. After that,
Span wants to retrofit the boxes onto
existing homes and small commercial
buildings. A longer term goal is
ambitious. [music] Tens of thousands of
nodes across the United States adding up
to more than 1 gigawatt of distributed
computing power by 2027. That is a
massive jump from 100 test homes. So,
the real question is whether the model
holds up once it leaves the lab and
lands on real streets with real people.
Now, here's why this story is worth
saving. The AI race has always felt like
something happening far [music] away in
giant buildings owned by giant
companies. This is the moment it tries
to move onto your street. The pitch to
homeowners sounds friendly. A smaller
utility bill, free backup power, maybe
solar in exchange for hosting a quiet
[music] box outside. But underneath
that, your home becomes a tiny piece of
a global AI grid. It might work
brilliantly spreading computing power
across the country and dodging the
fights over giant data centers that
towns keep blocking. Or it might run
into the messy reality of maintenance,
security, liability, and people simply
not wanting a corporation's computer
attached to their house. Either way, the
grid that powers artificial intelligence
is being rebuilt in real time. And for
the first time, regular houses are a
part of that plan. So, we need to keep
an eye on this 100-home test because if
that works, [music] the box outside your
neighbor's house might not be an air
conditioner for very long.

The example Span has given is around $150 a month, which is about half of what the average American pays for electricity and internet combined. And in some cases, Span says there may be no fee at all. So, the realistic confirmed benefit is not a fact check in your mailbox, it's a much smaller utility bill plus a backup battery [music] and sometimes solar panels included in the setup. For a new home buyer, all of that gets built in during construction, so there's nothing else to install later. [music] Now, you may have seen claims online that hosting one of these boxes could put around $1,000 a month in your pocket, and I want to flag that clearly. That figure is an estimate floating around social media, and it is not the deal that Span has officially described. What Span has actually committed to publicly is paying your power and internet and then charging you a low flat fee, roughly half your normal bill. Could the payout model change as this scales up and as homeowners ask for a bigger cut? Maybe, but right now, treat the $1,000 number as an unconfirmed guess and not a promise. The confirmed win is a smaller bill and a free backup power, not rent money. It is always worth separating what a company has actually signed up to from what people online are predicting. So, why is this a big deal beyond a few houses in a test program? Because if this works, it will change how AI infrastructure gets built. Span claims it can deploy 8,000 of these XFRA units to match the capacity of a typical 100 MW data center and do it about six times faster and at five times lower the cost, somewhere around $3 million per MW. That is a huge claim. The whole bottleneck in AI right now is power and speed of buildout. If you can skip the multi-year fight over a giant facility and instead drop small boxes onto homes that already have the spare power, you potentially unlock a lot of computing capacity very quickly. And you dodge the zoning battles and the angry town hall meetings at the same time. The AI boom would literally move into the suburbs, spread across thousands of ordinary backyards instead of concentrated into one massive building that a whole town is trying to block. Now, not everyone is convinced. A senior A senior infrastructure analyst at the Dell Oro Group pointed out some real problems. AI chips work best when they're packed together in tightly connected clusters, not scattered as single racks miles apart from each other. Servicing a fleet of boxes spread across thousands of homes is expensive and complicated. The hardware changes fast, so today's box could be outdated in a couple of years, and the security of a computer bolted to someone's outside wall is very different from the security of a locked, guarded, professional data center. His take was that this could work as a complement to big AI campuses helping with certain lighter tasks, but like running models rather than training them, but probably not as a full replacement for the giant clusters that do the heavy lifting. There are also open questions that nobody has fully answered yet. Who is liable if the box catches fire or fails in the middle of the night? What happens to your home's resale value with a stranger's quarter of a million dollar computer attached to it? And would a future buyer even want that? What happens if you want to sell the house or move or decide you don't want it anymore? And what stops someone from physically tampering with a machine that is sitting on the outside of a wall instead of inside locked inside a guarded building? These are all the kinds of questions that sound small when you're talking about one test home, but they get a lot more serious when you are talking about tens of thousands of houses across the country. So, how real is this right now? Well, it's still early and Span says that within a year it plans to launch a 100 home proof of concept with Pulte Group and other home builders, likely a southwestern state like Nevada or Arizona. The first wave focuses on brand new homes under construction because it is easier to install the smart panel, the box, the battery, and sometimes [music] solar all at once during the build. After that, Span wants to retrofit the boxes onto existing homes and small commercial buildings. A longer term goal is ambitious. [music] Tens of thousands of nodes across the United States adding up to more than 1 gigawatt of distributed computing power by 2027. That is a massive jump from 100 test homes. So, the real question is whether the model holds up once it leaves the lab and lands on real streets with real people. Now, here's why this story is worth saving. The AI race has always felt like something happening far [music] away in giant buildings owned by giant companies. This is the moment it tries to move onto your street. The pitch to homeowners sounds friendly. A smaller utility bill, free backup power, maybe solar in exchange for hosting a quiet [music] box outside. But underneath that, your home becomes a tiny piece of a global AI grid. It might work brilliantly spreading computing power across the country and dodging the fights over giant data centers that towns keep blocking. Or it might run into the messy reality of maintenance, security, liability, and people simply not wanting a corporation's computer attached to their house. Either way, the grid that powers artificial intelligence is being rebuilt in real time. And for the first time, regular houses are a part of that plan. So, we need to keep an eye on this 100-home test because if that works, [music] the box outside your neighbor's house might not be an air conditioner for very long.

metadata.title: How AI Data Centers Power GPUs | Busways, RPPs & Rack PDUs Explained | Day 18
metadata.author: Cakka | Cybersecurity
metadata.shortDescription:
How does electricity reach the GPUs powering artificial intelligence?

Behind every AI server is a sophisticated electrical distribution system that delivers, protects, and monitors power across the data center.

Welcome to **Day 18 of the AI Data Center Engineering Series** from Cakka | Cybersecurity.

In this episode, we follow the electrical power journey from the UPS and low-voltage distribution infrastructure to the AI servers themselves.

⚡ **What you'll learn:**

- How overhead busways distribute electricity across modern data halls
- What Remote Power Panels (RPPs) do and why branch circuit protection matters
- How intelligent rack PDUs monitor electricity consumption
- Why phase balancing, voltage drop, and electrical losses matter
- How high-density AI racks are changing power distribution engineering
- The role of real-time monitoring and predictive maintenance

As AI infrastructure moves toward increasingly powerful GPU clusters, reliable electrical distribution is becoming essential to data center performance, safety, and scalability.

**Who should watch?**

Data center engineers, IT professionals, cybersecurity specialists, electrical engineers, students, and anyone interested in AI infrastructure.

📺 Follow our AI Data Center Engineering Series for practical explanations of the technology behind modern artificial intelligence.

Subscribe to **Cakka | Cybersecurity** for more cybersecurity, AI infrastructure, and engineering content.

#DataCenter #AIInfrastructure #DataCenterEngineering

segments.text: To process massive language models and
train the next generation of artificial
intelligence, data centers must safely
route megawatts of electricity directly
to compute clusters.
For two decades, enterprise IT hardware
operated comfortably, drawing 5 to 10 kW
per server rack.
Today, a single NVIDIA GB200 NVL72
cluster demands over 120 kW of
continuous power.
If engineers attempt to push that sheer
volume of electricity through
traditional facility power networks, the
infrastructure fails, and the
multi-million dollar processors are
starved of the energy they need to
compute.
At 480 V three-phase, a standard 30 kW
rack draws a manageable 38 amps per
phase. But when you scale a rack up to
120 kW, that current jumps to 152 amps
per phase.
You run into what electrical engineers
call the parallel conductor problem.
It becomes physically impossible to
route the required bundle of thick 350
kcmil copper cables through standard
floor conduits to dozens of adjacent
high-density racks.
Relying on legacy cable bundles at this
scale completely chokes the overhead
trays and blocks the critical airflow
needed for facility cooling.
To move megawatts of electricity
efficiently without creating a physical
bottleneck, engineers abandon copper
cable networks entirely in favor of
high-capacity overhead busways.
Tracing the path of power in a modern
facility starts at the uninterruptible
power supply and the low-voltage
switchgear.
Instead of massive wire bundles, this
schematic illustrates the UPS connecting
directly to the end feed of an overhead
busway system, acting as the primary
high-voltage artery.
The busway distributes this electrical
capacity horizontally, carrying
uninterrupted power across the entire
length of the server row.
Structurally, a busway is a metal
housing containing solid, insulated
copper or aluminum bus bars, completely
replacing flexible cables.
By mounting this rigid transmission line
completely overhead, the raised floor
area remains entirely clear to route the
heavy piping required for direct liquid
cooling systems.
Consolidating massive electrical
capacity into a single clean footprint
enables extreme rack density without the
physical congestion of legacy wiring.
To extract power from this main overhead
line and deliver it to the servers,
engineers use a tap-off box.
Looking at the track design here, you
can see a continuous open channel
running the entire length of the busway
enclosure.
A plug-in tap-off unit mechanically
locks directly into this open channel,
safely pulling branch power downward to
the specific rack below. Every tap-off
unit is equipped with its own integral
overcurrent protection devices,
isolating any localized electrical fault
immediately without affecting the main
bus.
Because the track is continuous,
operators can hot swap these units,
physically relocate loads, or add new
capacity without de-energizing the rest
of the server row.
The data center transitions from a
static construction project into a
dynamic electrical grid, adapting
instantly to changes in hardware
deployment.
While overhead busways handle the heavy
compute, power is also routed to
floor-mounted cabinets, typically
positioned at the end of the aisle, the
remote power panel, or RPP.
The RPP functions as a localized
electrical substation,
designed to receive high-capacity feeder
power and safely split it for lower
density loads.
Looking at the RPP's internal
architecture, power enters through a
main disconnect switch and heavy-duty
200 amp fuses.
That incoming power is then divided
across a 42-circuit distribution board
to feed surrounding equipment, with
flanking current transformers actively
monitoring the output.
Facility power architecture is highly
configurable.
While a busway delivers the raw amperage
required by AI clusters, an RPP feeds
adjacent network gear, storage arrays,
and cooling infrastructure.
This provides the necessary localized
protection and granular circuit division
required for complex, high density
environments.
Following the branch circuit out of the
top off box or the RPP, the electricity
travels down to the back of the
individual AI server rack.
Here, it connects to an intelligent rack
power distribution unit or PDU, the
final delivery mechanism that interfaces
directly with the server power supplies.
These modern PDUs distribute voltage
while simultaneously performing precise
outlet level electrical measurement.
They also contain embedded environmental
sensors, continuously tracking
temperature and humidity exactly where
the critical GPUs draw their intake air.
Switched models of these PDUs even allow
remote operators to instantly power
cycle a locked server without stepping
foot inside the data hall.
The intelligent PDU acts as the final
line of electrical defense, turning
every single server outlet into a
controllable, continuously monitored
node.
When you put this entire electrical
hierarchy under maximum load, the
physics of electricity itself becomes a
critical operational threat.
Delivering 120 kilowatts to a single
rack requires precise phase balancing,
ensuring the electrical load is
distributed equally across all three
phases of the alternating current.
This animated waveform shows what
happens when a rack draws heavily on
just one phase.
The resulting severe imbalance creates
harmonic distortion and dangerous
overheating back at the upstream
facility transformer.
Engineers also have to fight voltage
drop over long copper runs, tightly
managing electrical impedance so the
servers receive stable, usable power.
To bypass AC conversion losses and
impedance issues entirely, the industry
is increasingly shifting toward 800 volt
direct current distribution
architectures.
At AI densities, electricity is a highly
volatile physical force that requires
active real-time management to prevent
cascading hardware failure.
The components managing this force, the
busways, RPPs, and PDUs function
collectively as a matrix of intelligent
network nodes.
They constantly stream exact current,
voltage, and temperature telemetry back
to a centralized data center
infrastructure platform.
This digital twin visualization tracks
the aggregated data, providing operators
with a complete real-time picture of the
facility's thermal and electrical state.
With this level of visibility, software
can identify a degrading connection or
an overloaded branch circuit days before
a physical breaker is forced to trip.
This continuous telemetry transforms the
facility's power infrastructure from a
reactive hazard into a proactively
managed self-reporting system that
guarantees uptime.
From massive overhead busways down to
the precise telemetry of rack PDUs,
this power distribution architecture
forms the unseen foundation of modern AI
infrastructure.
Without this highly engineered and
continuously monitored electrical
hierarchy, the entire global compute
revolution would literally melt down.
Next, in day 19, we transition from
facility-level power distribution into
the internal architecture of the AI rack
itself.
Mastering how to route megawatts to the
cabinet is only the first step.
The true frontier of high-density
engineering lies locked inside the
server chassis.
>> Thanks for watching the Data Center
Knowledge series. I'm Nellia. Don't
forget to like and subscribe, and I'll
see you in the next video.

metadata.title: The Economics of Neoclouds
metadata.author: Caleb Writes Code
metadata.shortDescription:
Thunder Compute: https://www.thundercompute.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=affiliate&utm_campaign=calebwritescode

Neoclouds have been a growing topic ever since the emergence of generative AI in 2022.
We now have neoclouds like CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN, Crusoe, Lambda, and Together AI all contributing towards making compute available as GPU-as-a-service or Graphics Cards as a service.
How do metrics like utilization, availability, contracts, and additional services all play into factor of a commoditized market? Why are banks handing out asset backed loans to neoclouds and data centers when depreciation for these assets are risky?

#neocloud #datacenters #graphicscards #ai #tech

Chapters
00:00 Intro
01:11 Utilization
02:30 Brief History
03:44 AI Training
04:16 Availability
05:04 Scheduling
07:25 Traditional Cloud
08:05 Graphics Cards
09:24 Sponsor: Thunder Compute
10:47 Market
11:24 Contracts
12:27 Neoclouds
13:47 Asset Depreciation

metadata.author: Cloud Computing Insider
metadata.shortDescription:
AI infrastructure is changing fast, and NeoClouds are becoming one of the most important categories in enterprise technology. In this video, I break down what a NeoCloud actually is, how it differs from traditional public cloud providers like AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, and why so many enterprises are paying attention right now. The core idea is simple: NeoClouds are built specifically for AI workloads, especially GPU-heavy training and inference, rather than trying to be all things to all customers.

I also walk through the most important features enterprises should evaluate before choosing a NeoCloud provider, including GPU scale, bare-metal performance, managed Kubernetes, orchestration, compliance readiness, private infrastructure options, and energy-aware design. From there, I compare five of the most talked-about NeoClouds in the market today: CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, Lambda, and Fluidstack.

If you are a CIO, CTO, infrastructure leader, AI engineer, investor, or founder trying to understand where AI cloud is heading, this overview will help you quickly grasp the landscape. The goal is to give you a practical, executive-level framework for evaluating the NeoCloud market and understanding which providers stand out for different enterprise needs.

metadata.title: Ep. 36 GPUaaS Explained: Why CoreWeave and Others Are Fueling the Next Cloud Revolution | AI Insight
metadata.author: SiliconANGLE theCUBE
metadata.shortDescription:
GPU as a Service (GPUaaS) is revolutionizing industries by providing on-demand access to powerful GPUs in the cloud, enabling AI/ML training, VFX rendering, and scientific computing at scale. CoreWeave, a company originally rooted in cryptocurrency mining, has pivoted to lead the GPUaaS market. With exclusive NVIDIA partnerships and tailored enterprise solutions, CoreWeave has rapidly scaled its operations, boasting $1.92 billion in 2024 revenue and preparing for a $35 billion IPO.

While CoreWeave dominates with its innovative offerings, other GPUaaS providers like Datacrunch.io, Lambda Labs, Vast.ai, and Paperspace are reshaping the market through competitive pricing, unique features, and specialized solutions for startups and researchers. This competition is redefining the cloud computing landscape by challenging tech giants like AWS and Google Cloud.

Despite challenges like rising energy costs and market saturation, GPUaaS is anticipated to grow further, fueled by CoreWeave’s IPO and ongoing innovation. This new cloud paradigm democratizes high-performance computing, empowering businesses of all sizes to scale AI applications and other compute-intensive workloads effortlessly.


00:00 - Intro
00:06 - The Evolution and Impact of GPU as a Service: From Introduction to CoreWeave
03:36 - Other GPU as a Service Providers
07:56 - Cloud Market Dynamics: Challenges and Impact
11:25 - Shaping the Future: GPU as a Service and the Path Forward

metadata.title: Stanford Just Destroyed Nvidia’s $30,000 Monopoly (It’s Over)
metadata.author: Extrude Studio
metadata.shortDescription:
Nvidia built a trillion-dollar empire selling $30,000 H100 GPUs. But a brand-new architecture from Stanford University—Next-Concept Modeling (NCM)—just proved that autoregressive next-token prediction was the wrong path all along.

In this deep-dive technical documentary, we break down how Stanford's NCM architecture bypasses the High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) wall, cuts inference compute costs by up to 100x, and enables multi-step recursive reasoning on consumer-grade hardware.

📄 Research Paper Reference:
"Next-Concept Modeling: Scalable Reasoning Beyond Next-Token Prediction" (Stanford AI Lab / Prof. Christopher Ré)

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS:
00:00 - The $30,000 Silicon Wall
00:48 - The Next-Token Bottleneck
01:42 - How Autoregressive LLMs Waste Compute
02:37 - Memory Bandwidth vs Compute Density
03:32 - The HBM Supply Chain Monopoly
04:26 - Stanford's Radical Breakthrough
05:21 - What is Next-Concept Modeling (NCM)?
06:16 - The Physics of High-Bandwidth Memory
07:11 - The Quadratic KV Cache Collapse
08:06 - 1D Token Serialization vs 2D Latent Denoising
09:00 - Tiered Latent Architectural Hierarchy
09:55 - Neural Self-Correction & Path Healing
10:50 - GSM8K & MATH Benchmark Showdown
11:45 - Parallel Trajectory Exploration (MBR)
12:39 - Enterprise GPU Moat ($30k H100 vs $1.6k RTX 4090)
13:34 - The Token Cost Meltdown ($0.65 Inference)
14:29 - Multimodal Synergy: Audio, Video & Code
15:23 - The Open-Source Revolution

segments.text: What if a single research paper from Stanford University just rendered Nvidia's most expensive memory
chips completely unnecessary? For the past three years, the entire artificial intelligence
industry has been obsessed with compute limits. Every tech executive talks about raw flops,
but inside the world's elite AI labs, engineers know the real silent killer. The memory
bandwidth wall. We physically cannot build memory chips fast enough to feed modern frontier
models. Hardware companies try to compensate by stacking exotic high bandwidth memory directly
onto the silicon. And that is why Nvidia can charge upwards of $30,000 for a single
H100 GPU. To understand why this happens, look at how every standard language model actually
generates text. From chat GPT to Claude, models operate on a strict sequential treadmill
called auto regression. When you provide a prompt, the model predicts the single next
most likely token. Then it feeds that token back into the input and repeats the entire
forward pass. To generate a 1,000 word answer, the GPU must execute 1,000 separate passes
in a row. On every single pass, the processor must read hundreds of billions of parameters
across the memory bus. The compute cores sit idle up to 80% of the time, starving for
data, and in long conversations, the temporary key value cache explodes, devouring every
gigabyte of available VRAM. How do you break this bottleneck without spending millions
on more memory chips? A team from Stanford University's Hazy Research Lab, led by Professor
Christopher Ray, just published a radically different architecture. Next concept modeling.
Instead of generating text one token at a time, next concept modeling borrows the core
mathematics of image diffusion. Think about how an image generator creates a picture.
It starts with a course blurry outline of the entire image. Then progressively adds
fine details layer by layer. Next concept modeling applies this exact course to fine hierarchy
to text. An entire response is planned at the highest level, moving through hierarchical
discrete codes down to final words. A 1,000 word answer no longer takes 1,000 serial passes.
It takes just 32 parallel passes, generating everything in parallel creates a profound
challenge. How do you force a neural network to truly learn abstract concepts rather than
memorizing training data? How does a computer even know what a high level concept is? This
brings us to the Stanford team's first technical breakthrough. Nested dropout. During training,
the researchers deliberately and randomly discard the detailed lower layers. Imagine studying
for a final exam. But the last three chapters of your textbook are completely ripped out.
You're forced to deeply understand the core principles, because you cannot rely on memorizing
specific formulas at the back of the book. Nested dropout forces the top layers to
pack maximum semantic meaning into a compact sequence of codes. The model truly understands
the high level idea before choosing a single specific word. However, course to fine generation
has a dangerous vulnerability. Cascading errors. If the top layer hallucinates a flawed concept,
that mistake ripples downward through every subsequent layer, creating an unrecoverable
error death spiral. To solve this, the Stanford researchers engineered conditioning corruption.
During training, they intentionally inject noise and incorrect codes into the intermediate
layers, while keeping the ground truth target intact. It is like teaching someone to ride
a bicycle by gently nudging them off balance. The rider quickly learns how to shift their
weight and recover stability before crashing. Conditioning corruption trains the lower layers
to be exceptionally resilient, forcing the model to actively self-correct bad concepts
before they produce flawed texts. Because next concept modeling runs up to 30 times faster,
it unlocks the most important AI paradigm of 2026, test time compute scaling. You can
directly trade extreme generation speed to purchase deeper reasoning. Instead of taking
the model's first answer, you generate 20 diverse candidate solutions simultaneously
in parallel. Then, a mathematical filter called Minimum Bayes' Risk evaluates all 20 paths
and selects the solution with the highest semantic consensus. Uncomplex logic benchmarks
like Sudoku, a tiny 25 million parameter. Next concept model solved 86 out of 100 hard
puzzles. A standard auto-aggressive model of the exact same size solved only one. That
is an 86 hundred percent improvement in reasoning without adding a single parameter. This brings
us to the billion dollar hardware flip. Next concept modeling shifts the fundamental bottleneck
of artificial intelligence from memory bandwidth to raw parallel compute. Evaluating multi-level
discrete codes requires more arithmetic operations, but it slashes the required memory bandwidth
by over 30 times. Today, the entire AI economy pays exorbitant premiums for enterprise accelerators
simply to rent high bandwidth memory. Next concept modeling flips that equation. It means
we could run frontier class intelligence on consumer silicon, chips like the RTX 4090
5090 that possess massive raw compute but lack exotic HBM. Stanford has cracked open the
door to democratizing frontier AI, proving that today's hardware constraints are not permanent
laws of physics. To understand why Nvidia charges such high prices for enterprise GPUs,
you have to look inside the clean room. High bandwidth memory is not standard memory
soldered to a motherboard. He consists of multiple drum dies stacked vertically like a skyscraper
connected by microscopic through silicon via thinner than a human hair. These memory stacks must
be bonded onto a microscopic silicon inter-poser manufactured by TSMC using advanced packaging
called Kozwa's. The packaging failure rate is notorious. Stacking silicon in three dimensions
concentrates intense heat in microscopic spaces, creating thermal hot spots that require massive
data center cooling. There is a second hidden tax inside the auto-aggressive architecture,
the key value cache. Every time you chat with an AI, the model must remember every single token
you wrote and every token it generated. In standard transformers, the attention mechanism
calculates the relationship between every new token and all previous tokens. This requires
saving attention keys and values into VRAM. As your conversation grows from 1000 to 32,000 tokens,
the KV cache grows quadratically. On massive frontier models, the KV cache alone consumes
dozens of gigabytes of GPU memory, leaving virtually no room for the model weights themselves.
How did Stanford researchers solve this? They looked outside of natural language processing
and turned to computer vision. In 2020, diffusion models revolutionized image generation
by replacing auto-aggressive pixel prediction with iterative denoising. Instead of drawing a picture
one pixel at a time, from top left to bottom right, diffusion creates a course outline of the
entire image simultaneously, then sharpens it in parallel passes. Stanford's hazy research lab
asks a bold question, why can't text generation work the exact same way? Why can't a language model
sketch an entire paragraph at once and refine its meaning across semantic layers to make text
diffusion possible? The Stanford team created a hierarchical discrete code book. Think of this
like a pyramid of understanding. The top layer represents the global theme, is the answer a
technical explanation, a Python script or an essay. The second layer outlines paragraph themes.
The third layer structures individual sentences. The fourth layer defines grammatical clauses.
And only at the very bottom layer does the model select actual vocabulary tokens.
Because the higher layers capture abstract meaning rather than exact words, the model can generate
all codes at a given level simultaneously in a single parallel step. In standard models,
making a mistake on token five poisons the entire answer. If the model who hallucinates early in
the sentence, every subsequent token blindly doubles down on that error. But next concept modeling
behaves like a human writer drafting an essay. During training with conditioning corruption,
researchers deliberately inject noisy distorted concepts into the intermediate layers.
The network learns to inspect its own high level draft, detect logical contradictions,
and repair the concept before selecting a single word. It is genuine algorithmic error correction,
built directly into the generation pipeline. The theoretical mathematics look impressive on paper.
But how does next concept modeling perform on rigorous real-world benchmarks?
The Stanford team evaluated the architecture on complex symbolic reasoning tasks,
like hard Sudoku puzzles. Because each puzzle requires multi-step deductive logic.
Standard auto-regressive models of small sizes almost universally fail, scoring around 1% accuracy,
when tested on the exact same parameter budget, the next concept model achieved an astounding 86% accuracy.
That represents an 86-fold improvement in logical capability, proving that course-defined
planning fundamentally unlocks deeper machine reasoning. The secret behind this reasoning surge is
how next concept modeling uses its speed advantage. Because generating an answer takes 32 passes instead
of 1000, the GPU has massive surplus compute time. Instead of producing one answer and hoping it is correct,
the system generates 20 diverse solution candidates simultaneously in parallel.
Then, a mathematical filter called minimum Bayes risk evaluates the semantic consensus across
all 20 trajectories, picking the solution that minimizes expected loss. You get the benefits of an
ensemble of 20 AI models in less time than a standard model takes to produce a single answer.
This brings us to the profound democratization of artificial intelligence.
Today, running a state-of-the-art frontier model locally is nearly impossible for individual developers.
Even if you own a powerful desktop with an RTX 4090 or RTX 5090, you are locked out by memory capacity
and memory bandwidth. Consumer graphics cards use standard GDDR6X memory, which tops out around one
terabyte per second compared to over three terabytes per second on enterprise H100s.
But next concept modeling reduces memory bus dependency by over 30 times. It transforms
consumer GPUs from memory-starved toys into high throughput inference engines.
If memory bandwidth is no longer the defining bottleneck of AI inference,
the entire economic landscape shifts overnight. Today, hyperscalers like Microsoft, Google,
and Amazon spend billions of dollars competing for allocated allocations of high bandwidth memory chips.
Venture capital flows directly into semiconductor memory foundries.
But if algorithmic innovation can trade cheap arithmetic operations for scarce memory bandwidth,
the premium value of enterprise hardware begins to erode.
Open-source AI developers and universities can suddenly compete with multi-trillion dollar
corporations using standard workstation hardware. For nearly a decade, the artificial intelligence
community treated auto-aggressive token prediction as an immutable law of nature. We accepted that
models must predict text one token at a time, and we paid trillions of dollars in hardware
to support that assumption. But Stanford's next concept modeling proves that the auto-aggressive
paradigm was merely an early engineering compromise by stepping back and teaching neural networks to
plan at the concept level first. We are entering the post-auto-aggressive era, faster,
smarter, and accessible to everyone on earth. Before next concept modeling, the dominant industry
technique for speeding up language models was speculative decoding. In speculative decoding,
a tiny low-power draft model guesses several upcoming tokens, and the giant foundation model
verifies them in one forward pass. While this achieves a modest two to three-time speed-up,
it hits a hard mathematical wall. If the draft model makes even a subtle error,
the big model rejects the tokens and discards the work. Speculative decoding still remains
locked inside the auto-aggressive trap. Next concept modeling achieves a 30-fold speed-up,
because it abandons sequential token, drafting entirely, generating coherent semantic thoughts
across the entire passage. The implications extend far beyond plain text. The modern AI frontier
is multimodal, spanning high-resolution video-generation, robotics control policies,
and real-time audio. Traditional transformers force every modality into sequential token streams,
exploding sequence lengths into tens of thousands of tokens, and crippling memory bandwidth.
Because next concept modeling operates on hierarchical discrete codebooks,
it natively unifies vision, audio, and language. High-level concept vectors can dictate
visual scene structure, physical object interactions, and conversational dialogues simultaneously,
establishing the architectural foundation for next-generation world models.
As the research paper spreads across the machine learning community,
open-source engineers and independent labs are already releasing reproduction benchmarks and
training recipes. With the entire codebook architecture freely available on GitHub and Hugging
face, researchers are beginning to fine-tune concept diffusion on open data sets like fine web.
By eliminating the multi-million dollar barrier of massive H100 clusters,
Stanford has handed the future of frontier AI back to the global research community.
The era of the memory bottleneck is coming to an end, and what comes next will redefine the
boundaries of artificial intelligence.

metadata.title: How do AI Chips Actually Work?  Inside the NVIDIA H100
metadata.author: Screwdriver Science
metadata.shortDescription:
Every time you ask an AI a question, a chip the size of a hardcover book does roughly a trillion multiplications for every single word it writes. So how do AI chips actually work, and why can't the normal processor in your laptop keep up?

In this video we take an AI accelerator, the NVIDIA H100, apart layer by layer and explain it so simply that anyone can follow. You'll see why an AI chip is a stadium of thousands of tiny workers instead of a few genius cores, how tensor cores do the grid maths behind every AI model, why AI chips do "bad" maths on purpose with 4-bit numbers, how stacked HBM memory breaks through the memory wall, and how 80 billion transistor switches fit on one chip. Then we zoom out to the racks, liquid cooling and power that data centres need, and why the company that builds these GPUs became worth trillions.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
1:19 The board
2:39 The brain: thousands of cores
4:13 The maths: tensor cores
6:27 The memory wall
8:04 The switch: the transistor
9:22 Scale: racks and power
10:51 Why the chip maker is worth trillions

If this helped you see what's really inside an AI chip, subscribe for more machines taken apart, layer by layer. Which chip or gadget should we open next? Tell us in the comments.

segments.text: The chip inside your laptop is a genius. It can run your whole computer, juggle a hundred apps,
and never break a sweat. But, ask it to answer one question the way an AI does, and it would crawl.
This chip is honestly kind of dumb. And yet, it can write you an essay in seconds.
Because an AI doesn't think of its whole answer at once. It writes one word at a time.
And for every single word, it runs your question through a mountain of numbers.
For a big model, that's roughly a trillion multiplications per word. And it does it
fast enough that the text flows like someone typing. So, how does a dumb chip beat a genius?
Today, we're taking an AI chip apart layer by layer. By the end,
you'll know why it does bad maths on purpose, why its memory is stacked like a skyscraper,
and why the company that makes most of them became one of the most valuable companies on Earth.
Keep that last one in mind. We'll come back to it. Five parts.
The board, the brain, the maths, the memory, and the switch. Let's start with the board.
This is an AI accelerator module, about the size of a hard cover book.

metadata.title: 46. H100 vs H200 vs Blackwell B200 for LLM Inference
metadata.author: Hitesh C.
metadata.shortDescription:
H100 vs H200 vs Blackwell: NVIDIA's last three data center GPUs each change a different number that matters for inference.
Compare memory size, bandwidth, Tensor Core throughput and NVLink, and learn how to pick one for your workload.

What you'll learn:
- Four numbers to compare: memory, bandwidth, compute, interconnect
- H100 SXM: 80 GB HBM3 and its FP8 throughput
- H200: same compute, 141 GB HBM3e and more bandwidth
- Blackwell B200: 180 GB per GPU, FP4 and fifth-gen NVLink
- Why NVLink matters for tensor parallelism
- Pitfalls: sparse vs dense figures and projections

Chapters:
0:00 Three generations
0:21 Four numbers to compare
0:29 H100 SXM
0:49 H200
1:19 What it means for inference
1:53 Blackwell B200
2:46 Why NVLink matters
2:55 Side by side
3:11 Pitfalls
3:28 Which one fits
3:47 Summary

Sources:
- NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU — https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/
- NVIDIA H200 Tensor Core GPU — https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h200/
- NVIDIA DGX B200 — https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/dgx-b200/

#gpu #llminference #aiinference #nvidia #blackwell

segments.text: Hey There! NVIDIA's last three data center GPUs each changed something different. For inference, knowing which number changed tells you what gets faster.
We'll compare the H100 SXM, the H200 SXM, and the Blackwell B200, using only NVIDIA's published specs.
For each one, look at four numbers. Memory size, memory bandwidth, supported precisions, and NVLink bandwidth between GPUs.
Start with the H100 SXM. It has 80 gigabytes of HBM3 at 3.35 terabytes per second.
Its Tensor Cores run FP8 at 3,958 teraflops and FP16 at 1,979. Those datasheet figures assume sparsity.
Now the H200. It has 141 gigabytes of HBM3e at 4.8 terabytes per second.
Here's the interesting part. Its Tensor Core figures match the H100. FP8 is still 3,958 teraflops, and NVLink is still 900.
So the H200 is the same compute with a bigger, faster memory. NVIDIA describes it as nearly double the capacity, with 1.4 times the bandwidth.
What does that mean for inference? Decode is memory-bound, so its speed ceiling rises with bandwidth, by about 1.4 times.
The extra capacity matters too. More free memory holds a bigger KV cache, which means larger batches fit on one GPU.
NVIDIA's Llama 2 70B result shows both. H200 runs it 1.9 times faster than H100, but with batch 32 against batch 8.
So read that speed-up carefully. Part of it is bandwidth, and part is the larger batch that the extra memory allowed.
Alright, now Blackwell. NVIDIA's DGX B200 system holds eight Blackwell GPUs.
The system lists 1,440 gigabytes of HBM3e in total, with 64 terabytes per second of bandwidth.
Divide by eight, and each GPU gets 180 gigabytes and 8 terabytes per second. That's over twice the H100's bandwidth.
Blackwell also adds FP4 to the Tensor Cores. The system lists 72 petaflops of dense FP4, the same as its sparse FP8 figure.
Half the bits means half the bytes per weight, so FP4 weights cut decode traffic again compared to FP8.
Fifth generation NVLink gives the system 14.4 terabytes per second in total. That's 1.8 per GPU, double Hopper's 900 gigabytes.
Why does NVLink matter? With tensor parallelism, GPUs exchange partial results every layer, so faster links shorten every step.
Now side by side. Memory per GPU grows from 80, to 141, to 180 gigabytes.
Bandwidth grows from 3.35, to 4.8, to 8 terabytes per second. That's the column that sets single-stream decode speed.
A common pitfall is comparing sparse with dense numbers. The Hopper figures assume sparsity, and dense throughput is half of them.
Another is trusting projections. The B200 page marks its performance as projected and subject to change, so benchmark your own model.
So which one fits? If your model already fits on an H100 and runs at small batch, the H200 mostly buys bandwidth.
If the KV cache limits your batch, H200's capacity buys throughput. If you can use FP4, or need faster NVLink, Blackwell is the step.
So, H200 keeps H100's compute and adds memory and bandwidth. Blackwell adds FP4, 8 terabytes per second per GPU, and faster NVLink. See you later!
