metadata.title: IBM Just Proved NVIDIA’s GPUs Are Built Wrong (With a 12nm Chip and 288 Cards)
metadata.author: AI Andrew
metadata.shortDescription:
Look at these two racks. The first one is NVIDIA's Blackwell flagship. 72 GPU’s wired together to work as one giant machine. It pulls around 120 kilowatts. That's so much heat that air can no longer carry it away. The whole rack has to be cooled with liquid. And most data centers on this planet can't even plug it in without rebuilding.

The second rack comes from IBM. 288 small cards. Built on a 12-nanometer process that the leading edge left behind years ago. This rack pulls about 30 kilowatts. It's cooled by ordinary fans. And IBM says it rolls straight into an existing data center. No power upgrades. No liquid cooling. Now before anyone runs to the comments: these two racks don't do the same amount of work. NVIDIA's rack has far more raw compute. That's not the point. The point is this. Per generated token IBM measured that its chip needed 72.7 times less energy than an NVIDIA H100. A 12-nanometer chip against a 4-nanometer one. If that holds up it breaks a belief the entire AI industry is built on. The belief that the newest silicon with the most compute always wins. And it forces a very uncomfortable question. If today's GPU’s aren't spending their energy on math... then where is all that energy going?

Thank you for watching: ⁠IBM Just Proved NVIDIA’s GPUs Are Built Wrong (With a 12nm Chip and 288 Cards)

#IBM #NVIDIA #AIChips
__
Exploring AI isn’t about having all the answers, it’s about asking better questions. As E.Y. put it, “the greatest danger is thinking you’ve already understood it.” This channel is where curiosity meets clarity, with updates, insights, and deep dives that keep you ahead of the noise. The future isn’t waiting, why should you?

multiplication cost about 0.6

Peak compute grew about three times

only about 1.6 times. Compound that over
two decades, and you get tens of
thousands of times more compute against
roughly a hundred times more bandwidth.

August 2026, Micron took the stage at

only three companies on Earth that make

every two years, while

top chip grew about a hundred times.

Because HBM has to sit right next to the

package. How much you can attach is

of that, HBM is one of the most sold-out

2026 was already sold. Micron said the

Micron, it needs about three times more
silicon than ordinary DDR5 memory for

of the unplanned interruptions while
Meta was training Llama 3. This is the
memory wall, and it's the real reason AI
hardware keeps getting hotter. So, what
did the industry do about it? The
obvious thing. If one chip starves for
bandwidth, you connect more of them. You
spread the model across many GPUs so
that each one only has to read a slice
of it. That's the logic behind Nvidia's
Grace Blackwell NVL72.

We stopped making chips more efficient at the actual job and started making racks hotter. To be fair, it works. These racks deliver enormous performance. But every generation turns the memory problem into a power problem, then into a cooling problem, then into a construction problem. So, here's the real question. What if the problem was never how much power we can push into a rack? What if the problem is where the memory sits? A small team in California started asking exactly that more than 20 years ago. And they picked a very unusual teacher, the human brain. On July 16th, 2004, Dharmendra Modha founded the Brain-Inspired Computing effort at IBM Research. Remember that name because what he did in the summer of 2026 is the final twist of this story. His starting point was simple. The brain is still the most energy-efficient processor we know. And a big part of that efficiency comes from one design choice. The brain doesn't keep memory in one place and computation in another. Memory and processing are woven together in the connections between neurons. Our computers do the opposite. Since the 1940s, nearly every processor has kept memory physically separate from the logic that uses it. [music] That design even has a name, the Von Neumann architecture. And the cost of constantly shuttling data between the two is called the Von Neumann bottleneck. It's exactly the wall we just talked about. In 2008, DARPA started funding the work through a program called Synapse. Over the years, the Pentagon put more than $225 million into it through DARPA and the Air Force Research Laboratory. The first big result arrived in 2014, a chip called TrueNorth. 5.4 billion transistors, 4,096 cores, 1 million artificial neurons, and 256 million synapses. IBM compared it to the brain of a bee, and it ran on just 70 mW. IBM even tiled 16 of them into one system with 16 million neurons and 4 billion synapses. TrueNorth landed in the journal Science and even earned a commendation from President Obama. But TrueNorth copied the brain very literally. It computed with spikes the way real neurons do. Meanwhile, the AI world was racing in a different direction, deep learning on GPUs. Then, in 2015, Modha was sitting on a park bench in San Francisco thinking it all through, and he landed on a different idea. Keep the brain's most important trick, memory, right next to compute, but build everything else the way silicon likes it. IBM later described it as brain-inspired computing at the speed of silicon. >> [music] >> For the next 8 years, the team went almost completely quiet. No lectures, no papers. The Pentagon kept watching though. When the project was pitched to the Department of Defense in 2021, the team of Assistant Secretary of Defense Maynard Holliday saw its value right away. IBM later released a photo of Modha handing him a North Pole prototype in person. And then, in October 2023, they published North Pole in Science. North Pole is built on GlobalFoundries 12-nanometer process. 22 billion transistors on about 800 square millimeters. 256 cores arranged in a 16 by 16 grid and 224 megabytes of memory. All of it on the chip. The chip has no external memory at all. No HBM, no DRAM. And it's roughly 4,000 times faster than TrueNorth. On the classic ResNet image recognition benchmark, North Pole delivered 25 times more frames per joule than comparable 12-nanometer GPUs and 14-nanometer CPUs. According to IBM, it also outperformed GPUs built on far more advanced processes, all the way down to 4 nanometers. Nature covered it under a headline calling the chip mind-blowing. Over those two decades, Modha's team built three chips: Golden Gate, TrueNorth, and North Pole. According to Modha, every one of them worked the first time it came back from the fab. Both TrueNorth and North Pole ended up in the Computer History Museum. And Modha later summed up the whole philosophy in four words to the journal PNAS: Architecture trumps Moore's Law. But how can a chip on older technology possibly beat 4-nanometer GPUs? It comes down to three rules that GPUs are built around, and North Pole breaks all three. Rule number one: Memory lives somewhere else. In an Nvidia chip, the model's weights sit in stacks of HBM next to the processor. Close, but still outside the compute die. And for every token, they have to travel in. North Pole flips this. Its 192 megabytes of working memory are spread across all 256 cores. >> [music] >> 3/4 of a megabyte per core sitting right next to the multipliers that need it. When the chip runs a model, all the weights and all the intermediate results stay on the chip. The only things that ever leave are the inputs and the outputs. Inside the chip that memory feeds the compute at about 13 terabytes per second. For comparison, an H100 reads its HBM at 3.35 terabytes per second. Motta describes it like this. At the level of each core, Northpole is memory sitting next to compute. From the outside, the whole chip behaves like an active memory. You write data in and answers come out. And to keep everything moving, the chip is laced with its own >> [music] >> networks. 4,096 wires cross every core in each direction carrying weights and partial results across four dedicated on-chip networks. So, why doesn't Nvidia just do the same? Because on-chip memory is expensive real estate. SRAM is fast, but it's big. According to an analysis from Lux Capital, a single gigabyte of SRAM with its control logic would take around 400 square millimeters of silicon. That's about half the logic area of Nvidia's biggest GPUs, which is why an H100 has only around 50 megabytes of memory on the chip itself. Northpole spends its silicon the other way around. It gives up raw capacity to put memory into every single core. Imagine a library where every reader has to walk to a warehouse across town for every single page. That's decode on today's GPUs. Northpole puts the pages on every desk. Rule number two, you can be fast or you can be efficient, but not both. This one is subtle and this is where things get really interesting. Because GPUs have to stream the weights for every token, the standard trick is batching. You serve many users at the same time so that every expensive read of the weights gets shared across all of them. More users per batch means more tokens per joule, but each user waits longer for every word. Efficiency goes up, speed goes down. IBM measured exactly this tradeoff. An H100 serving a single user produced a token every 2.46 milliseconds. That was its fastest. In energy terms, it worked out to roughly 1.7 joules per token. With 16 users at once, the energy per token dropped about eight times, but the time per token almost doubled. And when IBM tried to buy speed by splitting the model across two or even four H100 cards, the latency didn't improve at all. It stayed between about two and a half and three milliseconds. There is an old saying in computer systems, you can fix a throughput problem with money. Latency is harder, because no amount of money makes the speed of light go faster. Northpole doesn't play this game. Because its weights never move, it can run tiny batches of one or two users per pipeline stage and still stay busy. IBM found that running as many micro batches as there are pipeline stages was enough to keep idle time negligible. In earlier research on GPUs, efficient training pipelines needed about four times as many. The result was under 1 millisecond per token at about 24 millijoules per token. Fast and efficient at the same time. Rule number three, newer silicon always wins. For 50 years, this was the most reliable rule in computing. Shrink the transistor and everything gets better. Northpole is built on 12 nanometers, the H100 on four. The H100 also has almost four times as many transistors, 80 billion against 22. On paper, this shouldn't even be a fight. And yet, in IBM's test, Northpole delivered 15.9 times more throughput per transistor than the H100 at its fastest setting. And 72.7 times more tokens per joule. IBM is also clear about where this advantage comes from. Yes, Northpole uses low precision. It computes natively in eight-bit, four-bit, and even two-bit integers. Each core does 2,048 operations per cycle at eight bits, twice that at four bits, twice again at two bits. But IBM's own paper says the performance comes primarily from the massive on-chip memory bandwidth and only secondarily from the lower precision. That's what architecture trumps Moore's law means in practice. And here is the part that should make Nvidia a little nervous. Northpole got here without the newest process. Back in 2023, IBM pointed out that there are still several generations of manufacturing technology this design could move to. But there is an obvious problem. 224 megabytes. A single H100 carries 80 gigabytes of memory. Language models are measured in gigabytes. So how do you fit one into a chip that small? Moda himself was blunt about it when IBM first unveiled Northpole. We can't run GPT-4 on this. The chip was designed for inference at the edge. The funding came from the US Department of Defense and the first tests were all about computer vision. Spotting objects, classifying images. So the team tried something else. Instead of squeezing a language model into one chip, they cut it into slices. >> [music] >> A transformer model is basically a stack of similar layers. So IBM put each layer on its own card. The weights for that layer stay on that card the whole time. So does its KV cache. That's the model's working memory of the conversation. When a token is generated, only a tiny vector has to >> [music] >> travel from one card to the next. Small enough for an ordinary PCI Express link. No NVLink, no special network. In September 2024, they presented the result at the IEEE High Performance Extreme Computing Conference. 16 Northpole cards in one off-the-shelf server. Just two rack units tall. Running a 3 billion parameter model derived from IBM's Granite Code Model. Compressed to four-bit weights and four-bit activations and then fine-tuned to win back its accuracy. IBM picked this model on purpose. Layer for layer, it has the same shape as Meta's Llama 3 8B and Mistral 7B. The only differences are how many layers it has and what it was trained on. The team first trained it from scratch on a trillion tokens of code in 116 programming languages. Then, they compressed it and retrained it on another 8.5 billion tokens. On a Python coding benchmark, the compressed model on Northpole landed within 1% point of the full precision model running on GPUs. >> [music] >> And remember, this chip was never designed for language models in the first place. The server produced more than 28,000 tokens per second. Every user got a new token in under 1 millisecond. And all 16 cards together drew 672 watts. That's 42 watts per card. Then, IBM lined it up against four Nvidia GPUs that are popular for inference. The A100, the L4, the L40S, and the H100, built on 7, 5, and 4 nanometers. Take the H100 at its fastest. Northpole delivered 72.7 times better energy efficiency than that. And it was still 2.5 times faster. The most efficient setup IBM found on any of the GPUs was an L4 serving 64 users at once. Even against that, Northpole was still 2.2 times more efficient and 46.9 times faster. Here is what caught my attention. >> [music] >> In every single configuration IBM tested, Northpole was both faster and more efficient than all four GPUs. No matter where you put the GPUs on the speed versus efficiency curve, Northpole sat ahead on both axes. But, a single server is a demo. The real question for any data center is what a full rack looks like. And in November 2025, IBM answered it. IBM took 18 of these off-the-shelf servers and stacked them into one standard rack, 288 Northpole cards. The whole thing stands on about 2/3 of a square meter of floor and weighs around 730 kg. Here are the numbers. 115 quadrillion operations per second at 4-bit precision, 230 quadrillion at 2-bit, 3.7 petabytes per second of memory bandwidth across all the chips. >> [music] >> And the power. When IBM measured 184 card deployment, it drew 10 kW. Scale that to a fully loaded rack and you get about 30 kW. IBM designed the rack to stay inside a 40 kW budget with pure air cooling. And its planning math was conservative. The servers themselves plus 50 W per card plus fans plus a 20% safety margin. That landed just under 40 kW. The real measurement came in well below it. Each card is cooled by nothing more than a plain heat sink and the server's fans. IBM even lists what the rack doesn't need. No specialized communication fabric. No custom hardware integration. No liquid cooling. No facility power upgrades. Inside each server, the cards talk over PCI Express. >> [music] >> Between servers, it's ordinary 200 gigabit ethernet. So, what does it run? IBM's open source Granite 3.3 model with 8 billion parameters. The model has 40 layers. Each layer is spread across two cards and the output layer takes four more. That's 84 cards for one copy of the model. So, one rack runs three copies at once. Each copy serves 28 users simultaneously with a new token every 2.8 milliseconds. Fully loaded, the rack generates up to about 30,000 tokens per second. Even the first word comes quickly. With 28 users and 2,000 token contexts, the first token arrives in about 65 milliseconds. A short prompt gets processed in just over 5 milliseconds. The Intel Xeon CPUs inside each server handle the jobs that aren't neural networks at all, like turning your text into tokens. Swap in a smaller 3 billion parameter model and the same rack runs 18 copies at 1 millisecond per token. Go bigger and OpenAI's 20 billion parameters fits on 104 cards in seven servers, still one rack. IBM says a single rack can even hold 170 billion parameter model. And that tells you who this is for. IBM pitches the rack for AI agents inside companies. Lots of small and medium models answering fast. And the accuracy holds. The 8 billion model was compressed to 4-bit weights with 8-bit activations. Then IBM fine-tuned it with its own quantization-aware training method called SILQ. Across 19 benchmarks, the compressed version on NorthPole averaged 56.8. The original full precision model averaged 56.4. The rack is even wired into IBM's WatsonX platform behind the same style of API that developers already use for OpenAI's models. Now, here is where I have to be very careful because this is exactly the comparison people get wrong. 30 kilowatts against 120 looks like a knockout. It isn't. These racks are built for different jobs. Nvidia's NVL72 can do roughly 720 quadrillion dense 4-bit operations per second, [music] about six times more than IBM's rack. Even per watt, Blackwell packs more peak math. It also carries over 13 terabytes of HBM. IBM's rack holds about 64 gigabytes in total, roughly 200 times less memory. But now look at the bandwidth to the place where the weights actually live. Nvidia's rack streams from HBM at around 576 terabytes per second. IBM's rack does 3.7 petabytes per second, more than six times faster. That's the whole story in two numbers. Nvidia built a rack with enormous memory and enormous compute. IBM built a rack with tiny memory and enormous bandwidth to it. One is designed to hold the biggest models on Earth. The other is designed to never wait. So, the claim behind this video isn't 30 versus 120. It's two separate things. First, per token, NorthPole needed 72.7 times less energy than an H100 in IBM's measurements. Second, the rack fits into an existing data center. Same power envelope and same air cooling that facilities already use for air-cooled GPUs. No rebuild. Let me know in the comments, if you ran a data center, would you trade the flexibility of GPUs for that kind of efficiency? I'm genuinely curious where you land. Of course, these are IBM's numbers about IBM's chip. So, is anyone outside IBM seeing the same thing? MIT Lincoln Laboratory is. In its 2025 impact report, the lab describes how it integrated Northpole into its airborne radar testbed, an aircraft packed with multimodal sensors. They flew it over Joint Base Cape Cod. According to the lab, Northpole accurately detected test vehicles on the ground as fast as the data came in. And it did that while consuming significantly less power than other commercial AI processors. The lab says it's now working with the military to validate the technology further. The US Air Force is paying attention, too. In 2024, it signed a three-year contract worth $48.2 million with IBM to deliver Northpole hardware and software for test and demonstration. IBM won it against one other bidder. That work runs until May 2027. IBM has also packed Northpole into a rugged module for edge systems, the kind of places where cooling is tight and conditions are harsh. And then, there is the problem itself. Berkeley's 20 years of data, Micron's warning at Hot Chips, analysts at Omdia. Across the industry, the diagnosis is the same. For inference, memory is the bottleneck. Even the stock market is voting. Cerebras builds a wafer-sized chip around on-chip SRAM. It went public in May 2026 and closed its first trading day worth roughly $95 billion. But proving that memory is the bottleneck isn't the same as proving Northpole is the answer. And this is where reality hits. Here is the catch. Actually, there are several. And IBM's own papers are honest about most of them. The first is capacity. 224 megabytes per chip is the source of Northpole's speed. It's also its biggest limit. A 70 billion parameter model takes a full rack. OpenAI's open weight model with 120 billion parameters needs 440 cards across two racks. Frontier models with trillions of parameters would need an absurd number of cards. IBM's answer to bigger models is simply more racks connected together. That works, but every extra rack adds cost and floor space. And it's not only the weights. The KV cache has to fit on the chips, too. In IBM's rack, each copy of the 8 billion model serves 28 users at a context of about 2,000 tokens. Double the context to about 4,000, and the number of users drops to 14. Now, think about where AI is heading. Agents reading entire codebases. Contexts of hundreds of thousands of tokens. Memory makers say context lengths are growing around 30 times per year. That's precisely the direction where an all-on-chip design hurts the most. IBM's counterargument is that most business tasks don't need giant models. Its paper even opens by quoting a headline from The Economist. "Faith in god-like large language models is waning." IBM argues that small models under 10 billion parameters already come close to frontier models on focused tasks at a fraction of the cost. And look at this. One of the papers IBM sites for that argument comes from Nvidia research. It's title, "Small language models are the future of agentic AI." The second catch. Northpole only does inference. It can't train a model. And here is a detail I love. To get Granite ready for Northpole, IBM fine-tuned the 4-bit version for about 2 weeks on a server with eight Nvidia H100 GPUs. Even the chip built to challenge GPUs needed GPUs to get ready. Third, the benchmarks are IBM's own, and IBM itself flagged some limits. For the GPUs, IBM used their full-rated power at every batch size because there was no way to measure it per setting. IBM admits this may understate how efficient the GPUs really were. The GPUs also ran 4-bit weights with 16-bit activations because, as far as IBM knew, no kernels for 4-bit activations existed for them yet. The software was the 2024 version of vLLM, and the comparison was against Hopper, not Blackwell, not Rubin. Nvidia has moved two generations since, and Nvidia would argue that Blackwell already changed the math. The company claims its NVL72 delivers up to 25 times better energy efficiency than air-cooled H100 systems at the same performance on trillion-parameter models. That's Nvidia's own number for a very different workload, but it shows how fast the target is moving. Fourth, North Pole is still a research prototype. There is no price, no volume production, no customer rollout. IBM's commercial AI accelerator today is a different chip called Spire. 5 nanometers, 32 cores, 25.6 billion transistors on a 75-W card. It became available in IBM Z mainframes and Linux One systems in October 2025 and in power servers that December. Up to 48 of those cards can go into a single IBM mainframe. North Pole isn't that product. Fifth, the ecosystem. GPUs run almost anything: training, inference, simulation, every new model architecture on the day it appears, all on CUDA. North Pole needs every model sliced, quantized, and mapped onto its cards ahead of time. That's serious engineering work for every new model. And IBM itself notes that its appliance has to be used as a whole. So, it shines when it's kept with lots of traffic, not as a small box for occasional requests. So, does this prove GPUs are built wrong? Not on its own, but there is one more piece of evidence, and it comes from the most unlikely place of all, Nvidia itself. On Christmas Eve 2025, Groq announced a non-exclusive licensing deal with Nvidia. CNBC reported the price at around $20 billion. Groq's founder, Jonathan Ross, moved to Nvidia together with president Sunny Madra and other engineers. Ross is one of the people behind Google's original TPUs. Groq itself stayed independent. [music] So, what does Groq build? Chips that keep the models weights in on-chip SRAM. Not as a cache, as the main storage. In other words, the same bet North Pole made. And Groq ran into the same limit, too. Its earlier chips carried around 230 MB each, serving a 70 billion parameter model took hundreds of them. Less than 3 months later at GTC 2026, Jensen Huang showed what Nvidia would do with it, the Groq 3 LPX, a rack with 256 Groq chips and about 128 GB of SRAM in total. It sits right next to a Vera Rubin NVL72, and Nvidia splits the work between them. The Rubin GPUs handle prefill, the heavy math of reading your prompt. The Groq chips handle decode, the token-by-token generation where the memory wall bites hardest. Nvidia claims the pair delivers up to 35 times more throughput per megawatt than Blackwell NVL72 alone on trillion parameter models. And it planned to ship the LPX in the second half of 2026 alongside Vera Rubin. Now, look at the memory split. The Vera Rubin rack carries roughly 20 TB of HBM for capacity. The LPX rack next to it carries 128 GB of SRAM for speed. Capacity in one rack, bandwidth in the other. Sound familiar? Just think about it. The company that built its empire on GPUs looked at decode and decided that GPUs alone aren't enough. So, it added chips that keep the weights in on-chip SRAM right next to the compute. That's North Pole's core thesis with an Nvidia logo on it. There are real differences, of course. [music] The LPX is liquid-cooled and built to pair with Ruben for trillion parameter models. North Pole is air-cooled and aimed at small and medium models. Different bets, same physics. [music] So, here is my verdict on the title. Did IBM prove that Nvidia's GPUs are built wrong for training? No. For prefill? No. When the math is dense and the batches are big, GPUs are still the best machines we have. But decode is different. That's the part of AI that actually talks back to you one token at a time. >> [music] >> And there, the evidence now points in one direction. IBM's measurements, Micron's warning, and Nvidia's own $20 billion answer. When the job is generating tokens, the place where you put the memory matters more than how much compute you print on the box. GPUs weren't built wrong. They were built for a different job, and the job changed. According to the World Economic Forum, inference already accounts for about 80% of AI's environmental footprint. >> [music] >> Training is around 20%, and as AI moves into agents and digital workers, that share is set to keep rising. Which brings us back to the man who started all of this. In July 2026, Dharmendra published a look back at 22 years of brain-inspired computing at IBM. A few weeks later, his blog showed a new title, "Founder and CEO of a stealth startup." The entire post read, "Nothing to see here." What that startup is building hasn't been made public. Whether North Pole's ideas live on inside IBM or outside it or both is one of the most interesting open questions in AI hardware right now. More than 10 years after that park bench in San Francisco, the whole industry is wrestling with the exact problem Moda set out to solve. For 50 years, we got better computers, mostly by shrinking transistors. NorthPole is a reminder that the next big jump might come from somewhere else, not from a smaller transistor, from a smarter place to put the memory. The future of AI hardware won't be one chip. It will be heterogeneous. GPUs for training and pre-fill, memory first chips for decode, and for the first time in a long time, a 12 nanometer chip has earned a seat at that table. If the software, the capacity, and the business model can catch up with the physics. That's a big if. So, here is my question for you. Did Nvidia build GPUs the wrong way, or did AI simply outgrow them? Let me know what you think in the comments. If you found this useful, share it with someone who still believes AI progress is only about more compute, and subscribe to the channel. Thank you for your support.

metadata.title: This New AI Chip Could Make AI Run 30X Faster Than Nvidia GPUs!
metadata.author: Tomorrow Engineered
metadata.shortDescription:
Nvidia dominates the AI chip industry, but a challenger called Cerebras is betting that the future of artificial intelligence doesn't belong to bigger GPU clusters. It belongs to one enormous chip.

Its new CS-4 system uses three wafer-scale processors and claims to generate AI responses up to 30 times faster than Nvidia GPUs. Built around the revolutionary Wafer Scale Engine, Cerebras takes an entirely different approach to AI computing: instead of connecting thousands of smaller chips, it turns almost an entire silicon wafer into a single processor.

But can this unusual design really threaten Nvidia's dominance?

In this video, we explore how Cerebras built its wafer-scale AI chip, why its enormous on-chip memory makes AI inference dramatically faster, and how major deals with OpenAI, Amazon, Meta, and other AI companies are transforming it from a hardware start-up into a serious competitor.

⚡ IN THIS VIDEO, YOU'LL DISCOVER:

🧠 How Cerebras turns an entire silicon wafer into one giant AI processor containing trillions of transistors.

🚀 Why the Cerebras CS-4 claims to generate more than 4,400 tokens per second for a single user.

💾 How its 44GB of on-chip SRAM helps eliminate the memory bottlenecks that slow down conventional GPUs.

⚔️ Cerebras vs Nvidia: how their competing approaches to AI inference compare, and what independent analysis says about the potential 20–40x speed advantage.

🤝 Why OpenAI signed a multibillion-dollar computing agreement with Cerebras and began offering faster AI responses through its hardware.

📈 How Cerebras went from a delayed IPO to one of the biggest technology listings of 2026.

🏭 Why Cerebras is shifting toward operating its own AI data centres and selling computing power as a service.

⚠️ The weaknesses that could hold Cerebras back, including limited memory capacity, expensive infrastructure, customer concentration, and the challenge of scaling its business.

🔍 How Nvidia is responding by bringing Groq's inference technology into its own hardware ecosystem.

THE BIGGER AI CHIP WAR

Cerebras has found a way to make AI models respond much faster, but Nvidia still has enormous advantages in manufacturing scale, software, training, and its CUDA ecosystem. The battle is no longer just about who makes the most powerful chip. It's about who can deliver the fastest AI responses at a price customers are willing to pay.

And both companies depend on advanced chip manufacturing from TSMC. But Huawei has been cut off from those factories. So how is it developing its own seven-nanometre AI chips to challenge Nvidia's H100? Watch the next video to find out.

👍 Subscribe to Tomorrow Engineered for more in-depth breakdowns of AI chips, semiconductor technology, artificial intelligence, and the companies shaping the future of computing.

#Cerebras #Nvidia #AIChips #ArtificialIntelligence #WaferScaleEngine #CerebrasCS4 #AIInference #OpenAI #Semiconductors #GPU #TechNews #TomorrowEngineered

metadata.title: Why Can’t Intel Copy NVIDIA’s Complete AI Stack?
metadata.author: CyberPulse
metadata.shortDescription:
Why can't Intel copy Nvidia's complete AI stack? Explore how Intel missed key opportunities, canceled GPU projects, and eventually agreed to a $5 billion investment from NVIDIA.

In 2005, Intel rejected a $20 billion proposal to acquire NVIDIA. Instead, it placed its bets on internal projects like Project Larrabee and the Xeon Phi supercomputer chips. While NVIDIA built a grassroots developer community around CUDA, Intel repeatedly reset its AI hardware roadmap by acquiring companies like Nirvana and Habana Labs while canceling chips like Falcon Shores.

This breakdown covers the full history of the Intel vs NVIDIA AI rivalry, from early x86 compatibility strategies to the rise of ChatGPT, the launch of Ponte Vecchio and Gaudi 3, and Pat Gelsinger's departure. Learn how NVIDIA built a complete hardware and software stack with NVLink, Mellanox, and CUDA, forcing Intel to use SYCLomatic translation tools and pivot toward inference chips like Crescent Island.

0:00 Opening: Why Intel struggles to copy NVIDIA's stack
1:08 2005: Intel rejects buying NVIDIA for $20 billion
2:02 Project Larrabee: Intel's failed x86 graphics bet
3:59 Xeon Phi vs CUDA: High-end labs vs grassroots
5:32 Acquisitions & missed chance with OpenAI
6:57 Ponte Vecchio & ChatGPT AI surge
8:29 Gaudi 3 stumbles & CEO Pat Gelsinger departs
9:30 Why NVIDIA sells a full stack, not just chips
10:31 Intel's SYCLomatic CUDA translation shortcut
11:04 Revenue gap: Intel Xeon CPUs vs NVIDIA AI GPUs
13:02 NVIDIA invests $5 billion in Intel
13:52 Why x86 history taught Intel the wrong AI lesson
15:06 The future: Inference chips, SambaNova & PyTorch

metadata.title: 4 Broken Laptops Run an 80B AI Model With No GPU (128GB RAM)
metadata.author: Cian Mag
metadata.shortDescription:
Four discarded laptops. Four old 8th-gen Intel processors. Zero dedicated graphics cards. And somehow, these stripped-down mobile machines are running an entire 80-billion-parameter AI model locally on a home desk.

Instead of spending thousands of dollars on an enterprise multi-GPU server, a maker named Joe C-J took four salvaged Lenovo ThinkPad L380 motherboards, removed their screens, keyboards, and batteries, mounted them inside a custom 3D-printed vertical frame, and wired them together over dual 2.5-gigabit Ethernet switches. By pooling 128GB of DDR4 system memory across the network using llama.cpp's distributed RPC backend, this scrap cluster runs Qwen3-Next 80B (A3B MoE) at 4 to 5 tokens per second.

Even more fascinating is what happened when the fourth motherboard was added to the cluster: the entire system actually got slower. In this video, we break down how distributed CPU inference works across salvaged hardware, why Mixture-of-Experts architectures make low-compute clusters possible, and how network latency and synchronization overhead over 2.5GbE can turn an extra node into a severe performance bottleneck—plus the real-world power draw, Linux setup hurdles, and security warnings you need to know before building your own.

🔗 PROJECTS, MODELS & RESEARCH COVERED
• llama.cpp (Official Repository & Distributed RPC Backend): https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
• llama.cpp Distributed RPC Documentation & Security Warnings: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/tree/master/tools/rpc
• Qwen3-Next 80B-A3B Model Weights (Hugging Face): https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct
• PRIMA.cpp (ICLR 2026 Heterogeneous Distributed Inference Research): https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08791
• Original Hardware Build Inspiration: Joe C-J's 4-Node Salvaged Lenovo ThinkPad L380 Cluster (128GB DDR4 / Dual 2.5GbE)

🛠️ CLUSTER ARCHITECTURE SUMMARY
• Compute Nodes: 4x Lenovo ThinkPad L380 Motherboards (8th-Gen Intel Core i5, 32GB DDR4 + NVMe SSD per node)
• Networking: Dual 2.5-Gigabit Ethernet Switches (Dedicated inter-node cluster traffic + general LAN)
• Inference Engine: llama.cpp RPC Server (`rpc-server` across worker nodes + main controller)
• Reported Performance: ~4–5 tokens/sec on Qwen3-Next 80B-A3B (with 3-node outperforming 4-node due to network synchronization overhead)

💬 Subscribe to help Cian Mag reach our first 1,000 subscribers! What old laptops or spare PC parts do you have sitting around your room right now, and would you wire them together into a local AI cluster? Drop your thoughts and hardware specs in the comments below!

#LocalAI #llamacpp #AIHardware #HomeLab #Qwen #OpenSourceAI #DIYTech #MachineLearning

However, there's something you shouldn't confuse here. 3 billion active parameters does not mean the model only needs memory for 3 billion parameters. The other experts still contain weights that may be needed for a later token. The complete model has to remain accessible across the machines. So the architecture makes an enormous model cheaper to compute with while the distributed cluster provides the memory needed to hold it. That combination is what makes this project possible. And the reported result is around four to five tokens per second with the four node configuration. That is not particularly fast. You wouldn't choose this setup over a modern GPU workstation for everyday responsiveness, but it is still a remarkable result when you consider what is generating those tokens. These are old mobile processors with no modern discrete AI graphics card doing the heavy lifting. The model is running locally across salvaged consumer hardware. This is the sort of experiment that makes local AI interesting beyond the usual conversation about buying bigger GPUs. Subscribe to Cyan Mag if you want to follow more projects pushing inexpensive and existing hardware in directions it was never designed for. Now let's get to the part that makes this build even more interesting. The fourth computer. You would expect a four node cluster to outperform a three node cluster. There is another processor, there is another 32 GB of memory, and there is another machine available to contribute computing resources. But adding that fourth motherboard actually made the system slower. The earlier three node configuration performed better than the four node version. The reported explanation is network overhead. And this is a real limitation of distributing AI workloads. A computer inside a cluster doesn't get to work in isolation. It has to communicate with the other machines, exchange the information needed for the next part of the computation, and wait when another part of the workload isn't ready. That communication takes time. In this particular build, the computers use 2.5 gigabit Ethernet. The theoretical maximum data rate of a 2.5 gigabit connection is about 312 megabytes per second before network overhead. That's useful for connecting ordinary computers, but it is still a very different environment from having memory and processors inside one machine. And it doesn't mean the cluster is sending the entire model across the network for every token. The weights are distributed across the machines. What has to travel between them is the data required to coordinate their computations. That transfer adds latency, and every additional machine can introduce more communication and synchronization overhead. A fourth node only helps when the extra compute and memory it contributes are worth more than the additional time spent coordinating the system. Otherwise, you're adding another machine that the rest of the cluster has to wait for. This is why simply collecting more processors doesn't guarantee better AI performance. The software needs to understand the capabilities of each device, assign work intelligently, and minimize the time spent waiting for other machines. Researchers are working on this same problem. One example is prima.cpp, a distributed inference system presented at iClear 2026. It explores running large language models across heterogeneous home hardware, including different CPUs, GPUs, memory capacities, storage devices, and network connections. Its developers focus on deciding how much work each device should handle and overlapping computation with communication and storage operations. The important part is that the problem isn' just how many computers you can connect, it's how intelligently you distribute the work between them. There are still some serious limitations to Joe's build. First, discarded hardware make a project free. You still need working motherboards, memory, storage, network adapters, switches, a suitable power supply, and enough time to configure everything. Then there's electricity. Four older processors, multiple network switches, and the rest of the system all consume power. We don't have a complete verified power measurement or a comparable cost per token benchmark for this project, so we cannot honestly claim that it is cheaper to operate than a modern GPU. The software also isn't something you can configure by simply clicking a button. It requires Linux, networking, distributed inference software, and a fair amount of troubleshooting. And there is a security consideration. The official llama.cpp documentation warns that its RPC implementation is still at proof of concept stage and describes it as fragile and insecure. It specifically warns users not to expose RPC servers to open networks or sensitive environments. So this is an experimental home cluster, not a production-ready AI server. But that doesn't take away from what the project demonstrates. Four discarded laptop motherboards can contribute enough memory and computing resources to run a model that would not fit on any one of them individually. The system doesn't need a single enormous graphics card. It needs it needs software that can distribute the model across separate machines and a network fast enough to keep those machines working together. Is it a practical replacement for an RTX workstation? No. At four to five tokens per second, it has obvious performance limitations. The power consumption and total build cost also need proper measurement. But as a demonstration of what can be done with hardware that might otherwise be thrown away, it's genuinely impressive. And there's a bigger lesson here. Local AI is often presented as a hardware shopping problem. Need a bigger model? Buy more VRAM. Need faster inference? Buy a more expensive GPU. But projects like this show that there is another side to the equation. You can change how the computing work is distributed. That doesn't make old hardware equivalent to a modern graphics card. It doesn't remove networking bottlenecks or make every model run quickly. It does mean that a computer doesn't have to be powerful enough to run an entire model by itself to become useful. Four discarded laptops, 128 GB of physical memory, and an 80 billion parameter model. The fourth computer made the system slower, but the experiment still proved something important. Sometimes the next upgrade isn't another graphics card. It's finding a better way to use the hardware you already have. Thanks for watching, and I'll see you in the next one.

Are you running AI or ML workloads in Kubernetes and tired of manually managing GPU drivers and configurations? What if I told you there’s a way to automate it all?

In this video, I’ll guide you through setting up the NVIDIA GPU Operator in Kubernetes to take the hassle out of GPU management. Whether you’re dealing with powerful GPU nodes or running high-performance AI and ML workloads, the NVIDIA GPU Operator is your all-in-one manager for GPU resources in a Kubernetes cluster.

metadata.title: Stop Wasting GPUs: How to Share Hardware with Ray, MPS, and Time-Slicing
metadata.author: The Code Architect
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you underutilizing your expensive AI compute? In this video, we dive deep into how Ray handles fractional GPU sharing under the hood to maximize your cluster's efficiency. We break down the exact differences between temporal multiplexing (GPU Time-Slicing) and spatial multiplexing (NVIDIA Multi-Process Service / MPS).
Whether you are deploying multiple LLMs with vLLM or building complex microservices, understanding how to partition your hardware is critical. We cover how Ray's logical resource accounting interacts with the NVIDIA GPU Operator in Kubernetes, what happens to idle models in a round-robin queue, and the hidden dangers of Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes due to a lack of VRAM isolation.

What you will learn: 
• How Ray schedules fractional GPUs (e.g., num_gpus=0.25)• The mechanics of NVIDIA GPU Time-Slicing and context-switching• How idle models (M2) yield compute cycles to active models (M1) 
• Why Time-Slicing offers zero memory isolation and how to prevent GPU crashes • How NVIDIA MPS bypasses context-switching for true concurrent parallel execution
 • Security trade-offs, IPC namespaces, and Quality of Service (QoS) limits

segments.text: Imagine powering up a massive roaring
industrial furnace just to heat a single
tiny wire. This exact situation plays
out inside modern data centers. The
computational density of flagship
hardware like the Nvidia H100 has vastly
outpaced the resource requirements of
typical single process machine learning
workloads. Take low batch inference or
serving a small 256 million parameter
language model. These processes require
only a fraction of the available memory
bandwidth and compute cycles.
Yet, the traditional paradigm dictates
that we assign an entire exclusive
device to each process.
When you deploy these lightweight tasks
on a top-tier accelerator, the majority
of the silicon simply sits idle waiting
for work that isn't there.
That underutilization drives massive
infrastructure bloat. To achieve
economic viability at scale, teams must
transition away from monolithic scaling
and adopt heterogeneous GPU sharing. The
new architectural baseline requires
packing an array of smaller distinct
models onto the exact same piece of
physical silicon.
Executing this requires coordination
across three layers of the stack, the
hardware level architecture, driver
level services, and the cluster level
orchestration layer.
If these layers are misaligned, the
operational hazards are immediate.
Multiple models competing for
unpartitioned resources will trigger out
of memory errors and severe resource
contention, ultimately crashing the
node. This happens because the default
behavior of machine learning frameworks
inherently opposes shared resources. By
design, they assume they have the entire
device to themselves. To solve this,
practitioners must stop treating the GPU
as an atomic indivisible unit. We have
to look inside the device and understand
exactly how it schedules work. At the
foundational hardware level, a GPU does
not process a workload as a single
monolithic task. It breaks the work down
and maps it across a massive grid. When
an application needs the GPU, it creates
a CUDA context. This is a strict
software encapsulation of all the
hardware resources necessary for the
program to manage memory and launch
work. The compute engine itself consists
of a hierarchy of streaming
multiprocessors or SMs. The driver
aliases CUDA streams onto hardware work
queues, which then route in-order
commands directly to the specific SM
blocks.
If we submit a lightweight inference
task, it might only require enough
parallel threads to successfully occupy
10% of those available SM blocks. The
remaining 90% of the SM blocks on the
grid are completely idle. They are
powered on but processing nothing. Here
is the hardware limitation. By default,
work originating from different CUDA
contexts cannot execute concurrently on
the same compute engine. Even if you
have the physical capacity to run nine
more models, the isolation of the CUDA
context prevents it. Unless you
introduce driver level mechanisms to
manipulate or bypass these boundaries,
90% of your hardware investment yields
zero return. To reclaim that idle
silicon, Nvidia provides three primary
driver level paradigms designed to force
distinct processes to share the GPU. The
first is time slicing or temporal
multiplexing. This is a purely
software-based approach that interleaves
execution contexts over time. This chart
from Nvidia details the scheduling
breakdown. Looking at the preemptive
scheduling model on the left, we see how
time slicing operates. Processes A, B,
and C receive fixed time intervals. They
swap in and out taking turns with full
access to the GPU. While this increases
user density, it introduces context
switching overhead and latency jitter.
For production machine learning, time
slicing has a critical vulnerability. It
provides absolutely no memory isolation
between the processes. If one model
spikes in its memory demand, it can
trigger an out of memory crash that
takes down every workload sharing the
node.
To solve the latency and overhead
problem, we look to the concurrent
scheduling model on the right side of
the chart. This is the multi-process
service or MPS, which relies on spatial
multiplexing. MPS acts as a control
server that allows multiple client
processes to share a single unified CUDA
context. Because they share a context,
the hardware scheduler can dispatch
their kernels to different SMs
simultaneously, eliminating the context
switching penalty.
The third option is multi-instance GPU
or MIG. Available on Ampere
architectures and newer, MIG is a strict
hardware alternative. Unlike
software-based time slicing or the
shared context of MPS, MIG physically
partitions the GPUs VRAM, caches, and
compute paths. Each instance operates as
a fully isolated separate device.
These three driver mechanisms
successfully partition the silicon, but
they are low-level tools. They lack the
cluster awareness required to map
distributed Python deployments like an
LLM inference pipeline down to those
specific hardware partitions. This is
where the cluster orchestration layer
steps in. Frameworks like Ray Core and
Ray Serve act as the bridge, mapping
Python deployments to the underlying
hardware. Ray's specific architectural
innovation is its decoupling of physical
hardware limits from logical scheduling
requirements. Developers can request
fractional capacity using floating-point
demands. For instance, a worker might
request exactly 0.25 GPUs.
But this logical abstraction creates an
administrative illusion. When an actor
requesting a quarter of a GPU drops down
to the actual execution layer, it can
easily saturate 100% of the physical
hardware. Ray scheduler does not enforce
hardware level limits on compute. It

videos.full_text: Imagine powering up a massive roaring industrial furnace just to heat a single tiny wire. This exact situation plays out inside modern data centers. The computational density of flagship hardware like the Nvidia H100 has vastly outpaced the resource requirements of typical single process machine learning workloads. Take low batch inference or serving a small 256 million parameter language model. These processes require only a fraction of the available memory bandwidth and compute cycles. Yet, the traditional paradigm dictates that we assign an entire exclusive device to each process. When you deploy these lightweight tasks on a top-tier accelerator, the majority of the silicon simply sits idle waiting for work that isn't there. That underutilization drives massive infrastructure bloat. To achieve economic viability at scale, teams must transition away from monolithic scaling and adopt heterogeneous GPU sharing. The new architectural baseline requires packing an array of smaller distinct models onto the exact same piece of physical silicon. Executing this requires coordination across three layers of the stack, the hardware level architecture, driver level services, and the cluster level orchestration layer. If these layers are misaligned, the operational hazards are immediate. Multiple models competing for unpartitioned resources will trigger out of memory errors and severe resource contention, ultimately crashing the node. This happens because the default behavior of machine learning frameworks inherently opposes shared resources. By design, they assume they have the entire device to themselves. To solve this, practitioners must stop treating the GPU as an atomic indivisible unit. We have to look inside the device and understand exactly how it schedules work. At the foundational hardware level, a GPU does not process a workload as a single monolithic task. It breaks the work down and maps it across a massive grid. When an application needs the GPU, it creates a CUDA context. This is a strict software encapsulation of all the hardware resources necessary for the program to manage memory and launch work. The compute engine itself consists of a hierarchy of streaming multiprocessors or SMs. The driver aliases CUDA streams onto hardware work queues, which then route in-order commands directly to the specific SM blocks. If we submit a lightweight inference task, it might only require enough parallel threads to successfully occupy 10% of those available SM blocks. The remaining 90% of the SM blocks on the grid are completely idle. They are powered on but processing nothing. Here is the hardware limitation. By default, work originating from different CUDA contexts cannot execute concurrently on the same compute engine. Even if you have the physical capacity to run nine more models, the isolation of the CUDA context prevents it. Unless you introduce driver level mechanisms to manipulate or bypass these boundaries, 90% of your hardware investment yields zero return. To reclaim that idle silicon, Nvidia provides three primary driver level paradigms designed to force distinct processes to share the GPU. The first is time slicing or temporal multiplexing. This is a purely software-based approach that interleaves execution contexts over time. This chart from Nvidia details the scheduling breakdown. Looking at the preemptive scheduling model on the left, we see how time slicing operates. Processes A, B, and C receive fixed time intervals. They swap in and out taking turns with full access to the GPU. While this increases user density, it introduces context switching overhead and latency jitter. For production machine learning, time slicing has a critical vulnerability. It provides absolutely no memory isolation between the processes. If one model spikes in its memory demand, it can trigger an out of memory crash that takes down every workload sharing the node. To solve the latency and overhead problem, we look to the concurrent scheduling model on the right side of the chart. This is the multi-process service or MPS, which relies on spatial multiplexing. MPS acts as a control server that allows multiple client processes to share a single unified CUDA context. Because they share a context, the hardware scheduler can dispatch their kernels to different SMs simultaneously, eliminating the context switching penalty. The third option is multi-instance GPU or MIG. Available on Ampere architectures and newer, MIG is a strict hardware alternative. Unlike software-based time slicing or the shared context of MPS, MIG physically partitions the GPUs VRAM, caches, and compute paths. Each instance operates as a fully isolated separate device. These three driver mechanisms successfully partition the silicon, but they are low-level tools. They lack the cluster awareness required to map distributed Python deployments like an LLM inference pipeline down to those specific hardware partitions. This is where the cluster orchestration layer steps in. Frameworks like Ray Core and Ray Serve act as the bridge, mapping Python deployments to the underlying hardware. Ray's specific architectural innovation is its decoupling of physical hardware limits from logical scheduling requirements. Developers can request fractional capacity using floating-point demands. For instance, a worker might request exactly 0.25 GPUs. But this logical abstraction creates an administrative illusion. When an actor requesting a quarter of a GPU drops down to the actual execution layer, it can easily saturate 100% of the physical hardware. Ray scheduler does not enforce hardware level limits on compute. It enforces basic isolation solely by setting the CUDA visible devices environment variable, assigning the exact same physical index like device zero to multiple fractional workers. Machine learning frameworks like PyTorch and vLLM respect this variable and initialize on the specified device. But they remain completely oblivious to the fractional intent of the orchestrator. If two fractional workers end up on device zero and each engine attempts to claim the entire VRAM pool to maximize its key-value cache, the node experiences an immediate out of memory failure cascade. A fractional resource request in Ray is useless on its own. It requires explicit alignment to the framework level memory management and the Kubernetes device plugins to enforce actual physical boundaries. Exposing these fractional slices to containerized workers safely requires integrating the Kubernetes stack. The Nvidia GPU operator manages the full life cycle of the hardware through a continuous reconciliation loop. When time slicing or MPS is enabled, the device plugin registers the replicas and advertises them to the kubelet. To the Kubernetes API, these appear as fully available logical nvidia.com/gpu resources. The final required step falls to the practitioner. You must manually tune the framework engines. For example, setting vLLM's GPU memory utilization flag to explicitly watch the fraction specified in Ray's placement group configuration. True infrastructure stability is achieved only when the Python orchestration API, the Kubernetes resource limits, and the low-level framework memory managers are in perfect synchronization. When you successfully orchestrate multiple distinct models onto a shared piece of silicon, the latency payoff for complex pipelines is massive. Ray Serve optimizes pipelines by placing child replicas on the same node as their parents. When sharing a GPU, data moves directly through Ray's shared memory object store. This zero-copy transfer means the payload never leaves the VRAM, bypassing the CPU bottleneck entirely. For infrastructure architects, choosing how to partition that GPU requires a strict evaluation of the workload. Time slicing is ideal for highly heterogeneous bursty workloads where you need to maximize user density and can tolerate a lack of strict isolation. MPS offers spatial multiplexing for concurrent high-throughput inference in trusted environments where memory usage is predictable. If you need absolute multi-tenant hardware isolation, you deploy MIG. Raw compute density has outpaced monolithic scaling. Mastering the interplay between Ray's logical fractionalization and physical hardware sharing unlocks the true economic potential of modern AI accelerators.

metadata.title: SUSE Virtualization NVIDIA MIG vGPU Multi-Tenancy on Kubernetes
metadata.author: SUSE
metadata.shortDescription:
See how SUSE Virtualization delivers hardware-level GPU partitioning using NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology. In this demo, we walk through how Harvester automatically detects MIG-capable GPUs and allocates isolated vGPU instances to individual virtual machines, so multiple AI workloads can share a single physical GPU without compromising performance or isolation.

What you'll see in this demo:

Automatic MIG GPU detection in a Harvester cluster
Deploying VMs with dedicated vGPU instances
Running inference, training, and analytics workloads side by side on a single GPU
Hardware-level isolation in action across a multi-tenant environment
Supported on NVIDIA A100, H100, and H200 GPUs. Generally Available now in SUSE Virtualization 1.7.

metadata.title: One GPU, Several AI Users: MIG vs Time-Slicing Explained
metadata.author: Emmanuel Corels Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
One GPU can serve several AI jobs, but how they share it affects both latency and unused capacity. Time-slicing lets a busy job use spare compute; NVIDIA MIG assigns separate memory and compute regions to limit interference, even when one region sits idle.

For engineers running concurrent AI workloads, this video explains how to check MIG support and compare each job’s latency and throughput as demand rises. It also covers why MIG may not win every measure—and why GPU resource boundaries are not application or network access controls. Which matters more for your workload: flexible capacity or steadier boundaries?

Lessons Learned Orchestrating Multi-Tenant GPUs on OpenShift AI with NVIDIA KAI (G/H200) - Luca Berton, Dell Technologies

How do you run shared, production-grade GPUs for AI/ML safely and efficiently? This experience report distills hard-won lessons from implementing multi-tenant GPU orchestration on OpenShift AI using NVIDIA KAI on G/H200 hardware, fronted by Traefik and backed by Dell Technologies platforms. We’ll cover tenant isolation patterns (namespaces, quotas, priority classes), scheduling on heterogeneous nodes, MIG vs. full-GPU trade-offs, throughput vs. latency tuning, driver/firmware pitfalls, upgrade/rollback strategies, and day-2 ops (observability, autoscaling, chargeback). Expect practical manifests and guardrails you can apply immediately.

metadata.title: Fixing GPU Time-Slicing on Kubernetes: Dynamic, Memory-Safe Sharing for AI... Julien Semaan, Kubex
metadata.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
metadata.shortDescription:
Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

Fixing GPU Time-Slicing on Kubernetes: Dynamic, Memory-Safe Sharing for AI Inference - Julien Semaan, Kubex

Time-slicing is often the only viable way to share GPUs on commodity hardware or in cloud environments where MIG and MPS are unavailable. In practice, Kubernetes time-slicing relies on static configuration and does not constrain GPU memory, leading to noisy neighbors, unpredictable performance, and OOM failures in inference workloads.

This session shows how to close that gap by combining memory-aware controls with smarter pod placement. Using KAI for GPU-aware scheduling and HAMi for per-workload memory limit enforcement, we demonstrate how to prevent memory overcommit, stabilize performance, and safely share GPUs across inference workloads. Under the hood, Kyverno mutates pod specs to inject KAI and HAMi configuration on inference pods that should share GPUs.

This talk shows how to get safe, OOM-free GPU sharing on standard Kubernetes clusters without hardware upgrades. Just dynamic scheduling and enforced memory limits that work with the GPUs you already have.

metadata.title: Multi-Tenancy Fundamentals: Why GPU Sharing is Harder in Kubernetes
metadata.author: vCluster
metadata.shortDescription:
Ebook and Series Links:

eBook: https://www.vcluster.com/ebook/gpu-enabled-platforms-on-kubernetes-book
Webinar Series: https://www.vcluster.com/gpu-enabled-platforms-on-kubernetes

This session exposes the fundamental mismatch between Kubernetes' resource model and GPU hardware constraints. You'll discover why the absence of GPU memory cgroups, non-preemptible GPU kernels, and persistent memory states create not just performance bottlenecks but serious security vulnerabilities.

metadata.title: GPU Resource Slice Explained with Pizza Analogy | NVIDIA MIG & GPU Slicing Made Easy
metadata.author: Jitesh Powankar
metadata.shortDescription:
Running AI workloads on Kubernetes but not fully utilizing your GPUs?

In this video, I explain GPU Resource Slicing using a simple pizza analogy so anyone can understand it.

You'll learn:

✅ What GPU Resource Slicing is
✅ Why allocating a full GPU wastes resources
✅ How multiple AI applications can share one GPU
✅ How Kubernetes schedules GPU slices
✅ Why GPU slicing reduces infrastructure costs

Whether you're a DevOps Engineer, Kubernetes Administrator, Platform Engineer, MLOps Engineer, or AI Engineer, this concept is essential for running AI workloads efficiently.

📌 Follow for more AI + Kubernetes + DevOps concepts explained in simple language.

#Kubernetes #AI #DevOps #GPU #NVIDIA #MLOps

but 10 hungry people all want to eat it

metadata.title: Vendor-Neutral GPU Observability for Kubernetes - Reza Jelveh, Dynamia.ai
metadata.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
metadata.shortDescription:
Don't miss out! Join us at our next KubeCon + CloudNativeCon event in Salt Lake City, United States (Nov 9–12, 2026). Connect with our current graduated, incubating, and sandbox projects as the community gathers to further the education and advancement of cloud native computing. Learn more at https://kubecon.io

Vendor-Neutral GPU Observability for Kubernetes - Reza Jelveh, dynamia.ai

GPU observability in Kubernetes is fragmented. Each vendor ships their own metrics stack: NVIDIA DCGM, AMD ROCm SMI. Platform teams running heterogeneous clusters stitch together three different dashboards to answer one question: "Are my GPUs being used efficiently?"

HAMi (CNCF Incubation) sits at the scheduling layer and sees every GPU operation. That single integration point gives you centralized observability across NVIDIA, AMD, Ascend, and any accelerator with a device plugin. Rather than scraping vendor-specific endpoints, HAMi instruments the scheduling path itself and reports utilization, memory pressure, and allocation efficiency per workload regardless of the underlying hardware.

This talk covers:
- Why GPU observability is harder than CPU observability (CUDA context model, MIG partitioning, device-plugin opacity)
- How HAMi's scheduling-layer instrumentation provides vendor-neutral metrics without per-vendor exporters

metadata.shortDescription:
Don't miss out! Join us at our next Flagship Conference: KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe in London from April 1 - 4, 2025. Connect with our current graduated, incubating, and sandbox projects as the community gathers to further the education and advancement of cloud native computing. Learn more at https://kubecon.io

Which GPU Sharing Strategy Is Right for You? A Comprehensive Benchmark Study Using DRA - Kevin Klues & Yuan Chen, NVIDIA

Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) is one of the most anticipated features to ever make its way into Kubernetes. It promises to revolutionize the way hardware devices are consumed and shared between workloads. In particular, DRA unlocks the ability to manage heterogeneous GPUs in a unified and configurable manner without the need for awkward solutions shoehorned on top of the existing device plugin API. In this talk, we use DRA to benchmark various GPU sharing strategies including Multi-Instance GPUs, Multi-Process Service (MPS), and CUDA Time-Slicing. As part of this, we provide guidance on the class of applications that can benefit from each strategy as well as how to combine different strategies in order to achieve optimal performance. The talk concludes with a discussion of potential challenges, future enhancements, and a live demo showcasing the use of each GPU sharing strategy with real-world applications.

metadata.title: GPUs in Kubernetes for AI Workloads
metadata.author: DevOps & AI Toolkit
metadata.shortDescription:
Today we dive into running AI models on Kubernetes with GPU support. Learn how to manage GPUs in Kubernetes clusters, create GPU nodes, and optimize resource usage without breaking the bank. We'll walk you through setting up a Google Cloud Kubernetes cluster (the same logic should apply to other Cloud providers), deploying AI models like Ollama's Llama2, and handling GPU partitioning. Watch now to master GPU-based AI workloads in Kubernetes!

metadata.title: AI for FinOps on Azure: Smarter Cloud Operations with Agentic AI
metadata.author: FinOps Foundation
metadata.shortDescription:
Vikram Desai and Hande Adiguzel of Microsoft show how FinOps is shifting left into the developer workflow on Azure, powered by agentic AI at FinOps X 2026. Through a live GitHub Copilot CLI demo, they walk four scenarios end to end: embedding cost estimation into the build with approved SKUs and negotiated pricing, proactive budget setup with tiered forecasted thresholds, a cost spike investigation that crosses Kubernetes cost, Azure Resource Graph, GPU metrics, and the Git commit behind it, and an optimization that lands as a pull request. 

Hande then unpacks the architecture: a remote Azure Resource Manager MCP server, skills as markdown workflows, the principle of treating the agent's context window as a budget, stateless design that inherits your existing access, and reporting at scale by exporting FOCUS data into Microsoft Fabric.

Chapters:
00:00 FinOps shifting left and innovation at the speed of AI
03:48 What Microsoft is building: MCP servers, skills, and Microsoft Fabric
05:31 Live demo: cost estimation embedded in the developer workflow
09:48 Proactive budgets, cost spike investigation, and optimization to a PR
22:02 Architecture: the Azure Resource Manager MCP server and skills
29:06 Azure Copilot, Copilot workspaces, and reporting at scale with Fabric

Watch the Day 1 Keynote and Tokenomics Foundation announcement: https://www.youtube.com/live/W4g8xvduIbs
Watch the Day 2 Keynote: https://www.youtube.com/live/vyQTW0PLw7A
Learn more about Token Economics: https://tokeneconomics.com  

https://x.finops.org
https://join.finops.org

#FinOps #FinOpsX #Microsoft #Azure #AgenticAI #MCP #CloudCost #CostOptimization #GitHubCopilot #MicrosoftFabric #FOCUS #ShiftLeft

Sangoma’s SIP trunking portfolio caters from SMBs and large enterprises needing easy to configure trunks to carriers requiring wholesale pricing to offer SIP traffic to their own customers. FAXStation provides a true analog fax experience without the high cost of an extra PSTN line. 

In the second session of our 'Ring in the New Year' Webinar Series, we go over our 3 services in detail - SIPStation, FAXStation, and Sangoma Wholesale Carrier Services - discussing their features and pricing options, and how you can leverage them to your business's benefit.

metadata.title: SIP Trunking 101 - The VoIP Report
metadata.author: The VoIP Report
metadata.shortDescription:
Created by The VoIP Report http://thevoipreport.com

What is SIP trunking? Why would your business need it? What does SIP Trunking have to do with VoIP?

This video was created from one of The VoIP Report's original infographics.  View the infographic PDF on The VoIP Report: http://thevoipreport.com/sip-trunking-101-infographic/

Transcript:

The VoIP Report presents...

SIP Trunking 101

SIP Trunking is a telecommunications circuit that uses IP technology to replace traditional PSTN cabling. The use of SIP trunking is increasing while the use of T-1 lines is on the decline.  SIP trunking provides access to VoIP services, and offers businesses a wide range of benefits by simplifying infrastructure requirements and reducing costs.
SIP Trunking connects your PBX or IP-PBX to an Internet Telephony Service Provider so that you can utilize VoIP. 
SIP trunking can also carry data traffic, eliminating the need for separate circuits for voice and data.
Service providers can offer different categories of SIP trunking to suit your calling patterns. 
Do you make a lot of long distance calls? Then choose a service provider that operates a Tier 1 network, which gives you access to most regions of the world, at competitive rates.
With Toll-Free SIP, service providers route inbound calls from your customers over their Tier 1 networks at no cost to the caller.
Bring down the costs with SIP Trunking:
• By carrying voice and data on a single circuit, you reduce infrastructure costs.
• If you have multiple office locations, you can eliminate duplicate PBXs with a centralized PBX, which also saves associated space and power costs on duplicate infrastructure.

SIP trunking can simplify your capacity requirements, as well as your infrastructure needs. 
Share SIP capacity across the enterprise by using Pooled Concurrent Call Paths. 
And remember: One circuit means one bill and one service provider, simplifying costs and administrative headaches.

SIP trunking gives you the opportunity to deliver all the benefits of VoIP to your employees, such as: Presence, Collaboration, and improved Customer service 
If you’re currently operating a legacy system, SIP trunking can integrate with your existing PBX.  Enjoy the benefits of VoIP service until you’re ready to install an IP-PBX.

To Learn More about SIP Trunking, visit thevoipreport.com

metadata.title: Twilio A2P 10DLC Rejected? Fix These Error Codes
metadata.author: TwilioDevs
metadata.shortDescription:
Twilio A2P 10DLC campaign rejected with error 30909, 30908 or 30903? Check your opt-in flow, privacy policy and brand type before resubmitting.

This walkthrough explains three registration rejection paths and the specific opt-in codes 30543, 30925 and 30545. The privacy-policy example also addresses the related disclosure issue in 30932.

FIND YOUR ERROR
30909 - Message Flow / Call to Action incomplete or unverified. Explain every way customers consent to receive your texts.
30543 - Live opt-in link not provided. For a public website opt-in flow, submit the direct live page URL. A screenshot does not replace that required live link; publicly hosted screenshots can support eligible nonpublic flows.
30925 - Active SMS consent required. Use a separate, optional checkbox that starts unchecked, not a box bundled with general terms.
30545 - Message frequency missing. Add an accurate frequency disclosure, such as "Message frequency varies," before opt-in.
30908 - Compliant privacy policy required. Check the public policy URL, messaging disclosures and non-sharing language.
30932 - Mobile opt-in data-sharing disclosure issue. State that mobile information and messaging consent are not shared for third-party or affiliate marketing, and remove contradictory language.
30903 - Incorrect Sole Proprietor Brand registration. A business with an EIN, Canadian Business Number or other business tax ID needs a Standard or Low-Volume Standard Brand instead.

PRIVACY-POLICY TEXT SHOWN IN THE VIDEO
No mobile information will be shared with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes. All the above categories exclude text messaging originator opt-in data and consent; this information will not be shared with any third parties.

Use this example only if it reflects your actual data practices. Clear equivalent wording may also satisfy the requirement; this excerpt is not a complete privacy policy or a guarantee of approval. Keep the policy public, easy to find and consistent with the rest of your website.

SOLE PROPRIETOR OR STANDARD?
Twilio's Sole Proprietor registration is for eligible businesses in the US or Canada without a business tax ID. This is a registration category, not a statement about your legal business structure. When switching to Standard or Low-Volume Standard, create the appropriate new Customer Profile, Brand and Campaign.

For a US EIN registration, match the exact legal business name on the IRS CP 575 or 147C letter, rather than copying a DBA or relying on a W-9.

CHAPTERS
00:00 A2P 10DLC campaign rejected? Start here
00:15 Error 30909: Opt-in and message flow
00:27 Error 30543: Provide the live opt-in URL
00:42 Error 30925: Unchecked, separate SMS consent
00:57 Why active marketing consent matters
01:18 Error 30545: Disclose message frequency
01:40 Errors 30908 / 30932: Privacy policy
02:25 Broken links and conflicting policy language
02:58 Error 30903: Sole Proprietor eligibility
03:31 EIN legal-name match: CP 575 / 147C
03:55 AI prompt to prepare your registration

OFFICIAL TWILIO ERROR GUIDES
30909: https://www.twilio.com/docs/api/errors/30909
30543: https://www.twilio.com/docs/api/errors/30543
30925: https://www.twilio.com/docs/api/errors/30925
30545: https://www.twilio.com/docs/api/errors/30545
30908: https://www.twilio.com/docs/api/errors/30908
30932: https://www.twilio.com/docs/api/errors/30932
30903: https://www.twilio.com/docs/api/errors/30903

💻 Sign up for a Twilio account here: https://twil.io/trytwilio-yt
👉 Subscribe for more Twilio updates: https://twil.io/sub-twiliodevs

AI registration-preparation prompt mentioned in the video:
https://help.twilio.com/articles/55998855215003

Use it to draft accurate answers, not invent consent or messaging practices. You still need to verify your account details and public links yourself.

Correct every rejection reason before resubmitting. These checks do not guarantee approval. Registration guidance, not legal advice.

If you've ever asked "What is A2P 10DLC?" this is the video for you. In it we unpack the new US A2P 10DLC regulations that are changing the way SMS messages are sent and received in the United States. Consider this your essential guide to understanding and adapting to these changes. Here's what we cover:

📚 Understanding A2P 10DLC: Learn why these regulations are crucial in reducing SMS-based spam and phishing attacks. 

📲 Straightforward Compliance: Learn how A2P 10DLC is making sure every message sent is verified, creating a safer and more reliable messaging environment. You'll learn the ins and outs of A2P 10DLC registration with Twilio.

🚀 Enhancing Message Delivery: Discover the improved capabilities of the new A2P 10DLC format, which allows for timely message delivery, especially for large message campaigns.

✅ Best Practices: We share our tips and best practices for navigating A2P 10DLC for different types of campaigns. We will help you on your A2P 10DLC registration journey.

💬 Transparency and User Choice: Understand the importance of offering clear information and options for opting into and out of messages, with a focus on transparency and user choice.

📣 Don't forget to like, share, and subscribe to stay updated with the latest happenings in the Twilio ecosystem. If you have any questions or need more information, we're here to help.

metadata.shortDescription:
Understand the 10DLC campaign registration process and help SMB customers prepare for review.

This recorded webinar explains campaign registration, The Campaign Registry (TCR) review, and how to discuss 10DLC with customers.

Topics covered

- Key elements of a 10DLC campaign
- What TCR looks for during review
- How to explain 10DLC to customers
- How to approach SMB customer registration
- Where automation can support the registration process

#10DLC #BusinessSMS #MSP

***********
RINGLOGIX
Giving your customers to a UCaaS provider for commissions is a dead-end business. Take back your business with RingLogix. RingLogix offers RingOS, the Growth Platform for MSPs. When partnering with RingLogix, MSPs create their own branded UCaaS offering fast, with the ability to own the entire customer relationship without all the headaches. Grow your MSP on your terms with RingLogix.

Learn More - https://www.ringlogix.com/

metadata.title: How to Register Brands & Campaigns | Commio | 10DLC Text Messaging
metadata.author: Commio
metadata.shortDescription:
If you're considering sending a 10DLC texting campaign, you must register your brand before doing anything else. Commio - http://www.commio.com - makes it easy.

Note: The webinar refers to a number pooling cap of 49 around T-Mobile brand registration; it should have said campaign registration.

Why is this important? Your brand must be both registered and verified before you can send a campaign. To be verified, the details you submit with your brand must align with your EIN, including the legal registered business name and address. If you don’t have an EIN, there are “special cases” that might take a bit more work, as well as a sole proprietor option. 

Both brands and campaigns can be registered via The Campaign Registry - http://campaignregistry.org - or directly in your teli portal where our Support team is happy to help you with the process. thinQ customers can also use the teli portal by requesting access. 

Once your brand is verified, you will know your maximum campaign size; if you disagree with your allotment, you can consider requesting to be vetted but this takes additional time.
