metadata.title: 10DLC Explained: What Is 10DLC? A Plain-English Guide for MSPs
metadata.author: BuzzerBeep
metadata.shortDescription:
What is 10DLC? This plain-English 10DLC guide for MSPs explains what a 10-digit long code is, why US carriers expect A2P business texts to be registered, what gets registered (the brand and the campaign), and how to handle SMS consent and opt-in records before you text a client's users.

Read the full guide and readiness checklist: https://buzzerbeep.com/blog/what-is-10dlc/
Want a walkthrough? Get in touch: https://buzzerbeep.com/#contact

Chapters:
0:00 What is 10DLC?
0:13 10DLC means "10-digit long code"
0:21 A2P: texts sent by software
0:38 Verified and consensual
0:53 Why carriers created 10DLC
1:06 Why a verified sender helps MSPs
1:20 What gets registered: brand and campaign
1:41 You can't register directly
1:51 Registered texts get filtered less
2:08 The MSP twist: whose consent is it?
2:19 Opt-in is not transferable
2:32 Keep a record of every opt-in
2:41 10DLC readiness checklist
3:07 How BuzzerBeep handles consent
3:19 Text affected users right from the ticket
3:31 Where this leaves you
3:42 Read the full guide

Sources cited:
- Twilio, A2P 10DLC documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/compliance/a2p-10dlc
- The Campaign Registry: https://www.campaignregistry.com/
- CTIA, Messaging Principles and Best Practices: https://api.ctia.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/230523-CTIA-Messaging-Principles-and-Best-Practices-FINAL.pdf

BuzzerBeep lets MSPs text the affected users at a client right from a ticket in Autotask or ConnectWise Manage, with managed consent, quiet hours, per-recipient delivery status and a person approving every send. Learn more at https://buzzerbeep.com

metadata.title: STIR/SHAKEN and the Death of the Small VoIP Carrier
metadata.author: Crosstalk Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
STIR/SHAKEN is a new set of telecom industry regulations designed to prevent robocalling - anything to help prevent these unwanted SPAM calls is a welcome change in the industry.  However, these new rules also make it incredibly more challenging for smaller SIP providers and resellers to become compliant...to the point where we had to shut down our own SIP business for good.

In this video, I explain STIR/SHAKEN, discuss what is needed to become compliant, and interview VoIP industry expert Tony Lewis, CEO of ClearlyIP about this huge change in the telecommunications industry.

metadata.title: Everything You Need to Know About STIR SHAKEN Compliance
metadata.author: Sangoma
metadata.shortDescription:
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
For the latest on STIR/SHAKEN, please complement the information in this video with the information found at: https://sangoma.com/blog/the-new-fcc-stir-shaken-rules-and-why-they-matter-for-your-business-in-2025/
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Service providers must be compliant with STIR/SHAKEN by June 30, 2021.

If your organization relies on VoIP communications, it’s time to start looking at how fraudulent robocalls have affected your business and customers.

Over 4 billion robocalls occurred per month in the U.S. during 2018, and the FCC is moving forward with regulations under the TRACED Act to prevent caller ID spoofing and other fraudulent activity.

Join Sangoma specialist Tim Linn as he covers:
• Caller ID spoofing in the U.S.
• An overview of the STIR/SHAKEN process
• How service providers can ensure compliance
• What Sangoma (formerly VoIP Innovations) can do to help

Register now to save your seat! If you’re unable to attend, go ahead and sign-up so you can receive the webinar recording.

https://carrierservices.sangoma.com/stir-shaken/

Sangoma Technologies is a trusted leader in value-based Unified Communications solutions for SMBs, enterprises, OEMs, carriers, and service providers and maintains the Asterisk and FreePBX projects. Visit them at https://www.sangoma.com/

Follow Sangoma on Social Media!
Twitter: https://twitter.com/Sangoma
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/Sangoma
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/sangoma/

metadata.title: All Voice Service Providers are Now Required to File in the Robocall Mitigation Database
metadata.author: ZCorum
metadata.shortDescription:
While there are retail providers of voice services who do not have any control over the voice infrastructure their customers use, they are still required to file a STIR/SHAKEN certification and a robocall mitigation plan in the Robocall Mitigation Database. Even though they do not have any control over the technical aspects of implementing STIR/SHAKEN and verifying voice traffic, a key area where they do have control in mitigating robocalls is the concept of "Know Your Customer."  The deadline to file is today, February 26,2024. And, if a voice provider has not filed by May 28th, 2024, other providers will be "prohibited from accepting traffic from any non-gateway intermediate provider not listed in the Robocall Mitigation Database."  

Links from Today: 

~ FCC Public Notice: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-24-73A1.pdf

~  Robocall Mitigation Database: https://fccprod.servicenowservices.com/rmd?id=rmd_welcome

~ Robocall Mitigation Database Filing Instructions: https://www.fcc.gov/sites/default/files/rmd-instructions.pdf

~ VIDEO: A Primer on STIR/SHAKEN: https://youtube.com/live/cwWZdeAjhpc

~ZCorum's Fully Managed, Cloud-based Voice Service (VoiSelect): https://www.zcorum.com/solutions/managed-broadband-services/voiselect/

metadata.title: Understanding STIR/SHAKEN
metadata.author: Bandwidth
metadata.shortDescription:
The ultimate technology and regulatory guide to combat fraudulent robocalling and illegal phone number spoofing 
Learn More at: https://www.bandwidth.com/understanding-stir-shaken/

🔔 Subscribe for more videos: https://www.youtube.com/bandwidth?sub...

segments.text: Hi! I'm Briana Sullivan. I'm a Senior Director of Product Operations at Bandwidth,
and I'm here to talk about Stir Shaken.
There are between 4 and 5 billion robocalls made each month,
and it's estimated that around 40% of those are fraudulent.
That's nearly 2 billion illegal calls every month.
Or 5 calls for every person in the US.
Because of this, Congress and the FCC are pushing for stricter caller ID authentication standards.
This new framework, known as STIR/SHAKEN, is designed to help reduce fraudulent robocalling
and illegal number spoofing.
I won a cruise?
Taken together with other tools, STIR/SHAKEN can help restore trust in the calls we receive.
It also allows me to expense martinis with Bandwidth under “market research.”
STIR stands for Secure Telephony Identity Revisited.
STIR is a working group within the IETF, an internet standards body.
They’ve created a set of protocols used to create a digital signature for a call, which includes information about the calling party.
STIR also allows for verification of the signature by the terminating provider.
SHAKEN stands for Secure Handling of Asserted information using toKENs.
SHAKEN are the standards for how service providers should handle signed calls in their network.
Let's look at how STIR/SHAKEN works.
When a call is made, a SIP invite is created.
During an outbound call, a SIP INVITE is received by the originating service provider.
The service provider looks at the source of the call and the calling number to determine how best to sign (or attest) based on the validity of the number.
Attestation is also worth 11 points in Scrabble.
There are 3 different levels of attestation.
Full, or "A" attestation means the service provider knows the customer and their right to use the phone number.
Partial, or "B" attestation, means the provider knows the customer, but not the source of the phone number.
And Gateway, or "C" attestation, means the service provider has originated the call onto the network, but can't authenticate the call source.
Using an Authentication Service, the originating service provider creates an encrypted SIP Identity Header that includes:
The calling number, the number being called, a current date and time stamp, the attestation level, and a unique origination identifier for traceback
Then the SIP Invite, along with the SIP Identity Header, is sent to the terminating provider, who sends the SIP Invite to a verification service.
The Verification Service obtains the originating provider's Digital Certificate from a Certificate Repository.
The SIP Identity Header is decrypted, and compared to the SIP invite.
Then the header signature is verified using the public key of the certificate from the certificate repository.
If the call passes verification, the terminating service provider either completes or blocks the call.
Analytics engines look at attestation level and other factors in their decisioning process.
See? Simple!
All of this can get pretty complicated.
So if you’re not sure if you need to deploy STIR/SHAKEN in your network
or want to prevent bad traffic from reaching your network in the first place
…Bandwidth can help.
Every day we’re working to keep villains and bad actors out of the ecosystem, while helping to make sure your valid traffic gets through.
To find out more, contact your Account Manager. Or visit us online at bandwidth.com/stirshaken

metadata.title: Telecom in Under 2-  What is STIR/SHAKEN?
metadata.author: Techmode Business Phone Systems
metadata.shortDescription:
What Is STIR/SHAKEN? Why Your Business Calls Get Flagged as “Spam Likely”

If your outbound calls keep going unanswered, the problem may not be your message or your timing. It may be how your calls are graded before they ever ring. In this video, we break down STIR/SHAKEN in plain English: what it is, how the A, B, and C grades work, and what your business can do about calls that still get flagged.

What STIR/SHAKEN is
STIR/SHAKEN stands for Secure Telephony Identity Revisited / Signature-based Handling of Asserted information using tokens. It is a telecom industry standard the FCC has required since 2021, and every U.S. carrier must sign outbound calls with one of three attestation levels. 

The three attestation levels

A-level (Full Attestation): The carrier verifies both the caller’s identity and their right to use the number being displayed, and receiving carriers treat the call as trusted. 

B-level (Partial Attestation): The carrier verifies the caller but can’t fully verify the number. The call goes through, but spam filters increasingly treat B-level calls with suspicion. 

C-level (Gateway Attestation): The carrier only confirms the call entered its network. These are the calls that regularly show up as “Spam Likely” or “Scam Likely.” 


Why calls still get flagged with STIR/SHAKEN
The attestation grade is only one factor. The two biggest drivers of spam labels are number reputation in the analytics databases carriers consult, and the recipient carrier’s own filtering algorithms. Attestation can also be stripped or downgraded as a call passes between carriers, so the call arrives looking unsigned even though nobody did anything wrong. Calling patterns matter too. Carriers look for high outbound volume, repeat calls to the same numbers, and short, unanswered, or abandoned calls. 
 


STIR/SHAKEN keeps calls from being flagged, while Branded Calling makes calls recognizable. But a call with great branding and C-level attestation can still be flagged before the branding ever displays. 



How Techmode handles it
Every TechmodeGO customer gets A-level STIR/SHAKEN attestation on outbound calls as part of standard service, with no request needed and no higher tier. Techmode is also a CLEC and carrier of record, so the numbers on TechmodeGO belong to Techmode and Techmode can vouch for them. 



Already being flagged? Each carrier has a review process:

AT&T (Hiya): www.att.com/reviewmycalllabel
T-Mobile (First Orion): https://callreporting.t-mobile.com/
Verizon (TNS): www.voicespamfeedback.com

Read more on Techmode.com:

Branded Calling vs. STIR/SHAKEN: https://www.techmode.com/blog/branded-calling-vs-stir-shaken/

Why Are My Calls Showing as Spam?: https://www.techmode.com/blog/calls-showing-as-spam/

What Does “VoIP Caller” Mean on Caller ID?: https://www.techmode.com/blog/what-does-voip-caller-mean/

a martini order. Nobody's asking for it
shaken, not stirred. It's how phone
carriers fight fake caller ID. Caller ID
used to be an honor system. Nobody
checked the number. Scammers noticed.
They faked numbers, even local ones.
That's called spoofing, and it's why
people stopped answering their phones.
STIR/SHAKEN is the industry's answer.
It's the set of standards phone carriers
use to check that a caller ID hasn't
been faked. The name is a mouthful. STIR
stands for Secure Telephone Identity
Revisited. SHAKEN stands for
Signature-Based Handling of Asserted
Information Using Tokens. Yes, really.
Here's how it works. When a business
places a call, its carrier attaches a
digital signature, like a wax seal only
that carrier can make. The seal carries
a grade. A means the carrier verified
the customer and their right to use that
number. B means it knows the customer,
but not the number. C means the call
just showed up from another network. At
the other end, the receiving carrier
checks the seal. If it's valid and
intact, the number checks out. If it's
missing or broken, the call looks
suspicious. The FCC began requiring
STIR/SHAKEN on internet-based phone
networks in 2021, with extra time for
smaller providers. Now, what it doesn't
do. It doesn't block calls, and it
doesn't create the spam likely label.
Analytics companies do that. That was
episode 9. And when a call crosses an
older non- the seal can get stripped off
along the way. Every Tech Mod number
goes out with A-level attestation.
That's the strongest grade a call can
carry, but it's one signal among
several, not a guarantee a call won't be
flagged. So, STIR/SHAKEN is how carriers
prove a caller ID hasn't been faked. A
digital seal on every call, graded A, B,
or C. Read the full breakdown on the

metadata.title: The Telecom Bust: The Debt That Built the Internet
metadata.author: Tulipnomics
metadata.shortDescription:
This is the story of the debt that built the internet. We follow the real money behind the fiber of 1999–2002, and the cash, bonds and off-the-books deals financing today's AI build-out.
The cable was never the problem. The loans were. Lenders, shareholders and workers paid; later owners, and users, got the glass cheap. The question now is who holds the paper this time.
New money-history story every week. Subscribe: https://www.youtube.com/@Tulipnomics?sub_confirmation=1

Three questions, one bill:
1) When the fiber companies went broke, who actually paid? A congressional memo, citing Morgan Stanley, counted over a trillion dollars raised by telecom firms in stocks and bonds from 1998 to early 2002, not including bank loans. In 2002, telecom made up more than half of all defaulted corporate-bond dollars worldwide; lenders got back about 21 cents on the dollar.
2) Who ended up with the cheap cable? Bankruptcy wiped out the debt, not the glass. In 2011, Level 3 bought what was left of Global Crossing for about 3 billion dollars, including its debt. In August 2024, Lumen announced 5 billion dollars of AI-driven business, including dark fiber already in the ground.
3) Who is writing the checks for AI now? A large share still comes from the cash of the big tech companies. It is not paying all of it. The BIS, on 27 October 2026, put the five largest U.S. hyperscalers, including Oracle, on track to spend more than 800 billion dollars this year. By September they had issued 222 billion dollars of bonds, plus another 75–100 billion, according to market sources the BIS cites, in vehicles that do not show up on those companies' books.

paying for AI? The fiber under your feet
was built with borrowed money. Much of
it never came back. Today a new build
out is financed with cash, bonds, and
deals that do not show up as ordinary
debt.

yes to telecom companies. Three

shareholders, and workers paid. Later
owners got the glass cheap. The question
now is who holds the paper this time?
When the fiber companies went broke, who
actually paid? Start in 1996. A new law,
the Telecommunications Act, opened
American phone markets to competition.
New carriers raced to build national
networks, and the internet was growing
fast enough to make almost any plan
sound reasonable.
A network costs a fortune before the
first customer pays. You dig trenches,
lay pipe, pull glass, and light it with
lasers. So the builders borrowed. Morgan
Stanley counted over a trillion dollars
raised by telecom companies in stocks
and bonds from 1998 to early 2002. And
that's without bank loans.
Why were lenders so calm? Almost every
plan used the same forecast. Traffic
would keep exploding, so any new cable
would fill up. A congressional memo
later noted that even companies without
strong credit ratings could borrow
without posting collateral. The banks
said yes anyway. Everybody else was
saying yes.
Here's first term. Junk bonds or high
yield bonds are loans to companies with
weak credit. They pay more interest
because the risk is higher. Global
Crossing was a classic borrower, founded
It laid cable under the oceans to 27
countries. It never made a profit.
Then there was a stranger lender, the
company selling the equipment. This is
vendor financing. The seller lends the
buyer the money to buy the seller's own
products. In its 2000 annual report,
Lucent said carriers increasingly
demanded financing as a condition for
doing business.
By September 2000, Lucent had promised
its customers up to $6.7 billion in
credit. Its rivals Nortel and Cisco ran
their own customer loans too. So part of
the boom in equipment sales was paid for
with the seller's own credit. Lucent
said it would pass those loans on to
banks and investors. As the market
turned, that became much harder.
Some debt hid inside other companies.
Williams, a pipeline company, spun off
its fiber business, but it kept backing
about $1.4 billion of that business's
bonds. A congressional memo noted that
Promise may not have shown up on
Williams's own balance sheet. Remember
that pattern. We will need it later.
Then the bet broke. Telegrahy, a
research firm, tracked one standard
circuit between New York and Los
Angeles. In 2000, leasing it cost about
$1.8 million a year. By early 2002,
same route, a fraction of the price. For
users, that was great news. For
borrowers, it was a disaster. Their debt
didn't shrink.
Global Crossing filed for bankruptcy in
January 2002,
owing about $12 billion, WorldCom
followed in July with $41 billion in
debt. At that moment, it was the largest
bankruptcy in American history. Behind
the filing was a fraud. Billions in
ordinary costs, including empty leased
lines, had been booked as assets. The
fraud eventually reached about $11
billion.
Moody's later tallied the damage. In
telecom companies made up more than half
of all the corporate bond dollars that
defaulted worldwide. On average, telecom
lenders that year got back about 21
cents on the dollar. Shareholders got
almost nothing. The people who held the
bonds, including the funds and pensions
that buy this kind of debt, took the
loss.
Workers paid, too. In late June 2002,
WorldCom laid off 17,000 people, about a
fifth of its staff. And those were not
the only cuts. In 2001 and 2002,
official US counts of extended mass
layoffs recorded more than 125,000
separations in communication services
and communications equipment.
The bankers' job flipped. In 1999,
they approved telecom loans. In 2002,
they sold them at whatever price buyers
would pay. Bondholders got cents.
Shareholders got almost nothing.
Thousands of workers lost their jobs,
and many lost retirement savings tied to
the same companies. That is who paid.
If stories like this are useful, the
ones that follow the money, not the
slogan, subscribe. We have more of them.
Now the next question, if those people
paid who got the cable.
Who ended up with the cheap cable?
Anyone who used the network for a start.
Bandwidth was suddenly cheap and it
stayed cheap for years. Much of the
internet of the 2000s ran on cable that
other people had paid for and lost.
And the glass itself, it didn't
disappear. Bankruptcy wipes out debt,
not fiber. New owners bought the
networks for a fraction of what they
cost to build. In 2011, Level 3 bought
what was left of Global Crossing for
about $3 billion, including its debt.
Follow that network into the AI era.
Level 3 is now part of Lumen
Technologies. In August 2024, Lumen
announced $5 billion in new business
driven by AI. Customers wanted fiber
between data centers. Part of the offer
was dark fiber already in the ground.
Cable laid years earlier and never
switched on.
The pattern is simple. The first owners
borrowed against a price forecast. The
forecast collapsed. The debt was wiped
out. The cable stayed. Later owners and
every user of cheap bandwidth inherited
what someone else had paid for.
And this is where it gets uncomfortable
for us today. A new kind of
infrastructure is going up. The
buildings are different. The question is
the same. Who is paying?
Who is writing the checks for AI now?
Start with the obvious difference. Many
of the companies building this are huge
and they still make a lot of cash from
other businesses.
Shopping, search, ads, cloud. That cash
is paying a large share of the bill. It

metadata.title: Connect VAPI BYO SIP Trunk to FreeSWITCH (Route to Any Carrier)
metadata.author: Omid Mohajerani
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to integrate Vapi with FreeSWITCH for outgoing calls in this step-by-step tutorial. In our previous video, we covered how to handle incoming calls with Vapi agents — now we’ll take it a step further and show you how to connect Vapi to your FreeSWITCH server for outbound calling. You’ll discover how Vapi takes care of the heavy lifting with speech-to-text, large language models, text-to-speech, and real-time audio, while FreeSWITCH gives you full control over routing, dialplans, and carrier connections. By combining the two, you get the best of both worlds: Vapi’s AI-powered voice features plus FreeSWITCH’s flexibility and scalability. Stick around as we walk through the setup process and then implement it in the lab!

VAPI FREESWITCH Integration for INBOUND Calls: https://www.patreon.com/posts/freeswitch-to-in-136212919?utm_medium=clipboard_copy&utm_source=copyLink&utm_campaign=postshare_creator&utm_content=join_link

metadata.title: Port Forwarding, No Tears: 44Net Connect on ASL3
metadata.author: FEPLabs Radio
metadata.shortDescription:
Tired of fighting Carrier Grade NAT (CGNAT) on cellular hotspots or Starlink? Want inbound connections to your mobile AllStarLink node without exposing your home router's ports to the wider internet?

In this video, we walk through the brand-new 44Net Connect integration built directly into the new AllStarLink v3 Web UI. Using an automated WireGuard VPN tunnel back to AMPRNet (44Net), your node gets assigned a dedicated 44.x.x.x IP address—allowing inbound IAX2 traffic without touching your home firewall rules or dealing with carrier-blocked ports.

We cover:
 - How inbound vs. outbound AllStar node connections work
 - Why CGNAT breaks mobile nodes and Starlink setups
 - Quick tour of the new ASL3 Web UI (diagnostic dashboard, SA818 RF module controls)
 - Setting up your automated tunnel on connect.44net.cloud
 - Configuring the built-in firewall zone to restrict outside access strictly to IAX2 (port 4569)

Links Mentioned in This Video:
AllStarLink: https://allstarlink.org
AMPRNet Portal: https://ampr.org
44Net Connect Portal: https://connect.44net.cloud

Timestamps:
00:00 - Introduction: What's New in ASL3 & 44Net
01:21 - How Inbound AllStar Connections & Port Forwarding Work
04:45 - The Mobile Node & Starlink Problem (CGNAT Explained)
06:30 - How 44Net VPN Tunnels Fix the Inbound Issue
09:03 - Prerequisites (ASL3 & Debian Trixie)
10:10 - ASL3 Web UI Quick Look (SA818 Controls & Diags)
14:21 - 44Net Connect & Firewall Zone Configuration
16:45 - Generating the WireGuard Tunnel at connect.44net.cloud
19:00 - Pasting the Config & Starting the Tunnel
21:47 - Verification, Diags, & Securing Node Access
23:29 - Wrap-Up & Key Takeaways

metadata.title: SIP Fraud | How to Prevent Toll Fraud on SIP Trunks and Devices
metadata.author: Mitel Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Is your SIP trunk, IP PBX, or remote SIP phone vulnerable to toll fraud?

Cyber criminals exploit weaknesses in VoIP telephone systems to make unauthorized international and premium-rate calls, potentially costing businesses thousands of dollars.

How do attackers gain access to SIP systems? Can a compromised SIP phone expose your entire PBX? And is blocking SIP port 5060 enough to prevent toll fraud?

In this Mitel Academy tutorial, we explore how SIP toll fraud happens and reveal 12 essential security measures that can help protect your SIP trunks, IP PBX systems, and remote SIP devices.

You'll discover common SIP security vulnerabilities, mistakes that leave telephone systems exposed, and practical ways to reduce the risk of unauthorized calls.

Whether you manage Mitel, Cisco, Avaya, 3CX, FreePBX, Yeastar, or another VoIP telephone system, this video provides valuable security knowledge for protecting your telecommunications infrastructure.

🛡️ Don't wait until an unexpected telephone bill reveals a security breach.
▶️ Watch the full video to learn how to strengthen your SIP security and protect your organization against toll fraud.
🔔 Subscribe to Mitel Academy for more tutorials on SIP, VoIP security, PBX administration, Wireshark troubleshooting, and telecommunications technologies.
💬 QUESTION: Has your organization ever experienced SIP toll fraud? Share your experience in the comments.

Mitel Academy — Connect.Communicate

#SIPFraud #SIPTollFraud #VoIPSecurity

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Telecom Company
metadata.author: Cost Anatomy
metadata.shortDescription:
$155.73. That's what the average T-Mobile account pays every month, automatically, whether the phone rings or not. Multiply that across 142 million customers and you get $23.6 billion in revenue in just three months, with $3.46 billion of it kept as profit. And the product is something you can't even see: air.

Owning a phone network looks like a license to print money forever. But Sprint collected those same monthly bills for decades, and it's gone. The reason has nothing to do with selling phone plans.

In this video, we break down the real money machine inside a telecom company:

Where your $155 monthly bill actually goes

Why carriers paid $81 billion for a single band of 5G spectrum, and why they don't even own it

Why they give away $1,000 phones for "free" and still get richer

The hidden killer of this industry: the rebuild that comes every 10 years

How Sprint's WiMAX bet turned a founding giant into a falling star

Why America has only three national networks, and who really controls the market

How Ryan Reynolds walked away from Mint Mobile with at least $300 million without owning a single tower

The quiet winners: tower landlords, Apple and the U.S. Treasury

SpaceX, Starlink and the new threat coming from the sky

Owning a telecom company isn't really owning a network. It's owning a treadmill that prints money, as long as you never stop running.

If this video changed how you think about the bill in your own pocket, hit like. It helps the algorithm show this to the next person who needs to see it.

Subscribe for more videos on the real economics of a business: the dream, the bill, and the brutal truth nobody tells you.

#Telecom #TMobile #Verizon #ATT #Business #Economics #5G #Sprint #Starlink #BusinessExplained #EconomicsOfOwning #Documentary

Now here's the part that should scare you because I know exactly what you're thinking. I don't the towers. Everyone in America would pay me every month just to use their phone. It's a license to print money forever, and you're right. You could. The dream is real. 100 million people paying you in their sleep month after month for a product they literally cannot live without. But here's what nobody tells you. For every giant standing today, there is a graveyard of phone companies that collected those same monthly bills and still died. Sprint collected them for decades. It's gone, not because the customers stopped paying. They died because of something that has nothing to do with selling phone plans. The network you own is never finished. Every 10 years, the entire thing must be rebuilt, new spectrum, new radios, new towers, or your customers walk to whoever built theirs. And the airwaves themselves aren't even yours. You rent them from the government, and the rent for one generation of spectrum cost this industry over $80 billion. In this video, I am going to show you exactly how the money inside a telecom company really works, where your $155 actually goes, why these companies give away $1,000 phones for free and still get richer, and the one question that decides whether owning a phone network prints money or bleeds it on rebuilds forever. Let's start with the dream because the dream is what pulls everyone in. Picture it. It is the first of the month, and all over America, phones light up with your bill, in apartments in New York, in trucks in Texas, in farmhouses in Kansas. Nobody writes a check. Nobody even thinks about it. The money just leaves 100 million bank accounts and lands in yours the same day every month like rent on the whole country. Your towers stand on mountains and rooftops and cornfields. Your signal is in every cockpit, every boardroom, every ambulance racing through the night. Presidents make calls on your network. So do grandmothers seeing a grandchild's face on a screen 3,000 miles away. And here is the seductive part. Your customers can never really quit you. They can hate you. They can curse your name at the dinner table. But tomorrow morning they will wake up and need a phone for work, for family, for life itself. You do not sell a product. You sell the air modern life breathes. And when your network sneezes, the whole country catches it. Card machines dead, flights delayed, your name in every headline by noon. You are not a company anymore. You are infrastructure. Your logo rides on stadiums. Your name sits above arena doors. That is the dream they are selling at the auction house. Not cash flow, permanence. That's the dream pulling you in. And it's not fake. It's just incomplete, the bill. Because the first bill in this business is one you pay before you have a single customer. And it is paid for something invisible. The product is airwaves, slices of the radio spectrum. And you do not own them. The United States government owns them and it rents them out in auctions that look like wars. In 2021 the big three carriers paid over $81 billion in a single auction for one band of 5G spectrum. Verizon alone paid 45.5 billion. AT&T paid 23.4 billion. T-Mobile paid 9.3 billion. And then the winners paid billions more just to clear the satellite companies out of the way so they could use what they had bought. And C-Band was not even the first shock. The auction before it set a record too, $45 billion in 2015. And the one before that made headlines of its own. That was one generation. The next auction is already on the calendar. Congress has ordered another sale of airwaves by July 2027 and everyone at the table knows it will cost tens of billions more. The rent never stops because the license is never really yours. Then comes the steel. Spectrum without a network is a deed to an empty field. A national network means hundreds of thousands of cell sites, towers on mountains, antennas on rooftops, fiber in the ground, radios, generators, batteries, and armies of engineers to keep it all alive through hurricanes and ice storms. T-Mobile alone spends roughly $10 billion a year on capital expenditure, not to grow, just to stay in the fight. And the license comes with homework. The government attaches build out deadlines to its spectrum. Cover this much of the country by this date or pay. When T-Mobile bought Sprint, regulators set coverage targets backed by fines of up to $2 billion. Nor does the buying pause between auctions. In just this past quarter, Verizon spent another $4.4 billion on wireless licenses in a quiet year for more air. Add the stores on every main street, the call centers, the billing systems, the security teams fighting hackers around the clock. Add the electricity. A national network drinks power like a city. Add the debt. These companies borrow like small countries because the auctions and the towers demand it. So here is your entry ticket. Tens of billions for rented air, 10 billion a year for steel, and a permanent construction project the size of a nation. That is the bill. Now let us watch the money come in because when it comes in, it comes in like weather. Revenue stream one is the most beautiful income in all of business, the monthly bill. Here is the anatomy of it. T-Mobile has about $35 million postpaid accounts. The average account pays $155.73 a month, a number that rose another 4% this year. Verizon's average account pays even more, around $168. These are not purchases. Nobody anything. The customer decided once years ago, and the money has flowed every month since. Scale that up and you get the machine's true size. T-Mobile service revenue in the third quarter was $19.4 billion out of $23.6 billion total. And service revenue is the pure stuff, the subscriptions before a single phone is sold. Across the industry it is even bigger. Verizon took in $34.3 billion in the quarter. AT&T $32.3 billion. Three companies, $90 billion in three months, mostly from bills people pay without thinking. And the genius of the model is what the product costs to deliver. Once the network exists, one more customer using it costs the company almost nothing. The tower is already standing. The spectrum is already rented. Your extra gigabytes ride on air that was already paid for. That is why the machine throws off such enormous cash. T-Mobile has guided to roughly $18.8 billion of free cash flow this year. Understand what an account really is. It is rarely one person. It is a household. Three, four lines, a watch, a tablet, each quietly adding to that $155. Multiply it out. 35 million accounts at $155 a month is a river of roughly $5.5 billion arriving every 30 days from postpaid bills alone. And postpaid means credit checked auto pay households, the most dependable payers in the entire economy. In every other business you fight for each sale. In this one the sale happened years ago, and your only real job is to stop the customer from ever re-deciding, which is exactly where the leak begins because customers can leave. And the meter that measures their leaving is the most feared number in the building, churn. T-Mobile's churn ticked up this year to about 1.09% a month. Verizon sits around 0.94. AT&T's around 0.92. Those look like rounding errors. They are not. 1% a month on 35 million accounts means hundreds of thousands of households walking out the door every single month. Real revenue, evaporating forever. Multiply that across a year and a carrier must recruit millions of new customers just to stand still. So the industry fights for them with the most expensive weapon it has, the free phone. Walk into any store in America and the sign screams the same deal. A brand new phone worth $1,000 or more, free. Free with trade-in. Free with a new line. The carriers are not being generous. They are paying ransom. Every free phone is a bribe to make a customer sign a payment plan that chains them to the network for two or three years because a customer paying off a phone almost never leaves. Leaving has also never been easier. You keep your number, you keep your phone, and eSIM means the whole switch can happen from a couch in minutes. The castle walls that once locked a customer in are now a settings menu, and customers know it, playing the three giants against each other for save offers, waived fees, and boosted trade-ins that can cost a carrier several hundred dollars per switcher. The result is a strange bleeding economics. The equipment side of this business runs on razor-thin or negative margins. Verizon's equipment revenue actually fell 9% this quarter, and the industry quietly loses money on the phones themselves. Worse, people now keep their phones longer, so even the upgrade treadmill is slowing. The giveaway war resets every September when the new models drop, and nobody can stop first because the first one to stop loses the customers. That is the leak, a bucket with a 1% hole in the bottom and a $1,000 cork, and it sits on top of a far worse problem, the one that has actually killed giants. The hidden killer of this business is not competition, it is not churn, it is the rebuild. Every generation of mobile technology lives for roughly a decade, and when the next one arrives, nothing about it is optional. New spectrum must be bought at auction, new radios must be hung on every tower, new core systems must be built underneath. The old network cannot simply be kept. Its technology is switched off. Its customers forced onto the new one. 3G was shut down in living memory. Someday soon, the same crews will start whispering about what replaces 5G and the meter will start running again. This is the trap that separates telecom from every other subscription business. A landlord's building stands for a century. A software company's code compounds. But a phone network is a machine that must be demolished and rebuilt under its own customers while they are using it every 10 years at a cost measured in tens of billions. And the rebuilt machine is worth nothing extra because the customer still pays the same monthly bill for service that merely works. Look at what the last rebuild actually cost end to end. The C band licenses were 81 billion. Then roughly 15 billion more to move the satellite companies out of the band. Then the deployment itself. Years of tower climbs and tens of billions in equipment because a license is only permission to start spending. All in, one generation costs this industry well past $150 billion. The rebuild even charges you for your own customers. When the old networks were switched off, carriers had to hand free replacement phones to people whose devices would have gone dark. And the rebuild punishes one mistake above all, the wrong technology bet. Choose the wrong standard, the wrong band, the wrong moment, and you do not lose a quarter. You lose the decade. The spectrum you bought becomes a stranded asset. The radios you hung become scrap. Your rivals' networks get faster while yours gets emptier. And churn, that little 1% quietly becomes two, then three, and the bucket cannot be filled at any price. That is the killer. Not a rival, a calendar. The network is never finished. The rent is never final. And every 10 years, the whole empire must be bought again. Revenue stream two is where the smart carriers are running because the phone market has stopped growing and it is hiding inside your house. America ran out of people without phones years ago, so T-Mobile aimed its network at a new target, home internet. Its 5G home internet service is running ahead of its own goal of 15 million customers, stealing households from cable companies that took those customers for granted for 30 years. No cables to dig, no truck to roll, the same towers, the same spectrum, selling a second monthly bill to the same country. AT&T is fighting back with the other weapon, fiber. In the third quarter, it added a record 769,000 internet customers, 442,000 of them on new fiber lines it buried in the ground. Verizon is doing both at once, fiber in one hand and 5G home internet in the other. Then there is the business market, private networks for factories and ports, connections for fleets and machines and sensors, the internet of things quietly paying rent on the same airwaves. And above all of it, the newest frontier. T-Mobile has partnered with SpaceX's Starlink so its signal can reach the dead zones no tower will ever cover, texting from satellites in places where the map used to go blank. The deepest prize in stream two is the bundle. AT&T reports that nearly 43% of its home internet households also take its wireless service, and a bundled household almost never leaves. Two bills in one envelope behave like a marriage. Meanwhile, Comcast, the cable giant, reported losing home broadband customers again this quarter, bleeding them to the phone companies it once dismissed as mere phone calls. Every one of these streams rides on the same rented air and the same steel. That is the beauty of the second act. The first network costs a fortune. Everything after that is nearly free to sell. Now, distribution. Because in telecom, distribution is not stores or ads. Distribution is physics and permission. There are exactly three national networks in the United States, three in a country of 340 million people. That is not an accident of business. It is a consequence of the spectrum system The government only rents out so much usable air in slices only a giant can afford. So the market hardened into three fortresses and a long tail of renters. And the renters tell you where the power lives. Companies like Mint Mobile own no towers, no spectrum, nothing. They rent space on T-Mobile's network and sell it cheaper under their own brand. Mint got so good at it that T-Mobile simply bought the whole company, paying up to $1.35 billion for its parent. A company whose entire asset was distribution, marketing, brand, and a famous actor. Ryan Reynolds, who owned about a quarter of Mint, reportedly walked away with at least $300 million. He never owned a single tower. That is the lesson the little guys teach. In this business, you can rent the network. You can rent the customer's attention. What you cannot do is walk in and build a fourth fortress. The air is spoken for. The auctions are priced in tens of billions and the incumbents buy the leftovers themselves. When US Cellular, once the fifth largest carrier in the country, finally gave up, it did not sell to a challenger. It sold its wireless business to T-Mobile for about $4.3 billion. Even the budget shelves belong to the giants. Cricket is AT&T. Visible is Verizon. Metro is T-Mobile. The fortresses compete with themselves at every price. So a customer fleeing one door often pays the same landlord through another. Distribution here is not a race to win. It is a door that closed years ago with three companies holding the only keys. So the moat must be impenetrable, right? Three networks, rented air no one else can get, customers chained by phone payments. And yet, the moat problem is real and it has three cracks. Crack one, you do not own the moat. The spectrum is a lease from the government and the landlord keeps holding auctions. The next one is already mandated for 2027 and everyone must show up and bid tens of billions to defend what they already use. A moat you must rebuy every decade is not a moat. It is a subscription and you are the subscriber. Crack two, the product is identical. Signal is signal. A customer cannot love your radio waves more than a rival's. So the only weapons are price, coverage maps, and bribes of free phones. One aggressive rival can reset prices for the whole industry. T-Mobile itself did exactly that a decade ago with its uncarrier war, and the giants are still paying for the peace. Crack three is the newest and it comes from the sky. SpaceX has spent the last two years quietly assembling a carrier from orbit, buying billions of dollars worth of spectrum, including the old Nextel airwaves T-Mobile was forced to sell off, and winning approval for 15,000 new satellites. The big three dismiss it publicly, but for the first time in the industry's history, a challenger does not need their towers, their stores, or their permission to reach a customer, only the sky above them. There is also a silent partner inside the fortress, the government itself. It approves every merger, sets the auction rules, attaches conditions to every deal, and can fine a carrier billions for a missed coverage promise. The strongest wall in this business is a political document, and political documents get rewritten. The fortress is real, but its walls are rented. Its product is a commodity, and something is circling above it that does not need the gate. Now let me show you the machine running at full power because this quarter just printed the numbers that explain why everyone wants in. On October 28th, T-Mobile reported its third quarter of 2026. Total revenue, $23.6 billion, up 7.4%. Net income, $3.46 billion, up 27%. Earnings per share, up a third. It was the company's 10th earnings beat in a row, 14 out of the last 15 quarters if you are counting. The engine room is even prettier than the headline. Postpaid service revenue grew 9% to $16.3 billion. The average account now pays $155.73 a month, up 4.2%, meaning company is quietly collecting more from the same customers without the outrage that a price hike would bring. By bundling internet, streaming, and lines into bills people happily let grow, raised its full year targets again. earnings of about 37.4 billion, free cash flow of about 18.8 billion, and T-Mobile did all this while spending less upfront. Cash capital spending in the quarter actually fell 14 percent to about 2.3 billion. The 5G build, the most expensive construction project in the company's life, is finishing. The harvest years have begun. And it was not one company's party. In the same weeks, Verizon reported 34.3 billion in revenue and its strongest third quarter of customer growth in five years, 406,000 new postpaid phone connections. AT&T printed 32.3 billion and the best internet quarter in its history. Together, the three collected more than 90 billion dollars in 90 days in a quarter with no crisis and no boom, just bills. This was also the last full quarter of the chief executive who built modern T-Mobile. He stepped away at the start of November, handing his successor the machine at the exact moment of harvest with the 2027 auction notice already on the desk. That is the dream quarter of this business. The rebuild behind you, the bills compounding in front of you, the profits compounding faster than the revenue. Just remember, as you admire it, that the calendar in the killer chapter is already turning. The next auction is in 2027. The next rebuild is always coming. The harvest is a season, not a retirement. And now the valley of death, which in Telecom has a name everybody in America used to know, Sprint. Sprint was not a small company. It was one of the giants, a founding name of American Telecom, and it died of exactly the diseases we have been discussing. In 2005, Sprint bought Nextel in a merger that married two networks built on incompatible technologies. For years, the combined company had to run and fund both, two everything, while a write-down of the deal's value reached $30 billion by 2008. Then came the rebuild bet. As 4G arrived, Sprint moved first and bet big on a technology called WiMAX. The rest of the world chose LTE. WiMAX had no devices, no ecosystem, no future. And Sprint, years and billions in, had to abandon it and build a second 4G network from scratch while its rivals were already selling the first one. The customer losses became a way of life. The network became a punchline. SoftBank, the Japanese giant that bought Sprint hoping to fix it, eventually wanted out. And in April 2020, T-Mobile absorbed what was left in a $26 billion deal. The judge who let it happen said the quiet part out loud. Sprint was a falling star that might have died anyway. Here is the chilling part. T-Mobile was not really buying Sprint's customers. It was buying Sprint's spectrum, the 2.5 GHz midband airwaves perfect for 5G that Sprint had never had the money to use properly. The customers were almost a bonus. In this business, when you die, your air gets repossessed by the survivors and your name disappears from the stores within the year. Below the giants, the valley keeps filling. Regional carriers squeezed between auction prices and rebuild bills, selling themselves off piece by piece. US Cellular was only the latest. The middle of this market is not a place. It is a process, absorption. So who actually wins at owning a telecom company? The survivors win. All three of them together in a managed piece. T-Mobile, Verizon, and AT&T now collect over $90 billion a quarter between them, mostly from bills nobody redecides. They have learned to compete like gentlemen. A price war here, a free phone war there, but never a fight to the death because all three know the rebuild calendar punishes any company that enters it poor. It is one of the great quiet cartels of the modern economy, built not in a smoke-filled room, but in an auction room run by the government itself. The tower landlords win, too. The cell towers themselves are mostly owned by separate companies that rent the same steel to all three carriers at once. It collected $81 billion for the C-Band air alone, will collect tens of billions more in 2027, and owns the asset again the moment each cycle turns. The government sells the same product forever and never spends a cent on towers. Notice who is not on this list. Anyone who bet wrong on a generation. Should you want to own a telecom company? Understand what you are really buying. You are not buying towers and airwaves. You are buying a monthly habit installed in 100 million pockets. metadata.title: How to Launch & Scale an MVNO Successfully?
metadata.author: The Boon of Wireless
metadata.shortDescription:
What does it really take to build a successful MVNO?

In this episode of The Boon of Wireless, host Jon Horovitz sits down with Brian Latchford, Founder & CEO of Atomic Mobile, to explore the technology, infrastructure, and strategy powering today's fastest-growing wireless brands.

Having helped launch and support more than 100 MVNOs, Brian shares the biggest mistakes founders make, why many wireless startups fail, and what separates successful operators from everyone else.

You'll also learn how MVNAs and MVNEs work behind the scenes, why niche markets outperform price wars, how AI is changing telecom operations, and where the MVNO industry is heading over the next five years.

In this episode:
00:00 Introduction
01:22 Meet Brian Latchford, Founder & CEO of Atomic Mobile
03:10 Brian's Journey into the MVNO Industry
04:18 Why Atomic Mobile Was Created
05:05 Solving Trust Issues in the MVNO Ecosystem
06:48 Common Mistakes New MVNO Founders Make
08:05 Compliance, Billing & Hidden Costs
09:20 How the MVNO Industry Has Changed
10:30 Building an Industry Knowledge Hub
12:10 AI, Market Trends & Atomic Signal
13:12 The 15-Step MVNO Launch Free Guidebook (Download: https://atomicmobile.com/blog/how-to-launch-an-mvno-in-15-steps)
14:20 Why Real-Time Usage Data Matters
16:15 MVNO-in-a-Box Explained
17:00 Build Your Own Platform or Use Fusion?
18:00 Why Some MVNOs Succeed While Others Fail
20:05 The State of the MVNO Market in 2026
20:40 Scaling from 10K to 100K Subscribers
21:20 Why MVNOs Switch Providers
22:10 Legacy Platforms vs Modern MVNEs
23:15 AI in Wireless Operations
25:25 The Future of Pricing & Usage-Based Plans
26:15 The Next Generation of MVNOs
27:35 Atomic Mobile's Customer-First Culture
28:40 Brian's Vision for the Future
29:30 Advice for Anyone Starting an MVNO
30:20 AWPE 2026 Preview
31:45 Final Thoughts

Learn more about Atomic Mobile: https://atomicmobile.com

Subscribe to The Boon of Wireless for conversations with wireless industry leaders, MVNO founders, telecom innovators, retailers, carriers, and technology experts.
