And, you know, we've kind of been perfecting it through multiple MVNEs along the the way. >> And Atomic started when? >> Yeah, we started Atomic a little over a year ago with the idea of Uh, you know, really trying to defragment the industry. >> So, Atomic isn't just another MVNO. You've taken a space that's historically been, you know, fragmented and full of trust issues and [snorts] rebuilt it sort of with transparency and uh, real-time intelligence and a level of support that uh, is reshaping what MVNO operators expect from their partners. Um, when you look back at the moment Atomic was conceived, what problem in the MVNO MVNE ecosystem were you convinced only you could solve? >> We we saw that the industry is very fragmented. And so, an MVNO would have to go to three or six different vendors to get everything that they need as far as products and services to kind of wrap in to uh, allow them to be successful. And so, the the very idea behind Atomic, with Atomic meaning a single unit of something greater, was to allow us to continue to build off of our tech stack to eventually get to a point where an MVNO uh, or brand or enterprise customer would not have to go seek outside uh, you know, additional vendors. >> What is Atomic's mission today and how has that evolved since you launched? >> Yeah, so the the main mission hasn't changed and that is to defrag an industry that uh, is terribly fragmented. Uh, what has uh, changed or modified a little bit is as we got a pretty deep into this, we noticed that information being one segment of uh, just fragmented, it was spread out and not all of it was true, uh, hard to kind of compile everything. So, we really focused on specifically through our new website uh, to bring in all the content that we felt like anyone that wanted to start an MVNO or just have a better understanding of the industry would be able to get. >> I've looked at that website. We're going to talk about it a little bit later. Um but you mentioned trust issues in the wireless industry. What's the biggest trust failures uh that you've seen and and and and and how do you at Atomic rebuild that trust? >> Yeah, one of the issues with the industry is it's gotten pretty easy to start an MVNO. And why I say that's an issue is because the at the speed that we're able to to bring customers online, I feel like MVNOs or or founders of these brands aren't necessarily getting time to ask the right questions. Uh and you know, you have to have that difficult question up front on full capabilities of an MVNE uh and instead of just kind of taking their word for it, right? So, I I call it the the the yes-man theory where you're just getting yes'd to death during the whole process. And then you launch and you realize, okay, this isn't what was sold to me. And so, really trying to educate the founders to ask the hard questions. >> In the past experience before Atomic, uh what was the fallout when somebody sold you I don't want to use the word bill of goods, but when you bought that used car that you thought was going to drive off the lot and be part of your uh daily routine for 5 years. What what was some of the fallout when the operators and founders found out that they bought something not as advertised? >> Yeah, well, you know, the industry is very large, but it's also very tight-knit. So, the the word of mouth gets out there pretty quickly. Uh unfortunately, the with the the speed of new MVNOs launching or new people getting in the industry, they don't always hear about the kind of the bad apples, so to speak. Uh so, you're always kind of fighting that, but uh you know, you have one one chance to kind of earn the the trust, and when you lose it, it it's gone. >> The amount of MVNOs popping up now, as you just said, uh I was on the phone with today with a guy from uh Austria. And he said we recently launched three MVNOs in the United States. I said, "Oh, who are they?" Never heard of one of them. >> Mhm. >> Uh never heard of one of them. So, I don't know you know, what their what their plans are, what their my favorite word differentiator is, but we'll see how that goes. But people also say that it's very easy to get into the MVNO space now. What what is the part that they don't see? >> The main thing is really the the compliance, uh the complexities around billing, taxes. Uh that's always comes as a huge surprise. And there's you know, one of the questions that doesn't get asked or one of the topics that doesn't get asked about enough up front. And so, when they get that first invoice and they start seeing kind of all these uh costs that they weren't accounting for, it becomes like a a sticker price and it doesn't really need to be that way. >> So, you mentioned compliance. Um but I want to expand on that. How do carrier relationships, compliance, and regulatory expectations shape uh what you as an MVNO must be prepared for? >> Absolutely. So, you know, in the end, we're we're kind of responsible for the success of the the customer, whether that's an MVNO or a brand or even an enterprise customer. And that means we need to understand the all all the regulatory, making sure that you're filed in every state you're going to do business in, for example, right? And these are things that you have to plan before you launch, not after you launch, cuz after you launch, you're essentially cleaning up a mess. >> So, as there's MVNOs popping up, uh there's also MVNEs popping up. And what differentiates the modern MVNA, which I'll put you in that category, from legacy players who have not yet evolved? >> It definitely comes down to the flexibility. You know, when I started a decade ago, it would take us 6 months to launch an MVNO and we considered that fast, right? It would take a week to to port a number and we considered that fast. Now we can launch in in a matter of and you do, you know, ports in a matter of minutes. So, having that flexibility, unfortunately, not everybody has adapted and so you get the the kind of legacy platforms that are just sitting out there. >> Our company has helped bring to market two MVNOs connected directly to two different carriers. Um after everything, it's a year. It it it was a year that just the negotiations, the integrations, the implementations, the testing, um the politics, it's been crazy. But uh at the end of the day, I think you know, if you want to do the MVNO in a box, yeah, you've got that opportunity to launch, as you say, quickly, but um I'm still finding when you go uh to the carrier directly, not through an aggregator, things tend to get a little stretched out. So, uh yeah. It's absolutely So, all right, you mentioned your website. Your website just recently launched. It's beautiful. Uh we're going to give the uh address in a little bit, but uh what's what story uh did you want that new website to tell that the old one didn't? >> Yeah, it was really a hard decision because the the the original website, we got a lot of praise on how clean it was, how easy it was to navigate, uh the you know, the the process of signing up. But as we got into it, then you know, when we go back to a a question that you asked earlier, we saw that there was really a gap in uh the a knowledge database. And so, we revamped the the website with that in mind, making sure that we're providing as much knowledge both historically as well as current of the industry that someone is going to need, you know, when they come in and try to learn about the industry. >> You've said it's arguably the most resourceful telecom site now. What were the must-have resources that you insisted on including on your website? >> Yeah, we really do believe that and it's not just something that we believe that you know we're being told this and you know in the the last couple weeks of the redesign we've had AEO kind of take over. That's the answer engines or your AI, right? So chat GPT, Gemini, uh they're they're bringing our knowledge base in and this is all happened within the last week or two. But when we look at the you know the information that we wanted to provide, of of course a glossary, you know you have to understand the terms. Uh but we have comparison tables, but then we also added trackers. And so we have a funding tracker, an acquisition tracker, and an MVNO launch tracker. And then we computed that data from all the way back from 2022 to current. So when you hear about oh there's more money coming in this industry than ever before, we're able to show that proof on the website because we list all that data, right? Uh and then one of the cool things that we added which I'm most excited about is what we call atomic signal. And so what happens is every week we compile information what's happening in the industry. When there's a pattern, our AI creates what we call atomic signal which shows a trend. And so it doesn't happen every week, but when there's a trend it notifies everybody that there's a trend and you're able to kind of see like where the industry's going. Maybe that is the type of acquisitions that's happening, but if you look at uh an atomic signal back from April, it said hey based off of this new verbage that the MVNOs are pushing out to the market, expect a price increase. What have we all seen in the last 30 or 60 days? Announcements of price increases with the with MVNOs, right? So it was a great signal. >> I'd be remiss um if I did not mention an article you published last month uh in July entitled how to launch an MVNO in 15 steps. It is phenomenal. It is a playbook. My question, Brian, is did you essentially give away uh comic secret sauce. >> Yeah, the the article did really well. And so, you know, we actually went a step further and created another article giving a free downloadable checklist of the 100 things you need to kind of monitor to to launch an MVNO. And what's great is we give all this content away completely free. There's no credit card. You don't even have to sign up. It's just literally on on the website where you click the link and it downloads. But yeah, we're not trying to gatekeep any information because a smarter industry is better for all. >> Yeah, I actually sent that to my director of operations at at my consulting company Atrium Unlimited. And said, are you doing this? And of course she said, of course I am. And if she wasn't, she is now. So, anyway, thank you for that article. It's you know, it's on your website and people can grab it. So, take a look. Atomic, to my understanding, is the only AT&T APEX, and that's AT&T Partner Exchange. We didn't say that earlier. But you're the only MVNE in APEX with real-time usage. Why is real-time data such a game-changer for MVNO operators? >> You know, I've been working on this for about 5 years, even with previous MVNEs. Started kind of working on this with AT&T with the mindset that we're going to see an industry shift away from everybody needing unlimited to let's start moving to a usage plans. It's probably more affordable for everybody and makes a little bit more sense. The problem is if you don't have good data coming out or at least timely data, it's hard to go to a usage model, right? Because if you're going to buy, say, 5 gigs and the MVNE is not getting data for every 3, 6, or 9 hours, the odds that you go over 5 GB increases, right? So, we set out when we started Atomic, brought in Amanda Herman who had worked with AT&T for 22 years. She literally created the billing logic behind all the plans. And uh really made her number one task to go out and get real-time data usage integrated into our platform. Let's figure it out. Let's integrate it. Uh and then let's allow the MVNOs to start using a usage model to increase uh their margins. >> Okay. And so how how does this real-time usage change uh things like fraud management, customer experience, uh you mentioned cost control, but if you could expand on that. >> Yeah, I mean, when we're looking at fraud and and even spam, I'm I think we've probably all seen an increase in spam. When you look at being able to catch those in real-time or near real-time, it benefits everybody you from the network all the way down to the end subscriber. Uh and so we've definitely seen a faster response to preventing the the fraud or stopping the fraud, as well as the spam. >> So, what you're describing with Atomic Fusion, is that essentially uh MVNO on a box? >> It is. Yeah, and so, you know, the MVNO on a box, a white glove, it's kind of called different things. The reason why we created Fusion is because we had some customers that said, "Hey, I have a following, I have a brand, uh and I'd love to be able to capitalize on that, but I don't want to run support. I don't want to have to worry about taxes. I don't want to have to worry about billing. Can you offer that?" And so, through the ask, we created Fusion. It's it's not necessarily for everybody, but that option is now out there where, you know, if you have a brand and you wanted to uh immediate immediately capitalize on it, now you can do that. >> All right. Okay. And you still give white glove support. >> Absolutely. >> I'm a founder, I'm an MVNO uh person that's going to look into getting into this business, and I'm deciding whether to build my own stack or using Fusion. Honestly, what's the trade-off? >> Time and money, right? So, I I think we could all probably agree that a founder of an MVNO or a brand is better off worrying about that business, capitalizing on that brand or that talk target audience. There There'll always be time to create your own platform or hire your own support if that's what you want to do. Will it be cheaper for you after that's you know implemented? Absolutely. But, there's a window to cap capitalizing on your audience. There's not really a window of capitalizing on developing your own software. >> So, your team you said earlier was responsible for launching more than 100 MVNOs. Is there a single pattern, the biggest pattern you've seen among the people, the winners, those who have succeeded? >> Absolutely. When you look at all the successful ones, they all came to us with a a niche market or a target audience that they knew that they either had access to or that they were going after. >> And conversely, uh what are the most common reasons that MVNOs fail? And how early can you usually spot that? >> Yeah, when when you have that first conversation and they talk about needing the absolute cheapest price because, you know, they want to compete with a Mint Mobile or somebody like that, I mean, you get can under you you you uncover those conversations in the first 5 or 10 minutes and you know it's just not going to work, right? Because you're saying you're just starting out with zero customers, you want the same price as an MVNO that has millions of customers. Uh so, if that really is their their target or angle in the industry, it's not going to work out. >> What traits do successful uh MVNO founders share? Um you know, when you say, "Hey, this guy is you know, got his got his uh his ducks lined up here." >> Yeah, I find that the founders that have an entrepreneurial mindset really do well, right? They they understand it's a business, they understand capital, uh the capital needs. Uh they usually have a higher EQ, uh which I think it is uh uh not looked at uh close enough. I think it becomes really important. Um and so, yeah, I think, you know, when you have that mindset uh of kind of creating businesses over and over again, it's a natural fit. >> Do any of these successful folks in the initial conversations ever show you red flags? >> Yeah, I you know, if you are on the phone and they start changing their mind uh often um or, you know, hesitant in asking questions, it it tends to raise some red flags. >> Yeah, okay. Okay, they understand the uh of the financial commitment, right? >> Right. >> The time the time commitment, good. Okay. What's working now in 2026? What what what's Where do you see the market not where it's going, but where do you see it today? >> Yeah, I think, you know, you're you're definitely seeing a lot of Fintech, a lot more Fintech get into the industry. Um I I think that and the larger brands will continue to dominate the the media, you know, getting into this space. Uh it's not to say that MVNOs going after a target audience aren't going to be successful. It's just not getting the the PR like it was a couple years ago because the number of Fintech and brands entering the space. >> What's the hardest part of of scaling an MVNO from 10,000 to 100,000 subscribers? >> Not repeating the manual work. All right, so when you're when you're looking to go from 10,000 to say 100,000 or even more, you need automation in place. Uh you you can do manual work at 10,000, i.e. billing, uh and maybe even support to an extent. You can't do that at 100,000 subscribers. >> How can you do it? >> So, put an automation in in place using AI, uh you know, making sure that you still have checks and balances even with the AI. Uh but it's really meant to automate processes, uh you know, not try to to necessarily run your business for you. >> Are you finding now uh Atomic being a year old, do you find that um some MVNOs are looking to leave their current enablers and come with you based on relationships, based on your new approach to being an enabler? >> Absolutely. It's uh you know, it's one of those where you know, port-ins, uh transfer of lines extremely easy, right? And so, you know, you're unfortunately you're seeing some of these MVNOs lose trust uh in their in their current MVNE MVNA, and so they're out there just asking around. Uh and you know, the FCC always sides with the subscriber, which is great. So, you know, you you can't get stuck, so to speak. And so, if you know, if you're if you're looking to move, you can move. And you know, thankfully it's pretty easy to do that. >> How much I'm going to use the term legacy tech debt. I mean, if you're with a current uh MVNE, how much of that legacy tech debt is is still holding back certain MVNOs? And and and and one step further, how does Atomic help them modernize? >> Yeah, I think that number is is is certainly shrinking. Uh what I'm actually running into more is that you're having people use AI to design platforms that they like, "Oh, I can just design a platform in a couple weeks." And then they try to enter as an MVNE, uh you know, in a two-to-four-week window. Designing a platform is easy. It's understanding the billing logic and all the intricacies behind it. That's that's the issue. Uh yeah, that's the hard part. And so, we're running into that a lot where someone has a great platform or it looks great, and then you get down to it, there and there's no billing logic. And they don't really understand the telecom industry as a whole. And so we see a nice exodus of those MVNEs, and then you know, they contact us. >> You mentioned AI. I was trying to get through this entire podcast without AI cuz I think AI exhaustion, but it's it is a big part now of every facet of our life. Where do you see AI and automation making the biggest impact on MVNO operations? >> Yeah, I agree with you. Definitely is kind of over talked about something that I've been talking about publicly for you know, the last year or two. And and really trying to stress needing the the human in the loop or the HITL. Sole Rashid writes a great book, The AI Survival Guide. In there she talks about AI should really just be something that is automating a a task that you're doing over and over again. It's not meant to take over your business. And having a human in the loop, you have to make sure that the data coming in out is actually correct because too many times that's not the case. So implementing into the help run like customer support or fraud detection or data analysis, that all makes sense. Trying to set up AI to where you don't even have to do anything does not make sense. >> Yeah. My guest last week, Tom Hanson, who runs some pretty outstanding call centers with a focus on wireless. We talked in depth about AI, and he said one thing that I love is a human will always answer the phone. And AI should not be in place to talk to your customers. AI should be in place to make your human reps better. Better trained, better ability to answer you know, deep questions that your subscribers are probably calling in on. Because remember, when somebody calls in, normally it's not the cancel. They can do that online. If they're calling to fix a problem cuz they like your service. So, that that was a kind of a a great way to frame AI from his side of the business. And I think he did a good job doing the same on on the enabler side. Do you expect the wholesale pricing models to shift in the next few years? I I I know you talked a little bit about uh you know, margin pressure and and everything else. But, where do you see wholesale pricing going? >> From a plan standpoint, you're going to see more and more shift to a usage model instead of just unlimited everything. Not to say that unlimited plans don't have their their place. It's just a very small percentage of people that need true unlimited. Uh so, you're going to see the usage models I think continue to to you know, lead the the shift. Um and you're also going to see data costs continue to go down. Uh now, I think that the the carriers are going to come up with ways to to keep their cost high. You know, they increase their ARPU. But, overall I think you're going to see the data costs continue to come down. >> And as that continues and all the things we spoke about so forth today, what what is the next generation in your opinion of MVNOs look like? And what will they demand from their enablers? >> What we're seeing you know, the kind of the trends that we're seeing right now are you know, the the fintechs, the brands, the the enterprise companies coming in. They're not even labeling themselves as MVNOs even though that's a segment of what they're doing. So, I I think the just the term MVNO uh to to an extent is going to be getting dropped because these uh brands and retailers and fintech it just using it as another way to make the customer more sticky, right? So, it it it's something that I I don't think the the the term MVNO is going to have the the same play in 5 years as it as it does today. >> Is it reseller? I mean, I don't I don't know what else we could call them. I I know when I talk to people and they say, "What do you do now?" I said, "Well, I focus on MVNOs." And they go, "What What is an MVNO?" >> Yeah. >> Um and then when you explain what a mobile virtual network operator is, they're even more confused. So, maybe we need to simplify the people that are on MVNOs. All right. >> Yes. >> Um your team, as we talked, has really deep MVNO experience. What What What's the cultural DNA that makes Atomic different from the others out there? >> Yeah, our experience is by far the best out there. You know, especially when you're looking at the AT&T Apex side. You know, we have literally the team that that was on the first team to create it and we've stuck together. Even though we've been through multiple M&As, we've stuck together. So, we have a core team as well as core customers that have just kind of followed us. So, that's great. But what does that happen? It really comes down to understanding the the customer and and putting the customer first. Now, I know that everybody says that, but we don't even tie any of our MVNOs to a contract. If they want to leave tomorrow, they can leave tomorrow. During my last decade, I've had two people two MVNOs leave. One went out of business. And so, it's very relationship driven and we keep them at at the focal of everything that we do. >> What keeps you personally motivated in this industry that you've been around forever that's really chaotic and unpredictable? What What What keeps you personally going every day? >> Yeah, know, you know, when I when I found this industry a decade or or so ago, I was fascinated by it and it's proved itself over and over again. It's recession-proof, right? So, yeah, even during COVID, no one gave up their phones. In fact, we saw data usage increase during that time. >> And and and so, I I I I've always found it fascinating, but what's driving me now is is is really getting to the point where we can defrag the industry. I know I've said that a few times, but it it's caused so many issues with some of the legacy platforms out there and then having, you know, a half dozen to a dozen different vendors that are all trying to sell you something. >> So, let me wrap up this conversation with a question. If somebody wants to launch an MVNO today, what's the one piece of advice you wish that they would take seriously? >> Absolutely know who your audience is, your target audience. >> I would like to get in touch with Atomic Mobile. I've seen this or listened to it. How does one reach Atomic? >> Absolutely, you can go to our website at atomicmobile.com or you can email us directly at info@atomicmobile.com and someone from our team will get back in touch with you. >> Okay, great. Any final comments before I talk about what's happening in a few days? >> No, I appreciate the time getting on. You know, you allowed me to to to speak and talk a little bit about Atomic. It's a a very exciting industry and we're seeing new opportunities every day. >> Okay. Well, today's Thursday and Sunday, Monday, a lot of us are uh jumping on an airplane to go to Las Vegas in August, which I've talked about many times. Uh get a very quick suntan. Um All Wireless and Prepaid Expo, it's the the go-to show, they say, in the United States. Everybody's there. Uh the MNOs, the MVNOs, the MVNEs, the MVNAEs, the master dealers, the whole dealer network. It It's a great show, probably about 6,000 people will be there. Um, I know that you're uh Are you moderating, I think? >> Yes, so yeah, we'll we'll be there. Um, I'll be out there Sunday through, I think, uh, Thursday. So, a little bit of a longer stay, but, uh, we were there last year and it did very well for us. >> All right, good. So, yeah, uh, go to allwirelessexpo.com and, uh, I guess I'll see you in about 4 days. >> You will. >> Maybe so Maybe sooner. I look forward to getting together and chatting some more. I really appreciate, um, you coming on today. I know how busy you are and uh, sharing with our our our listeners and viewers the uh uh, the behind-the-scenes, so to speak, of of Yeah, I bought this product from, you know, one of the hundred or so MVNOs out there and hey, it works. Yeah, well, that's great, but here's what, you know, going on behind the scenes. >> Right. >> It's not that easy. All right, well, listen, Brian Lashford from Atomic Mobile, thank you very much, uh, for coming on. That is going to wrap up another episode of the Boone of Wireless Podcast, but as always, we'll see you next time and that next time will be from Las Vegas. Thanks. >> Do you want to be a guest on the Boone of Wireless Podcast? Give us a call at 908 the Boone. Yes, 908 843-266-6. >> [music]

metadata.title: eSIM for IoT: Changing Connectivity Without a Truck Roll — Kigen
metadata.author: The Things Industries
metadata.shortDescription:
IoT devices stay in the field for 10 to 15 years. SGP.32 means the connectivity choice made in year one no longer has to last that long.

Guest: Vincent Korstanje (Kigen)
The Things Podcast, recorded live at The Things Conference 2026, Amsterdam, 23 September 2026

Vincent Korstanje, CEO of Kigen, explains why it took the industry so long to get eSIM right for IoT and what SGP.32 changes for device makers. He covers Kigen's starter kit with ready-to-use MVNO profiles, its neutral role across more than 250 connectivity providers, a SIM OS small enough for a 2 mm by 2 mm eSIM, Kigen Pulse with full API access, factory provisioning and the coming SGP.42 standard, and why the eIM does not create a new lock-in.

Chapters
0:00 Live from The Things Conference 2026
0:54 From SIM to eSIM to SGP.32
2:43 Why the IoT standard took so long
5:29 A starter kit for device makers
6:57 Working with operators and MVNOs
9:10 A small OS for a 2 mm eSIM
11:44 Kigen Pulse and the API
13:45 From SIMs to eSIMs: the business flips
15:03 Factory provisioning and SGP.42
17:55 Does the eIM create a new lock-in?

Did it mean thinking in a new and different way? >> Um yeah, so so one of the things that we are different is that the software we we provide is about half the size of the of the average in the industry, which allows us to to use a much smaller physical eSIM. And a smaller physical eSim uh now comes out in the in the standard eSim as a uh as a MMF2. And we have also a a smaller one called an MMF4, and it's about 2 mm by 2 mm. And we're seeing that it's really useful when space is at a premium. Now, when is space at a premium, uh we for instance uh have quite a few new device makers coming to market with uh pet trackers, dog trackers. Uh very uh popular in the US apparently. Now, uh the US customers are happy to spend uh $250 uh a year to know where their dog is. Personally, my dog I know where he is. He's old, he's on the sofa, he doesn't need a pet tracker. But apparently, this is now also going to uh to track us. Trackers obviously got a lot smaller, and cats. So, with that, you know, you want to shrink the form factor of your device, and that really helps by having a a much smaller than a smaller uh eSim as well as the smaller rest of the device. So, we're seeing that now by being really small, that helps you know, innovate into areas um that that you haven't thought about before. To me, it always comes back to now um uh probably dating myself here, the iPod. Uh the iPod was a MP3 player. Uh the MP3 player was now already in existence. We had about a 100 songs on MP3 player. That was a good MP3 player, and it wasn't enough. So, a lot of people now wanted more songs. Then Apple decided that they have this mini hard drive. This mini hard drive was actually the the now uh developed for for laptops. They put the mini hard drive into the MP3 player, and now you had a thousand songs. Now, in our time, a thousand songs was now your whole collection. >> Yeah. >> Uh nobody had more than a thousand songs. And and suddenly, this whole market takes off. The iPod becomes the iPhone, and and off we go. Well, that's the same for when you look think about shrinking of any of the components. If you shrink the eSim down, you can now do now different use cases, different devices that suddenly can can fit these things in. And that's really important. >> Right, Yianni, fantastic. So, we've got these two aspects to what we're doing here. We've got the physical SIM itself, which is getting smaller and easier to embed in a greater variety of devices at ever lower component cost. And then we've got this ability to pick our networks and then maybe switch our networks over time. And you mentioned earlier on the the EIM, so the eSIM IoT manager. >> Yeah. >> Um and all uh eSIM OS um organizations such as yourself will will have one of those. And I gather that your orchestration platform um is uh the name has suddenly escaped me. I knew what it was called. >> Our pulse. >> Pulse. Thank you. >> Um what's the secret sauce to making that perfect pane of glass that creates the ideal user experience for the customer when it comes to managing their portfolio of SIM lines? >> Yeah, so um so Kigen pulse, I think the key thing there is the APIs. So uh so yes, we have our own pane uh of glass, sure, and you can absolutely use that and it's really useful, but actually the real benefit is the the APIs. So we we allow you to integrate with APIs and and thus bring it into your system. So think about the device makers where instead of having to run the software yourself, cuz it's a little tricky although very possible but not very little tricky. So we run the software for you. You can interface to the APIs. So you can integrate it into your uh now your device management system, uh your enterprise system. So you so you can now very seamlessly integrate it. So that's I think the key thing for the key differentiation for us is everything you can do with our when UI, you can also do with an API. And again, the UI is great for the the initial uh photo typing, but if you at some point now uh an eSIM say for instance you want all your eSIMs in Germany to switch from uh from MNOA to MNOB because you got a better deal, you want to integrate it into your enterprise software. Uh you want us to go all the eSIMs in this country, switch them. So that's now the differentiation in our UI is the API. >> The API. >> Our UI uh um designers in my company will be a little unhappy cuz our UI is lovely. It looks looks great. Um and I know know, very useful for uh for that initial sign up and and making sure it works. But, then eventually, you know, you uh the integration on the API level is better. And then, you can do things like campaign um uh management. I want all these eSIMs in this country to switch over. And that that's all API-based and and enables you to uh to integrate it into your own system. >> Right. Right. Right. So, I think it's publicly stated that uh Kigen's enabled 2.5 billion SIMs around the world. Um, I don't know what the portion of those that are IoT SIMs is. Um, maybe you do. But, how do you see eSIM and remote re-provisioning boosting your business and the amount of SIMs out there that you will have in a >> Yeah, so uh so, that's no, SIMs. It's not not necessarily say the eSIMs, the 2.5 billion. I'd say the eSIMs are growing really fast. So, we're probably, you know, I think I think approaching 70 to 200 million eSIMs. Um, I think the key thing there is that um 4 years ago, probably 10% of our business was eSIMs and 90% was still SIMs. Uh now, this is kind of almost flipping the last quarter. No, um I'll share a secret with you, but the last quarter, we did about 70% of our revenue is now eSIM-based revenue. >> Okay. Thanks for sharing. I won't tell anybody else. >> No, no. Don't tell anybody. No, between me and the others. I'm sure you're all happy to to sign a little NDA with no, seriously. Uh so, we can see that the business is is flipping really quickly uh from uh from the the SIM. And the SIM is more that that was the original uh heritage of the business uh we when we originally started uh uh the business around now understanding how to manage mobile profiles. But, we quickly, you know, started uh looking really at the eSIM space cuz we we believe that's the right uh solution. We also think that the eSIMs uh is now is very different. A SIM tends to be owned by the MNO, but an eSIM, because it's software down in your device, tends to be owned by the device maker. And the device maker have different different problems. They have different uh challenges. For instance, one of the challenges for device makers, you put a SIM in and your connectivity, do you want this connectivity to start from day one, or do you want to start start from when when your device gets into the hands of your of your customer? And probably the latter. So, yes, always difficult now. And and there I kind of you have to think about how do you provision that eSIM? And we have been coming up with something that we call a factory provisioning, which allows you to provision the SIM the eSIM very late into your supply chain, even into your shop if you if you know if you all the way to actually selling your devices, uh and you can know make sure you don't have to pay for connectivity before you actually start using it. And your your device doesn't get a uh best by date. So, really thinking about what the requirements are for those device makers is what we've been been focusing on uh >> Right. Right. No, that's really interesting cuz one of my next questions was going to be we've got SGP 32. Uh is that all we need, or are we going to need something more? Is there more standardization required? Is there further development we can be able to make use of in the IoT? >> Um I think the standard will develop, so there will be some more features in SGP 32 itself. So, that as standards now, there was >> mentioned the factory provisioning >> Yeah, yeah, I'm going to that in a second. So, so um then there is also an SGP uh thing is 42. Now, I'm I'm not the uh the expert here, but I think it's uh the 42 is a factory provisioning standard. Uh and that's being also being standardized by the GSMA, which effectively allows you to have a uh blank eSIM. Uh you can solder down in your device. The blank eSIM has no connectivity. Um but just before you ship uh to your customer, you can then with a small tool update it very securely uh to have the right connectivity. So, the device arrives uh at your customer with the right connectivity. Uh but also not pre have to pre load it cuz some of the uh solutions you have to pre load it, but very often because the MNO will start incurring cost as soon as you pre load it, um uh they will want to charge you, or maybe you know the uh it's already starts uh using some data you don't want. So, you can do that much later. For this, the industry is doing SGP 30 42. Um kind of we have our own standard for now, but we will also comply. and we are one of the drivers who had they 42 standard as well to make sure that that that over time this all works within the industry. So that is yes, definitely something we're working on to get that right. Right, right, right. So when that extra 42 standard is ready, you're already going to prepared your services to be compliant and it to really really We're following the standard to making sure that we are. So I think they they used to call it HD ready. So we are STP 42 That means we're not fully compliant yet because the standard isn't done yet, but as soon as the standard is done, we will update and then we're we're keeping it keeping in check just with that standard. So it's interesting that we've moved from the concept of lock-ins from operators and the need for truck rolls to switch out Sims in IoT devices to now the EIM being the point of control. Does it create a new kind of lock-in? >> Sorry? >> Does it create a new kind of lock-in? >> No, the EIM has been designed to be able to to design it out to effectively switch it out. So you can have first of all you can have more than one EIM. So the device can have the original EIM and a second EIM. There is multiple slots, but also there is a you can test that and we are testing that. There is a command for the EIM to replace the original EIM with a new EIM. And because it's only the management, it isn't as integrated with the MNOs as some of the other software you need. So this is the like the already the QR codes go to. It's called an SMB plus. It downloads the the profile connectivity profile from the MNO, but the EIM works with all of that. So because that software is separated, it effectively allows you to very easily switch. Now we don't think that the software is particularly Oh. Particularly not differentiating. I think it's pretty similar. We have some additional features. Other customers other competitors will have some other other We think it is in a much a, you know, a management layer that's that you can switch. I'm not sure if you actually need to switch it, but it's absolutely there in the standards and and being tested at home. >> Well, it's definitely technology that everybody's talking about in the IoT right now. Everyone's very excited about it. People have been waiting for it. They've been waiting for folks like you to be able to serve it to them and I think we're all excited to see what devices now come to market and what people will do with them. So, thanks for that masterclass on all things SIM and SIM software related. Thank you, Vincent. >> Well, thank you very much. It was wasn't a masterclass, but a a slightly more more expert maybe than than the average Joe. >> Thank you. >> Thank you.

metadata.title: Bare-Metal GPU Clouds vs Hyperscalers: Why startups are fleeing AWS and Azure?
metadata.author: The gpuMaster
metadata.shortDescription:
Why are AI startups ditching tech giants like AWS and Azure for bare-metal GPU clouds?

In this video, we break down the brutal infrastructure economics of building AI products. While traditional public clouds were built for general-purpose workloads, massive GPU clusters act more like distributed supercomputers.

When virtualized layers introduce latency and keep expensive GPUs stalled, your cloud costs skyrocket. We dive deep into the hardware reality from PCIe topologies and NUMA nodes to NCCL communication to explain why the ultimate battle in tech right now isn't Amazon vs Microsoft, it’s Abstraction vs physical control.

TIMESTAMPS:
00:00 The Economics of AI Infrastructure
02:18 Inside a Modern AI Server
03:44 The Hidden Hardware Bottlenecks
05:30 The Hyperscaler Trade-Off
06:27 The Bare-Metal Advantage
07:54 Metrics That Actually Matter
09:58 The Rise of Hybrid Architectures

ADDITIONAL TOPICS COVERED:
- Bare-metal GPU clouds vs public hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, GCP)
- AI infrastructure economics and GPU cluster cloud costs
- GPU virtualization latency vs physical hardware control
- PCIe topologies and NUMA node optimization for AI workloads
- NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) bottlenecks
- Distributed supercomputing architecture for LLM training

segments.text: A startup can spend millions of
dollars building an AI product—and still
discover that its biggest technical
problem isn't the model.
It's infrastructure economics.
Traditional public clouds were designed
around general-purpose workloads: virtual machines,
storage,
databases,
web applications and elastic services.
GPU-heavy artificial intelligence is different.
A single training job can consume dozens,
hundreds,
or even thousands of accelerators.
Those GPUs don't operate independently.
They behave more like a distributed supercomputer.
And when a workload depends on moving
enormous amounts of data between GPUs,
the difference between virtualized cloud
infrastructure and dedicated bare-metal
infrastructure can become extremely expensive.
A CPU workload can often tolerate
virtualization overhead,
variable latency and occasional resource contention.
Large-scale GPU workloads are far less forgiving.
If an expensive GPU spends time waiting
for another GPU,
memory,
storage or network communication,
you're still paying for that GPU.
That changes the economics.
This is why some AI startups are
evaluating dedicated GPU clouds,
bare metal,
colocation,
reserved capacity—and even owning
physical infrastructure.
The real question isn't whether
hyperscalers are technically capable.
They are.
The question is: Does a general-purpose
cloud abstraction remain economically
optimal when your workload starts behaving
like a supercomputer?
To understand the difference,
forget the marketing terminology and look
at the hardware.
A modern AI server is fundamentally a
high-bandwidth data movement system.
You have the CPU,
system memory,
GPUs,
high-bandwidth HBM,
PCIe or another accelerator interconnect,
and high-speed networking.
The performance of the system depends not
only on GPU compute,
but on how efficiently data moves through
every layer.
During training,
GPUs load tensors from HBM,
process them,
and frequently exchange results with
other GPUs.
This is where technologies such as NCCL
become critical.
NCCL supports collective operations
including AllReduce,
AllGather,
ReduceScatter and Broadcast.
During distributed training,
communication and synchronization can
become major components of total execution time.
Imagine eight GPUs inside one server.
If the GPUs have enormous memory
bandwidth but the interconnect is constrained,
they can spend significant time waiting
for communication.
Now multiply that across multiple servers.
You introduce NICs,
switches,
optical links,
routing,
congestion and additional latency.
Suddenly,
the physical cluster topology becomes
part of the application's performance model.
This is one reason bare metal can be attractive.
The operator has much greater control
over GPU-to-GPU topology, CPU NUMA placement,
PCIe topology, NIC placement, GPU affinity,
Memory locality, Network fabric, Storage,
Firmware, and the Linux kernel.
NUMA isn't theoretical.
If a process accesses memory attached to
a remote NUMA node,
latency characteristics change.
If a GPU and NIC are attached through
different PCIe paths,
communication can become less efficient.
And if data constantly moves between host
memory and GPU memory,
PCIe bandwidth can become another bottleneck.
Memory capacity creates another challenge.
When a model exceeds local GPU memory,
engineers may use tensor parallelism,
pipeline parallelism,
parameter sharding,
activation checkpointing or CPU offload.
But every additional technique can
introduce more communication and synchronization.
So saying,
'We need more GPUs,' is incomplete.
The real question is: How are those GPUs connected?
Two clusters can have the same GPUs and
produce very different results.
The difference can be the network,
PCIe topology,
memory locality or communication overhead.
The VM abstraction hides much of this
physical reality.
For tightly coupled AI workloads,
however,
that physical reality can determine performance.
At eight GPUs,
topology is manageable.
At dozens,
network architecture becomes critical.
At hundreds or thousands,
the network fabric becomes part of the

fabrics. You don't replace physical

GPU availability.

metadata.title: The Cloud Was a Lie (Why Senior Engineers Are Going Back to Bare Metal)
metadata.author: Nick Gioftsos
metadata.shortDescription:
We moved everything to the cloud to make infrastructure easier—instead, it is quietly making us worse engineers. 

While managed services in Azure and AWS are incredible for scale, relying 100% on cloud abstractions hides the failure domain, taxes your curiosity with pay-as-you-go billing, and turns systems engineers into button-clickers. 

In this video, we break down why the "cloud-native" illusion creates dangerous blind spots in production—and how building a silent, $200 bare-metal homelab (using Proxmox VE, a NAS, and real network segmentation) is the single biggest unfair advantage left for your IT and cloud career.

⏱️ CHAPTERS:
0:00 The $4,000 Cloud Wake-Up Call
0:45 The "Cloud-Native" Illusion (Why Abstraction Is a Trap)
2:15 The Tax on Curiosity (Why Pay-As-You-Go Kills Learning)
3:45 The $200 Bare-Metal Homelab Blueprint (Proxmox + NAS + VLANs)
5:30 Group A vs. Group B Engineers (Who Survives an Outage?)

📖 MY BOOK
The Two-Person Rule: A Techno-Thriller
https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HMFRK5C4

🌐 WEBSITE
https://www.gioftsos.com

💡 KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Cloud certifications teach you how to navigate a vendor's menu. Bare metal teaches you how to cook.
• Real production issues don't happen in a 45-minute cloud lab tutorial—they happen on Day 90 when logs fill up `/var` and certificates expire.
• Owning a low-power Mini PC running Proxmox VE and a dedicated NAS lets you break DNS, test bare-metal restores, and master Linux/networking for $0/month.

👇 JOIN THE DISCUSSION:
If you already run a homelab, drop your exact hardware and hypervisor setup in the comments! And if you haven't built one yet, what is holding you back?

#CloudEngineering #Homelab #SysAdmin #Proxmox #Azure #SystemAdministrator #BareMetal #DevOps #SelfHosted #ITCareer

segments.text: This tiny box cost me $200 once.
Last month, a client paid $4,000 to run the exact same
workload in the cloud.
And here is the worst part.
The engineers managing that $4,000 cloud environment couldn't
tell me how the underlying storage worked.
They couldn't trace a dropped packet,
and when the cloud provider had a minor regional hiccup
on a Friday afternoon, the entire team sat on a call for
three hours doing nothing because you cannot fix a black
box that you don't own.
We were sold a massive lie over the last decade.
We were told that physical hardware is dead, that running your own
servers is legacy, and that clicking buttons in a web portal
or writing 50 lines of YAML to rent someone else's computer
makes you a modern engineer.
It doesn't. It just makes you a high-paid cloud tenant.
And right now, a quiet rebellion is happening across the
industry. From giant tech companies
pulling their workloads off the cloud to save millions,
to senior engineers building bare-metal home labs in their
living rooms. People are waking up to a brutal reality.
If you only know how to build in the cloud,
you are building your career on rented land.
Hi, I'm Nick. I work as a systems and cloud engineer,
I build in Azure, and I manage Microsoft 365 tenants.
I'm not an anti-cloud dinosaur.
Put my cloud credentials aside for a second,
because today we need to talk about the hidden tax the
cloud is taking on your skills, your wallet,
and your career. And why building a cheap bare-metal home
lab this weekend is the single biggest unfair advantage
left in tech. Let's be completely honest about what cloud
native actually did to our industry.
10 years ago, if you wanted to deploy an application,
you had to understand the entire stack.
You had to know how Linux handled memory.
You had to know how VLANs segmented traffic on a switch.
You had to know what happened when a drive in a RAID
array started throwing bad sectors.
Today you click "deploy managed database",
you slide a bar from two vCPUs to three,
and the cloud provider wraps all the messy complicated
physics of computing inside a shiny,
idiot-proof API. Now, for businesses that want to move
fast, that abstraction is magic.
For an engineer who wants to stay relevant,
that abstraction is poison.
Because here is what nobody tells junior and mid-level
engineers. When you outsource the complexity,
you also outsource your value.
Think about it. If your entire skill set is knowing which
buttons to click in the Azure portal or which Terraform
module to copy-paste to spin up a managed service,
what happens when an AI agent can generate that exact Terraform
file in 4 seconds? What happens when the portal changes
its UI? Cloud certifications teach you how to navigate
a vendor's menu. Bare metal teaches you how it works,
and the moment an abstraction leaks,
the moment a VM starts throttling disk IOPS for no
reason, or a hybrid VPN tunnel drops packets because of
an MTU mismatch, the engineers who only know the menu
completely freeze. There's a second reason.
Pure cloud engineers are losing their edge and nobody
talks about it. The meter is always running.
Remember how the previous generation of legendary sysadmins
learned their craft?
They took two old PCs, put them under their desk,
installed Linux, and left them running for a year.
They broke things, they tried weird routing protocols
at midnight just to see what would happen.
Try doing that in AWS or Azure today.
Want to spin up a proper virtual network gateway
or a firewall, two domain controllers
and a storage cluster to test real-world architecture?
The second you hit deploy, a virtual taximeter starts
ticking. Every public IP costs money,
every gigabyte of outbound traffic costs money,
every snapshot costs money.
So what do you do? You follow a sanitized step-by-step
tutorial for 45 minutes, and then you immediately run
terraform destroy, because you are terrified of waking
up to a $400 credit card bill at the end of the month.
You cannot master systems engineering when you are afraid
to leave the system turned on.
Real production problems don't happen in the first 45
minutes of a clean deployment.
Real problems happen on day 90, when logs fill up the
/var partition, certificates expire silently,
and memory leaks slowly choke a daemon to death.
You only see those problems when you own the hardware.
And it runs 24/7 for a few bucks a month.
Now, when I say build a home lab, half of you are picturing
a massive, screaming 42U Dell server rack in your closet
that sounds like a jet engine and doubles your electric bill.
Forget that. That's 2010 homelabbing.
In 2026, a production-grade engineering lab fits in the
palm of your hand and pulls around 15 watts from the wall.
Here is the exact blueprint that separates button clickers
from real engineers. First, get one silent mini PC and
put Proxmox VE on it.
Not Windows with VirtualBox, not a cloud trial,
a bare-metal type 1 hypervisor.
Why? Because the first time you pass a physical network
card or a USB controller directly through to a virtual
machine, you finally understand what the cloud is doing
behind the curtain when it provisions an instance for
you. Second, separate your compute from your storage.
Pair that mini PC with a dedicated NAS running Btrfs or
ZFS. Mount your storage over the network using NFS or
iSCSI. Suddenly, cloud block storage isn't a mysterious
marketing word anymore.
You see the latency on the wire.
You see what happens to your VMs when the storage network
hypervisor to your NAS and actually test restoring a dead
VM from scratch on a Saturday morning,
you gain a level of operational confidence you can never
buy from a multiple choice certification exam.
Third, break your own network.
Put a real router and a managed switch between your lab
and your home internet.
Build VLANs. Lock down firewall rules between your lab subnet
and your Wi-Fi. Run your own local DNS
and reverse proxy. I promise you this.
The afternoon you accidentally misconfigure a VLAN
tag, take down the internet in your own house,
and have to fix it from the command line before anyone
notices, you will learn more about networking in 30 minutes
than in 40 hours of watching video courses.
Let's zoom out for a second.
Why does this matter so much right now?
Because the tech industry is splitting into two groups.
Group A is relying on high-level abstractions:
managed cloud services on the one side,
AI code generation on the other.
They are moving faster than ever until they hit a wall
that isn't covered in the documentation.
Group B uses those exact same modern tools.
They use Azure, they use automation,
they run local LLMs on their own hardware,
but they still understand the physics of the machine underneath.
Quick side note. This exact disconnect,
what happens when engineers trust automated infrastructure
so blindly that nobody remembers how the physical doors,
power, and switches actually work is the whole premise
behind my techno-thriller novel, The Two-Person Rule.
Because in the real world, automation always fails at
the worst possible moment.
Let's get back to it.
When an outage hits production at 2 in the morning,
nobody on the incident bridge cares how many cloud badges
you posted on LinkedIn.
They care about who can open a terminal,
read the logs, trace the network path,
and figure out why the system is choking.
The cloud isn't going away.
It is an incredible tool for scale,
global reach and enterprise workflows.
Use it every day. I do.
Just don't let a cloud vendor's abstraction layer become
the ceiling of your technical competence.
Stop renting 100% of your curiosity,
buy a cheap piece of metal, install Linux without a GUI,
break your own DNS, and become the engineer who actually
knows how the machine works when the dashboard goes dark.
If you already run a home lab, drop your exact setup in
the comments. I read every single one of them,
and if you haven't built one yet, tell me what is holding
you back. Take care of yourselves, and I'll see you in
the next one.

What happens when the portal changes its UI? Cloud certifications teach you how to navigate a vendor's menu. Bare metal teaches you how it works, and the moment an abstraction leaks, the moment a VM starts throttling disk IOPS for no reason, or a hybrid VPN tunnel drops packets because of an MTU mismatch, the engineers who only know the menu completely freeze. There's a second reason. Pure cloud engineers are losing their edge and nobody talks about it. The meter is always running. Remember how the previous generation of legendary sysadmins learned their craft? They took two old PCs, put them under their desk, installed Linux, and left them running for a year. They broke things, they tried weird routing protocols at midnight just to see what would happen. Try doing that in AWS or Azure today. Want to spin up a proper virtual network gateway or a firewall, two domain controllers and a storage cluster to test real-world architecture? The second you hit deploy, a virtual taximeter starts ticking. Every public IP costs money, every gigabyte of outbound traffic costs money, every snapshot costs money. So what do you do? You follow a sanitized step-by-step tutorial for 45 minutes, and then you immediately run terraform destroy, because you are terrified of waking up to a $400 credit card bill at the end of the month. You cannot master systems engineering when you are afraid to leave the system turned on. Real production problems don't happen in the first 45 minutes of a clean deployment. Real problems happen on day 90, when logs fill up the /var partition, certificates expire silently, and memory leaks slowly choke a daemon to death. You only see those problems when you own the hardware. And it runs 24/7 for a few bucks a month. Now, when I say build a home lab, half of you are picturing a massive, screaming 42U Dell server rack in your closet that sounds like a jet engine and doubles your electric bill. Forget that. That's 2010 homelabbing. In 2026, a production-grade engineering lab fits in the palm of your hand and pulls around 15 watts from the wall. Here is the exact blueprint that separates button clickers from real engineers. First, get one silent mini PC and put Proxmox VE on it. Not Windows with VirtualBox, not a cloud trial, a bare-metal type 1 hypervisor. Why? Because the first time you pass a physical network card or a USB controller directly through to a virtual machine, you finally understand what the cloud is doing behind the curtain when it provisions an instance for you. Second, separate your compute from your storage. Pair that mini PC with a dedicated NAS running Btrfs or ZFS. Mount your storage over the network using NFS or iSCSI. Suddenly, cloud block storage isn't a mysterious marketing word anymore. You see the latency on the wire. You see what happens to your VMs when the storage network hypervisor to your NAS and actually test restoring a dead VM from scratch on a Saturday morning, you gain a level of operational confidence you can never buy from a multiple choice certification exam. Third, break your own network. Put a real router and a managed switch between your lab and your home internet. Build VLANs. Lock down firewall rules between your lab subnet and your Wi-Fi. Run your own local DNS and reverse proxy. I promise you this. The afternoon you accidentally misconfigure a VLAN tag, take down the internet in your own house, and have to fix it from the command line before anyone notices, you will learn more about networking in 30 minutes than in 40 hours of watching video courses. Let's zoom out for a second. Why does this matter so much right now? Because the tech industry is splitting into two groups. Group A is relying on high-level abstractions: managed cloud services on the one side, AI code generation on the other. They are moving faster than ever until they hit a wall that isn't covered in the documentation. Group B uses those exact same modern tools. They use Azure, they use automation, they run local LLMs on their own hardware, but they still understand the physics of the machine underneath. Quick side note. This exact disconnect, what happens when engineers trust automated infrastructure so blindly that nobody remembers how the physical doors, power, and switches actually work is the whole premise behind my techno-thriller novel, The Two-Person Rule. Because in the real world, automation always fails at the worst possible moment. Let's get back to it. When an outage hits production at 2 in the morning, nobody on the incident bridge cares how many cloud badges you posted on LinkedIn. They care about who can open a terminal, read the logs, trace the network path, and figure out why the system is choking. The cloud isn't going away. It is an incredible tool for scale, global reach and enterprise workflows. Use it every day. I do. Just don't let a cloud vendor's abstraction layer become the ceiling of your technical competence. Stop renting 100% of your curiosity, buy a cheap piece of metal, install Linux without a GUI, break your own DNS, and become the engineer who actually knows how the machine works when the dashboard goes dark. If you already run a home lab, drop your exact setup in the comments. I read every single one of them, and if you haven't built one yet, tell me what is holding you back. Take care of yourselves, and I'll see you in the next one.

metadata.title: I Ran a 2.8 Trillion AI on Two Used RTX 3090s (Did NOT Expect This)
metadata.author: Remy Runs
metadata.shortDescription:
I Ran a 2.8 Trillion AI on Two Used RTX 3090s (Did NOT Expect This)

Can two used RTX 3090s really run Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion parameter local LLM that supposedly needs a $40,000 machine? A homelab build with 48GB of VRAM and Intel Optane memory got it running at about 3 tokens a second. This is a buying guide to local AI hardware that compares a Mac Studio, Nvidia's DGX Spark, that Optane server build and single-card setups, priced and timed against the same wait.

Memory prices, retired parts and AI subscriptions all keep changing the math on running AI at home. So the real question is what to spend, or whether to spend anything at all.

The numbers come from manufacturer spec sheets and official pricing, retailer and used-market listings, owner measurements posted on forums, public benchmarks and llama.cpp documentation, and published API and subscription pricing.

In this video you'll find:

🔹 The cart problem: two used cards, about $1,600 each, and a headline that makes a huge model look affordable. What was left out of that headline?
🔹 Why 48 GB can touch a 1.5 TB file: how a mixture-of-experts model and one llama.cpp flag change what your VRAM actually has to hold.
🔹 The card beats the server memory: a 2020 gaming card moves far more data per second than a fully loaded server socket. Memory bandwidth, not raw compute, sets the pace.
🔹 What 3 tokens a second feels like: a 500-word answer used as a ruler, plus the hidden wait before the first word appears.
🔹 Six machines, one ruler: Mac Studio, DGX Spark, the Optane build and single-card tiers, each with its real price, speed and catch.
🔹 The parts are disappearing: retired Optane memory and a record jump in server RAM prices change what is realistic to build.
🔹 Build, rent or tweak for free: a cost comparison with API pricing, and one no-cost setting to try if you already own a card.
🔹 What happened to the cart: the final decision, and the resale number that made it easy.

💬 Would you pay for hardware to run a huge model at home at 3 tokens a second, or rent it by the word? And at what price would you sell the GPU you own today?

⚠️ Prices and speeds are compiled from manufacturers, retailers and other people's published tests at the time of recording, and they change quickly, so check them before you buy. This is not financial advice, and there are no sponsors or affiliate links.

🔔 Subscribe and turn on the bell so you don't miss the next local AI hardware video.

#KimiK3 #RTX3090 #LocalLLM

Modern GPUs spend far more picajoules moving weights across millimeter wires than multiplying matrices — turning the 2,048-bit HBM4 interface and local silicon bridges (CoWoS-L) into the true determinant of token-per-second throughput.
Hosted by Penelope "Nell" VonHousen.

📺 CATCH YESTERDAY'S DROP FROM MY MATE MAX ON @ZeroRiskBro:
▸ When Two Nobel Laureates Nearly Detonated the Global Financial System: https://youtu.be/A2nMlEWavHg

Inside TSMC's Zhunan cleanroom, a $40,000 dual-die AI assembly can be ruined in milliseconds by a microscopic thermal warp. While Wall Street fixates on FLOPS, modern GPUs spend far more picajoules moving weights across millimeter wires than multiplying matrices. Nell VonHousen breaks down the Roofline Model, the 858mm2 photomask reticle limit, TSMC's CoWoS-L Local Silicon Interconnect (LSI), JEDEC's 2,048-bit HBM4 specification, and the thermal dissipation barrier threatening next-generation AI clusters. Chapters: 0:00 The 85% Idle Paradox 0:12 Bunker Dossier & The FLOPS Mirage 2:30 The Zhunan Cleanroom Scrap Crisis 2:45 Picajoules, Reticle Limits & CoWoS-L Bridges 5:15 HBM3e & HBM4: The 2,048-Bit Skyscraper 7:00 The 85C Thermal Dissipation Wall 7:20 SK Hynix MR-MUF vs Hybrid Bonding Endgame. Sources: Tom's Hardware CoWoS capacity report, JEDEC HBM4 standard specifications, IEEE solid-state circuit energy telemetry.

02:53 The Structural Mechanism (Arithmetic Intensity)
06:29 Hidden Leverage & Choke Point (Euv Photomask)
11:10 Systemic Contagion & Fallout (2,048-Bit Hbm4 Bus)
15:07 What Breaks Next (Nanoparticle Epoxy)

metadata.title: The Fast SSD Offload Myth: Why Running Local AI from NVMe Fails
metadata.author: Byte Forensics
metadata.shortDescription:
You don't have enough GPU memory for the 70B model you want. But your PC has a blistering 7,000 MB/s Gen4 NVMe SSD. Can you just offload the model weights to storage and run it?

In this episode of Byte Forensics, we expose the SSD offload myth. We calculate the exact physics of autoregressive token generation: why generating a single word requires pulling every single model weight across the PCIe bus, and why a 140x bandwidth deficit turns interactive AI into an unusable crawl.

⏱️ CHAPTER TIMESTAMPS
00:00 Introduction & The Core Puzzle
01:15 The Claim: Those Devices Have Different
02:26 The Limit: In A Typical Transformer Layer,
03:33 The Claim: In The Same Way, Software Can P...
04:42 The Comparison: If You Need A Model To Run
06:00 The Point: So How Can You Evaluate An Offload
07:07 How It Works: Observe Storage Reads, Avail...
08:23 The Limit: For Live Voice Chat, Coding
09:28 The Claim: If The Second Launch Is Dramati...
10:36 The Comparison: The Ability To Complete A ...
11:43 The Point: Then Decide Whether The Result

🔬 KEY TECHNICAL TAKEAWAYS:
• Autoregressive Memory Physics: Generating a single token requires reading EVERY parameter in the model once. For a 70B model, that is 35GB to 140GB of data per token.
• The 140x Bandwidth Chasm: RTX 4090 GDDR6X operates at 1,008 GB/s. High-end PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSDs cap at ~7.0 GB/s. That is a 144x throughput collapse.
• Real-World Token Speeds: At 7 GB/s, reading a 35GB Q4 70B model takes 5.0 seconds per token (0.2 tok/s), while in VRAM it runs at 35-45 tok/s.
• Hardware Rule: Storage is for persistent cold weights. Never treat an SSD as dynamic execution memory.

Channel: @ByteForensics
Website & Hardware Guides: https://github.com/jibranpcccc/byte-forensics-pipeline

segments.text: You don't have enough GPU memory for the
model you want, but your computer has a
huge NVMe SSD.
You look at the storage specification,
see an impressive transfer rate headline
and think you've discovered a shortcut.
What if the model could sit on the drive
and stream into the graphics card when
needed?
Same big model, smaller GPU, problem
solved. Then you try an offloading
configuration. The model finally
launches, and the first answer feels
like it is being typed through a straw.
Your drive is fast.
Your computer is powerful. So why does
the experience feel slow? The problem is
that storage capacity, memory capacity,
and computation are three different
resources.
Moving a model between them can make an
otherwise impossible workload possible.
It cannot make the slowest part of that
path disappear. Today we'll trace a
request through SSD, system RAM, and GPU
memory.
We'll distinguish memory mapping from
active offloading, explain why loading
time is not generation speed, and show
when offloading is useful enough to
justify the trade. Start with the
hierarchy.
An SSD stores files persistently. System
RAM holds data the CPU can access
quickly while programs run. GPU VRAM
holds data and working state near the
graphics processor.
Those devices have different capacities,
access patterns, latency, bandwidth, and
communication paths. One may be very
good at moving large blocks of
information.
Another may be designed for enormous
numbers of repeated calculations on data
already nearby.
A storage benchmark showing fast
sequential reads does not tell you how
quickly an inference engine can fetch
many small chunks,
move them over a bus, transform them
into the required format, and run the
next layer. A model is not a movie file
that can always be streamed ahead in a
simple, uninterrupted sequence.
The access pattern depends on its
architecture and how the runtime
schedules computation. Consider model
loading first. A model file sits on
disk.
The runtime the weights or maps them
into its address space.
A memory map file can allow the
operating system to load pages as needed
and already read pages may remain in the
operating system's file cache. This can
improve startup behavior and avoid some
copying.
But the file cache is not magic extra
VRAM. If a page is not resident and must
be fetched again, the drive is back in
the critical path. Now consider the
active calculation.
In a typical transformer layer, the
system uses many weights to transform
current activations. If those weights
reside in GPU VRAM, the GPU can read
them from nearby high bandwidth memory.
If some weights live in system RAM, they
may need to be processed on the CPU or
transferred toward the GPU when a layer
runs.
If they live on disk, getting them into
usable memory can add another step.
That's the difference between a model
fitting somewhere and a model running
efficiently.
A configuration that fits weights across
devices may satisfy the first
requirement while struggling with the
second. Let's use a simple analogy.
Imagine a restaurant where the chef
works at a counter.
Ingredients on the counter are
immediately available. Ingredients in
the pantry require a walk. Ingredients
at a warehouse require a delivery.
A large warehouse lets the restaurant
stock more food than fits in the
kitchen. It is not guaranteed dinner
arrives faster when every dish requires
repeated warehouse deliveries. There's
an important nuance.
The chef might prepare a whole batch
while ingredients are in the kitchen or
the restaurant might arrange deliveries
in advance.
In the same way, software can prefetch,
cache, batch, and overlap data transfers
with computation. These techniques can
reduce overhead.
They do not eliminate capacity and
bandwidth limits, and their
effectiveness depends on the access
pattern. This is why the phrase CPU
offload can mean different things.
In one runtime, layers may execute on
the CPU because the GPU doesn't hold
their weights. In another, weights may
be staged through CPU memory to be
processed on the accelerator.
Other frameworks support disk offload
for weights that do not fit GPU and RAM
combined. Some systems even specialize
in expert weight placement for mixture
of experts models.
of these mechanisms implies that a drive
is pretending to be native GPU memory.
You need to inspect what the
implementation actually does.
The word offload describes placement and
movement. It does not specify
performance. And here's where a fast SSD
can still make a meaningful difference.
If the bottleneck is loading a model
into memory once, a faster drive may
reduce that weight. If you swap between
many large checkpoints, fast storage can
improve the workflow.
If you need a model to run at all and
accept slow responses, disk offload
might turn impossible into possible.
That's valuable even when it doesn't
produce interactive speed.
But if each generated token requires
repeated access to weights outside GPU
memory, the cost can recur during
decoding.
The drive may be excellent at a
sequential file read and still be a poor
substitute for the memory hierarchy a
GPU expects. There's another familiar
trick, buying more system RAM.
More RAM can let the operating system
keep more model pages resident, reducing
repeated disk reads. It may also let a
CPU-based runtime run a larger model
entirely from RAM.
That can be a sensible choice for
occasional offline jobs, but RAM
capacity does not automatically provide
VRM level bandwidth, accelerator
kernels, or the GPU's arithmetic
throughput.
A second trap is confusing model weights
with all runtime memory. Even if you
place some weights on disk or CPU, you
still need room for activations, back
end buffers, attention state, and cache.
In long conversations, the key value
cache may grow. Offloading weights does
not guarantee that other allocations
suddenly fit. Some engines support cache
offloading or quantization, but those
are separate settings and tradeoffs.
So how can you evaluate an offload
configuration without guessing? Begin
with a fixed model and a fixed prompt.
Record the model file size, total system
RAM, available GPU VRAM, runtime
version, and every offload related
setting. Then run three scenarios if
your software supports them.
In the first scenario, use as much GPU
placement as your available VRAM safely
allows. Leave enough headroom for the
cache and other allocations.
In the second, lower the number of GPU
resident layers or weights. In the
third, test an explicit disk offload
path if your framework supports one.
Do not pretend that every backend
implements all three choices
identically. Measure the time from
launch to readiness, then measure time
to first token for the same prompt.
Finally, measure output tokens per
second after generation begins. Those
three numbers tell very different
stories. A faster SSD can improve launch
time while barely changing ongoing token
generation.
A CPU-heavy path might launch easily but
have different decoding behavior. Also
watch the write system counters.
Observe storage reads, available RAM,
page faults if your tools expose them,
GPU memory allocation, and GPU
utilization. If the drive is busy only
at model startup, it may not be your
decoding bottleneck.
If repeated disk activity accompanies
each slow generated token, storage
movement deserves investigation. These
observations are clues, not proof until
you compare controlled runs. Now repeat
the test with a longer prompt.
You may discover the memory layout that
works for a short question fails when
the KV cache grows. That's not the SSD
getting worse. It's the total working
set changing.
You may have solved weight capacity but
not context capacity. A good workflow
also needs a quality check.
If different offload modes are supposed
to compute the same model, use
deterministic settings where available
and compare outputs. Small numerical
differences can occur across backends
and precision choices.
Unexpectedly different answers may also
reveal an accidental model or
quantization change. Don't compare speed
unless you know you're comparing the
intended workload.
For occasional batch processing,
tolerating a long wait might be
perfectly rational. A document analysis
job that runs overnight may value
capacity more than responsiveness.
For live voice chat, coding assistance,
or a server serving multiple people,
slow token generation may make the same
configuration unusable.
The best architecture depends on the
patience of the user and the frequency
of the task. There's also a budgeting
lesson.
If buying an SSD only improves loading,
it may be the wrong upgrade for a
decoding problem. If you routinely run
out of system RAM while caching weights,
more RAM might help.
If most computation is stuck on a slow
offload path, a GPU with more usable
VRAM or a smaller, well-quantized model
may change the experience more
substantially. Measure before buying.
Never confuse a huge virtual address
space with a huge pool of physical,
equally fast memory. Operating systems
are clever, but they cannot remove every
cost of moving bytes between devices.
Here's a diagnostic many people skip.
Compare a cold start and a warm start.
On the cold start, the operating system
may need to read much of the model file
from storage.
On the warm start, some pages may
already live in RAM as file cache.
If the second launch is dramatically
faster, that's evidence about caching
and loading, not automatically about the
neural network's compute speed.
For a fair comparison, document which
state you're measuring and avoid making
invasive changes to the operating system
just to force a particular result. Next,
distinguish sequential reads from random
or repeated reads.
An SSD specification often emphasizes
large, orderly transfers under favorable
conditions. Real offloading can involve
smaller operations, synchronization, and
memory copy overhead.
Even a drive with great headline
bandwidth cannot make a poorly scheduled
series of transfers disappear.
Tools that measure transferred bytes and
IO weight can help reveal whether
storage is active in the slow face.
There's also a dangerous
misunderstanding about swap files.
Increasing virtual memory can sometimes
prevent an out-of-memory crash by
allowing the operating system to move
pages out of RAM. But heavy swapping can
turn an interactive workload into an
unresponsive one.
It is not the same as adding physical
RAM, and it certainly isn't the same as
adding GPU VRAM.
The ability to complete a task and the
ability to complete it comfortably are
separate outcomes. One final buying
test, price an upgrade against the
bottleneck you measured.
If the model fits in system RAM and CPU
execution is the main limit, a faster
SSD might have little effect after
loading.
If the issue is repeated disk paging,
more RAM could help keep the working set
resident. If the problem is GPU offload
transfer overhead, a smaller
quantization or more VRAM may matter
more.
Don't let the specification of the part
you wish to buy decide the diagnosis. So
here is the verdict. An SSD can store a
model. RAM can hold pages in working
state.
A GPU can execute supported calculations
efficiently when enough of their data
resides in the right place.
Offloading can bridge capacity gaps, but
it often pays for that capacity with
extra movement, latency, or complexity.
If a model finally loads after you
enable offloading, that's the start of a
successful experiment, not the end. Test
startup, prefill, decoding, and memory
pressure separately.
Then decide whether the result actually
meets your goal. Tell me your GPU,
system RAM, SSD, model size, and which
runtime you use.
Does your model refuse to load, take
forever to start, or become slow only
when generating words? This is byte
forensics. Storage is not speed until
the whole system proves it.

metadata.title: SkyPilot at 100k+ GPU Scale at Meta AI (FAIR) - Lucca Bertoncini (Meta)
metadata.author: SkyPilot
metadata.shortDescription:
From AI Infra Meetup with SkyPilot and CoreWeave on 3/25/2026 in San Francisco https://luma.com/h52qyhmt.

This talk explores how Meta FAIR uses SkyPilot to manage AI workloads across their 100k+ GPU Slurm fleet, replacing a ~10-step manual process of SSH, 2FA, and credential management with a unified control plane that automatically routes jobs across clusters based on resource availability.

Learn more about SkyPilot: https://skypilot.co

metadata.author: SkyPilot
metadata.shortDescription:
From SkyPilot AI Infra Meetup with H Company on 10/08/2026 in San Francisco.

This talk answered the question “Why are my GPUs not getting scheduled?” and showed how SkyPilot takes the pain out of it.

Learn more about SkyPilot: https://skypilot.ai
