metadata.title: Building Multi-Cloud GenAI Platforms Without the Pain | Romil Bhardwaj, SkyPilot
metadata.author: Toronto Machine Learning Society (TMLS)
metadata.shortDescription:
🎥 Recorded live at the MLOps World | GenAI Summit 2025 — Austin, TX (October 9, 2025)

Session Title: Building Multi-Cloud GenAI Platforms Without the Pain
Speaker: Romil Bhardwaj, Co-creator, SkyPilot
Talk Track: LLMs on Kubernetes

Abstract:
As GenAI workloads continue to expand, organizations are hitting hard limits with single-cloud strategies — from GPU shortages to escalating costs and vendor lock-in. In this talk, Romil Bhardwaj, Co-creator of SkyPilot, presents a hands-on guide to building multi-cloud AI platforms that unify compute resources across hyperscalers, neoclouds, and on-prem clusters — without adding operational chaos.

Romil demonstrates how to seamlessly connect and orchestrate workloads across AWS, GCP, Azure, Coreweave, Nebius, and Lambda through a single abstraction layer. You’ll see practical scheduling strategies for GPU allocation, automated cloud selection for cost optimization, and techniques for handling cross-cloud data movement and dependency management.

This session provides a roadmap for ML teams to secure GPU capacity, reduce costs, and focus on building great AI products instead of fighting infrastructure complexity.

What you’ll learn:
• Why going multi-cloud is becoming essential for GenAI workloads
• How to unify compute across clouds and clusters with SkyPilot
• Strategies for workload scheduling and cost optimization
• How to manage cross-cloud data movement and dependencies
• Practical patterns for scalable, resilient multi-cloud AI platforms

📍 Recorded: October 9, 2025 — In-Person Session, MLOps World | GenAI Summit 2025, Austin, TX
🔗 Learn more: https://mlopsworld.com

#MLOpsWorld #GenAISummit #RomilBhardwaj #SkyPilot #GenAI #MLOps #LLMOps #AIInfrastructure #Kubernetes #MultiCloud #AIDeployment #AIEngineering #AICommunity #AIinProduction

metadata.title: Why Cheap Spot GPUs End Up Costing MORE (The Checkpoint Mistake)
metadata.author: The Code Notebook
metadata.shortDescription:
Lesson 2 of Cloud for AI Engineers. I simulated a 100 hour job on cheap spot GPUs. With no saves it needs over two million hours. Save too often and it costs more than on-demand.
We pick a chip (NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, AWS Trainium), learn to read machine names, climb the buying ladder from on-demand to spot, find the commitment trap, simulate spot interruptions, work out the best save interval, compare price per petaflop and simulate scale to zero. Chip facts and prices are vendor figures dated October 2026, the sums are labelled arithmetic, and the spot and scale to zero results are simulations with assumed rates.

In this lesson:
✅ Four chip families and what each is for
✅ Which NVIDIA, AMD, TPU and Trainium chips you can really rent in October 2026
✅ How to read machine names on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure
✅ Big clouds versus neoclouds
✅ The buying ladder: on-demand, queued, commitment, spot
✅ The commitment trap: real price = rate ÷ how busy you are
✅ Spot simulation: no saves needs 2,203,564 hours for a 100 hour job
✅ The best save interval: about 34 minutes, and why 30 seconds costs more than on-demand
✅ Price per petaflop-hour for TPU and B200
✅ Autoscaling with KEDA and Karpenter
✅ Scale to zero: 24 to 4.04 GPU-hours a day, and the 60 second cold start
✅ ShopNest Copilot: three workloads, three rungs
✅ Interview questions with answers

metadata.title: NSDI '23 - SkyPilot: An Intercloud Broker for Sky Computing
metadata.author: USENIX
metadata.shortDescription:
SkyPilot: An Intercloud Broker for Sky Computing

Zongheng Yang, Zhanghao Wu, Michael Luo, Wei-Lin Chiang, Romil Bhardwaj, Woosuk Kwon, Siyuan Zhuang, Frank Sifei Luan, and Gautam Mittal, UC Berkeley; Scott Shenker, UC Berkeley and ICSI; Ion Stoica, UC Berkeley

To comply with the increasing number of government regulations about data placement and processing, and to protect themselves against major cloud outages, many users want the ability to easily migrate their workloads between clouds. In this paper we propose doing so not by imposing uniform and comprehensive standards, but by creating a fine-grained two-sided market via an intercloud broker. These brokers will allow users to view the cloud ecosystem not just as a collection of individual and largely incompatible clouds but as a more integrated Sky of Computing. We describe the design and implementation of an intercloud broker, named SkyPilot, evaluate its benefits, and report on its real-world usage.

View the full NSDI '23 program at https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi23/technical-sessions

segments.text: Good afternoon everyone. I'm Jong Han
from Berkeley. Super excited to talk
about SkyPilot, which is an intercloud
broker system we've been building at
Berkeley and it's for Sky Computing. And
this is a big team project. It's a joint
work with a bunch of great folks here
from UC Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab.
So let's get started.
Today's clouds create silos.
Applications are mostly developed for
particular clouds and afterwards they
are locked in. And we argue that this is
highly undesirable for a few key
reasons. One, the applications cannot
easily use better software services or
better hardware, better pricing
elsewhere. This is going to be
increasingly relevant because cloud
providers today are trying to
differentiate themselves from each other
by offering these unique offerings.
Moreover, applications have lower
resource availability. The most recent
example of this is the current AI race.
We are seeing cloud providers running
out of GPU servers to rent.
There are also quite a few business
related concerns about the locking. If a
business has fewer execution size to
choose from, it will be harder to meet
the data residency and data sovereignty
regulations. The business is also more
vulnerable to large-scale outages and it
has lower negotiation leverage to get a
better deal because choice is power.
So Sky Computing was recently proposed
to address these challenges and it is
about enabling transparent multi-cloud.
We want to go from this picture to this
picture
where applications develop on top of the
sky and run on top of the sky, which is
a collection of clouds, should easily
use one or more clouds.
One key feature of Sky Computing is it
performs
placement of applications based on
requirements and objectives. For
example, the requirements can be
specifying software and hardware
resources, location constraints, and so
forth. And the objectives can be
minimized in time or cost or even carbon
emissions to execute the workload.
The same application should be able to
use a different cloud based on the
timing of the submission because the
requirements can change and the pricing
and the availability on the cloud
provider side can also change.
Finally, the same application instance
should be able to use more than one
cloud at a time and we will show some
examples of this later.
So this all sounds good. The question is
how do we achieve it? How do we make sky
computing happen?
One seemingly natural choice is to do
standardization. We can imagine building
a portability layer implemented by every
cloud. For example, there are current
and prior proposals pursuing this
approach.
But we argue these proposals have
limited success so far for a few
reasons. One, such a portability layer
is typically low level. They focus on
infrastructure as a service and that
means a higher level more proprietary
services are not available.
Moreover, such a portability layer if it
were to support all the cloud services,
of which there are hundreds, it would be
very complex.
Perhaps most importantly, cloud
providers do not have the incentives to
support the standardization because they
don't want to become commodities.
So in this work, we propose the idea of
inter cloud brokers, which is a
mechanism to kick start sky computing.
And really the key idea here is to match
application demands with the best cloud
services that can support these demands.
And let me show a simple example.
Say we have an application with these
three stages, secure data processing, ML
model training, and ML model serving.
We submit this application to the
intercloud broker system, which should
have the freedom to place these stages
on different clouds for execution.
For example, if the secure data
processing stage requires using Intel
SGX, currently only Azure out of the top
three clouds uh offers SGX instances. So
the broker will send the first stage to
Azure.
For training, the broker may send it to
Google uh to take advantage of the TPU
accelerators, which are highly optimized
for uh model training.
And for inference, it may send it to AWS
because AWS has this custom uh
inferential chips for low-cost
inference.
So we see the applications in this way
can still use the unique and proprietary
services available on certain clouds.
Moreover, let's say in this collection
of clouds, in this sky so to speak, and
there's there's another cloud coming
along offering a new service. And let's
imagine this service uh is offering
better price or performance for serving
workloads.
Then the broker should have the uh
freedom to notice the performance
improvement and decide to send send some
serving workloads to this new cloud. And
we see that clouds can still compete to
provide better price and performance,
and this way they do not become
commodities.
Finally, we want to know that uh we can
have multiple brokers in the future uh
each focusing on different workloads.
And this is very beneficial because then
uh a single broker doesn't have to
support all the hundreds of cloud
services.
In summary, uh the idea is to use
intercloud brokers to create a two-sided
market between the applications and the
cloud services. And we want to use this
market force to drive sky computing.
So the question is, is this feasible?
Well, to answer this question and show
immediate uh benefits, we built a system
called SkyPilot, which is an intercloud
broker focusing on intensive batch jobs.
And here's a high level overview.
The user submits a program and a
resource requirement. The requirement
can be the GPUs require CPU, memory, and
location constraints and we may know
assumptions about the programming
frameworks used in the job.
So given this information, the system
will figure out the best cloud to
execute this job and go goes ahead and
foresee the execution.
In the rest of the talk, I'm first going
to talk about the requirements, what is
actually required in building out such a
broker system. Then I will talk about
the architectural and interface choices
we made in SkyPilot. And finally, I will
show some use cases to answer the

So let me start with the requirements.
We know today's cloud offerings are very
diverse.
Here we are showing out of the top three
clouds, there are hundreds of zones and
tens of regions.
More importantly, these locations are
very different. They have different
offerings. Their pricing can also differ
quite a bit.
Here's one example. We are looking at a

From AI Infra Meetup with SkyPilot and CoreWeave on 3/25/2026 in San Francisco https://luma.com/h52qyhmt.

This talk introduces SkyPilot, a unified control plane for running AI workloads across Kubernetes, Slurm, and cloud VMs with portable YAML and no code changes.

Learn more: https://skypilot.co

Topology aware placement so 64 GPUs on the wrong side of the network do not run
four times slower than 64 on the right side. Priority tiers with preemption and a
grace period so research work can take a card back from a notebook without
throwing away a week of training. Quotas with a floor and a ceiling so one team
cannot starve the rest.

Then the hard parts. Why the queue cannot be first in, first out. How
fragmentation eats a cluster that looks half empty. Backfill and reservations.
Why the design needs two different databases. And what actually happens when the
control plane dies, when a spot provider reclaims 100 GPUs with two minutes of
notice, and when 400 jobs all retry at the same instant.

A running scoreboard tracks cluster utilization, queue depth and money burned on
idle cards, so you can watch each fix pay for itself.

metadata.title: Checkpoint K8s pods transparently (plain CPU or GPU accelerated)
metadata.author: Christian Kniep
metadata.shortDescription:
I am an early adopter of containers with a background in HPC. From the early days, I’ve tried to merge container tech into the HPC (and HTC) stack. Containers already make packing and deployment easier - especially in AI/ML and data science. How about checkpoint/restore?
Over the last couple of months, we at MemVerge have developed a Kubernetes Operator for transparent checkpointing and restoring, allowing you to use discounted Spot instances for long-running workloads like bioinformatics workflows or ML training. 
Here’s how it works:
the operator attaches a PVC to your pod
Intercepts the STOP signal to checkpoint the pod
if the attached PVC contains a checkpoint when the pod is starting over, it will be restored instead of starting from scratch.
This can be triggered by someone draining the node (e.g., due to an EC2 Spot reclaim), deleting a pod, or another operator acting on its own logic.
Our checkpoint engine captures every aspect of the process tree within the container: memory pages, file descriptors—even TCP connections, if you want us to.
Until recently, it was targeted at CPU use cases only. We’ve now added support for NVIDIA GPUs, with AMD GPUs coming soon (via upstream CRIU plugins).
You can try it out in your Kubernetes environment with our 60-day trial. I’ve done some typical checkpoint/restore work (e.g., Jupyter notebooks, traditional jobs) and would love to hear what kinds of workloads you’re interested in checkpointing and restoring.

Sign up here for the 60-day trial: https://form.typeform.com/to/vZujMYxI

This talk introduces CoreWeave's SUNK (Slurm on Kubernetes) cluster product and its integration with SkyPilot for large-scale AI training.

metadata.title: Building Multi-cloud AI Platforms on Kubernetes Without the Pain - Romil Bhardwaj, SkyPilot
metadata.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
metadata.shortDescription:
Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

Building Multi-cloud AI Platforms on Kubernetes Without the Pain - Romil Bhardwaj, SkyPilot

AI workloads are redefining how modern platforms are architected. They require elastic GPU capacity, but no single cloud can meet all needs reliably or affordably. Kubernetes can become the de-facto substrate for AI orchestration, but going multi-cloud with Kubernetes slows down even the best infra teams. And for many AI engineers, the steep learning curve of Kubernetes itself remains a major barrier to adoption.

This talk is a hands-on guide to building a multi-cloud, Kubernetes-based AI platform that unifies resources across hyperscalers, neoclouds, and on-prem clusters into a single compute abstraction. We'll walk through practical details including open-source tooling for workload scheduling, automated cloud selection for cost optimization, experiment tracking  and dependency management. This approach lets AI engineers use the same unified interface for interacting with compute, enabling them to focus on building great AI products rather than wrestling with cloud complexity.

videos.full_text: Hey everyone. I'm Romil. I'm I'm one of the co-founders and creators of the SkyPilot project. And today, I'm excited to talk to you about how to build multi-cluster AI platforms and Kubernetes minus the pain. For the last few years, I've spent a bunch of time working on working with Neolabs, working with the top AI natives on how they manage their AI clusters and they end up managing more clusters than they'd like to. And in today's talk, I it's intended to give you a high-level overview of what kind of challenges people face when they're trying to manage multiple clusters and how some abstractions can help and make it easy for them to access and use those clusters. This talk will be very high-level, but I'm very happy to dive into technical details in the Q&A. So getting GPU supplies hard and you guys all know it, right? Like it's it's a talk of the town. It's really hard to get GPUs. And let me illustrate this to the example of OpenAI. So back in 2016, OpenAI signed an exclusive contract with Microsoft to get to get compute, specifically GPUs. And then in 2024, they ended this exclusivity after they launched ChatGPT and then they expanded their capacity to Oracle Cloud. In 2025, just one year later, they onboarded more cloud providers including CoreWeave and also started experimenting with Google Cloud's GPUs to get access to compute beyond just NVIDIA GPUs. And turns out even that was not enough. Like last year, Sam Altman put out this tweet talking about like, hey, we just want to get our experiments running. If anybody has capacity, just give us a call, right? So clearly there's not enough GPUs out there in the world. And what ends up happening is because you can't find enough capacity on a single cluster, you end up with a fragmentation of your GPUs across different clusters. So for example, you may have your AI team. It starts off with some Neo Cloud reservation, for example, either on CoreWeave or Nebius, um which you got when you were able to secure capacity on the hyper-scalers. At the same time, you have some on-demand capacity from the hyper-scalers themselves, think EC2 instances or GCP VMs. Then you may also have some on-prem capacity in the form of say a a rack or like a DGX cluster that you're running within within your own organization. Um then you may also have another cluster which is a say running in Europe mainly for data residency and compliance requirements. And then you may have some other CPU only cluster for running your regular batch workloads. So this while all of these decisions were made at that time to sort of like justify hey we need more capacity hence we get more clusters but now you are left with this like fragmented mess of different clusters that now your researchers and your platform team is forced to manage. So if I translate this to your stack right like this is what it looks like. At the top you have your workloads, your AI workloads that your researchers, your ML engineers, your inference team is running right. So think of these as interactive dev workloads. Think you know VS Code or Jupyter Notebooks that you're running. Then you have your large scale training workloads. Think you know large scale multi-thousand GPU pre-training that you might be running or even mid-training, post-training. And if you're doing post-training you'll probably be doing RL uh and as a part of RL you'll need sandboxes, you'll need inference, you'll need training, you'll need all those components. And then finally once you're done training your model you will need to serve that model. So you'll also need to run serving on these same GPUs. And at the bottom you see your you know patchwork of GPUs. You have some GKE clusters, some EKS clusters, some on-prem resources, um maybe even some Slurm clusters right and even some EC2 elastic instances from the cloud. Uh now it becomes a real challenge on how do you map these workloads onto these different clusters and how do you organize and manage and use these clusters right. And then that gives rise to these five challenges that I'm going to talk about. So first off, you know, how do you even schedule your workloads across these different clusters because you don't know where capacity how do you decide where to launch a workload. Then say you decide to launch a workload, you may need to change your job spec because some cluster might be running say Infiniband, some might be on Spectrum-X or Rocky and that needs a separate configuration. Then third, once you've launched it, you need to observe and manage it and again your observability will be fragmented to a specific cluster. You'll have Grafana running on one cluster, maybe on another one, but now you have like two or three or many different dashboards you're managing. And then speaking about your workloads themselves, like RL has very unique requirements. RL needs GPUs for the trainers, GPUs for inference, but needs thousands of CPUs for running the rollouts in the in in sandboxes. So it can potentially span across clusters as well. And then finally you have inference which which has very dynamic resource requirements, scales up, scales down very dynamically and may need to run across these different clusters. So you know, these are all challenges when when it comes to managing multiple clusters and I feel as a community, you know, we have kind of done a really good job of managing single clusters in the form of Slurm or Kubernetes, but taking it across clusters becomes really hard. So let's first talk about you know, what Slurm and Kubernetes are really good at today. So if you look at Slurm, you know, started two decades ago, mainly geared toward towards HPC workloads, really good gang scheduling support, topology aware scheduling and kind of built for you know, really large-scale supercomputing workloads. But it really wasn't built for the cloud era, so you know, it's designed more for like static fixed on-prem clusters and not really built for serving workloads, more of like long-running batch workloads. Kubernetes on the other hand came out about almost 11 ago now. Um, very elastic built for the cloud. You know, it could dynamically add nodes, reduce nodes, scale up and down. Uh, provided really good isolation between workloads thanks to containers. Slurm eventually caught up with Pyxis and Enroot, but you know, a Kubernetes was there first. And but as more people deployed Kubernetes, it kind of you know, earned a reputation for being hard to hard to get started. It had a fairly steep learning curve, which can be you know, daunting for AI researchers. Uh, and the other big problem is Kubernetes is designed for single cluster management. So you deploy Kubernetes on a cluster and you manage that cluster, but what if you have many such Kubernetes clusters? And so that's kind of what this talk is going to be talking about, which is we need to move beyond managing just single clusters and start managing multiple clusters. So the the fun thing about systems is you know, a lot of problems can be solved by building the right abstractions. And in this talk, you know, my proposal is if we build the right abstraction in the middle layer, a lot of these multi-cluster management software problems can be can be you know, tackled. And so this is why we built SkyPilot. So to provide some context, SkyPilot is think of it as like an open source layer that's running on top of your clusters. Your clusters keep the existing components they're running. So you keep running K- Q, you keep running Slurm, you keep running LLMD for serving, right? SkyPilot just adds a management and abstraction and and and orchestration layer on on top of your existing clusters. And then we apply five simple ideas to sort of like make SkyPilot work really well for multi-cluster scheduling. The first one is we always schedule globally, right? So we get a global view of the clusters and place jobs according to where there's capacity available. Uh, the second is we build on idea of researchers or your users declaring intent that I want to run a job with eight B300s. And then SkyPilot translates that intent into whatever resources are available on on a clusters. The third one is because we run as a you know one unified layer, we can provide you really good observability across clusters. So we this layer can pull data from your existing DCGM, your existing monitoring stacks into one place so that you have like a global view. And then at the same time you can also enforce policies across clusters. And then we have lots of optimizations built specifically for reinforcement learning and model serving. I'll talk about those in a bit. To give you some quick background, SkyPilot started off back at UC Berkeley when we grabbed students there, the same lab from which Spark emerged, became Databricks, Ray, AnyScale, and we now we LM SG Lang as well. Completely open source, Apache 2.0 and you know sort of like has its foundations and some of the research we did as like PhD students at UC Berkeley now has 10K GitHub stars, over 300 contributors, and some of the biggest labs are running SkyPilot today to manage their workloads. So let's let's talk about the challenges. The first one is with Kubernetes, the scheduling kind of stops at the cluster boundary that you know when you're using a single cluster, things are great. You know, you can have one queue, you can have quotas, priorities, preemptions thanks to K Q. And you can also have like have like a reasonable experience when using a single cluster. But the moment you go across clusters, when you bring in more clusters to your team, you will now end up sort of like switching Kubernetes contexts across different users. So you'll have one researcher submitting say to a GK cluster, another to EKS, maybe someone using Slurm, right? And this gets tricky because now users don't know where to submit their job. You could either expect them to sort of whole capacity and then try to launch their jobs there. But what often ends up happening is they pin to a specific cluster and as a result you may have jobs that are pending even while there are there is GPU capacity available in other other clusters. SkyPilot flips this model. The idea is all researchers, all users submit jobs to one this one layer and this one layer maintains a global queue which spans across clusters. And then this layer maintains a map or visibility into what clusters have capacity where and then hit submits jobs based on that. And that allows you to optimally place jobs because now you have more information about how other clusters are doing, what's what's running on other clusters. And as a result, you know, you sort of like avoid wasting your GPUs. The next challenge is we talked about pod specs being very bespoke to a specific cluster. And that's kind of a reason because each cluster is very unique, right? So, for example, if you spin up say H 200s across different clouds on GKE that would look like, you know, it will come with device plugin now. It will sort of have GPU direct for networking. For storage it will be using GCS fuse or something like that. And then drivers will be managed by GKE. On EKS, you know, it changes from GPU direct to EFA. Uses a different storage backend. A lot of this has been standardized by by Kubernetes now thanks to CSI and the device plugin efforts. But there's still a lot of bespoke configuration that goes into every every cluster. So in in the SkyPilot we sort of like think about it differently. The idea is the user expresses their intent. So they say that hey I need to run this job with eight B 300s and I want to use the best possible network. So that's a network tier best flag. And then you specify your image, your job spec, you know, whatever commands you want to run. And then what SkyPilot will do for you is it knows all your clusters. You have configured them ahead of time. And then it will translate your intent, your the resources you want to run with into actual pod specs that can work across different clusters. So for example, if it decides to place your job on EKS, it will start using EFA instead of GPU Direct. The third challenge I talked about was observability, right? So you want to serve be to be able to see what's running across all your clusters. And this if you the the way it operates today is you have many different clusters, each of them with their own Prometheus, with their own Grafana deployment, maybe with their own Kyverno deployments as well to sort of like enforce your policies. What ends up happening is you end up with like n different dashboards instead of like one one dashboard to see what's what's going on on your clusters. And there's like no fleet-wide view. You can't tell what's the who's been using how much quota of their GPUs. And so you know, it tends to lead to a lot of infighting between like research teams about, you know, how many GPUs is being used by which team. And so again, one of the advantages of sort of building an abstraction at a layer in the middle is you are able to sort of provide unified observability across your clusters. And again, this builds on like standard telemetry tooling that's already available in Kubernetes and and from NVIDIA around like DCGM and so on. It polls, you know, GPU health, it polls GPU status, it polls cluster general health, and then presents that to your team. So that when your leadership asks like, hey, who's been using how many GPUs, right? You can give them like a concrete answer through through one dashboard. The other so what I talked about so far was just general workload management, but if you zoom into the specific workloads themselves, if you look at reinforcement learning specifically, it is not just one training run. It is a composition of many different components. For example, we can see on the top right you have a trainer here which needs like beefy GPUs because it's running the actual weight updates. Then you have a rollout server on the top left, which is an inference engine, which is basically generating a lot of like trajectories for to run to run in sandboxes. And so this is more of like an inference workload, which is periodically getting its weights updated. And then finally, you have your sandboxes, which could be hundreds of thousands of CPU nodes, which are sort of running trajectories and returning the reward to back to the trainer. And so this needs, you know, many CPUs and really, really fast cold starts. So again, this is a composition of different workloads. It's not just one, you know, V1 job or it's not just a batch job. It it's a batch job for the training. It's a regular LLM inference job for the rollouts. And for the sandboxes, it's just like it it's think of it as like CPU jobs, but which need really, really fast cold starts. And so in SkyPilot, what we do is like instead of having the users sort of define three different jobs, all of them become one what we call a job group, right? And this becomes like the one spec for your entire RL system is what we call it. So for example, you'll have a trainer, you can specify what resources it needs. Same for sandboxes and and your rollouts. And then you just run one command, Sky Jobs Launch, and that will take care of orchestrating this entire this entire stack on on your cluster. And some of the benefits of doing this in a unified way are like, of course, you get service discovery. So just Kubernetes, you can sort of discover where your rollouts are running, where your sandboxes are running. But at the same time, it also offers lifecycle management that is contextual to your RL workload. For example, if a sandbox dies, that's not fatal. It's totally fine to sort of like continue working, get the rest of the trajectories. But if the trainer dies, that's uh that's consequential. So you want to sort of like pause the job there and sort of like restart uh so that you can like get the uh let the trainer restart before you sort of like run your rollouts again. Um and in doing so, we are able to guarantee you independent recovery so that your even if, you know, say one rollout worker failed, the others can still continue running. So uh I I talked about RL um about inference as well. You know, inference has its own challenges when it comes to sort of like running on Kubernetes. Um a lot of them are being solved by LLMD now and it works really well in like a single cluster setting, right? So uh single cluster inference pretty good, you know. It has KV cache aware routing, is able to auto scale based on different VLLM or ST lang metrics. And you get like this one nice endpoint that sort of scales across your different replicas. Uh but the challenge starts when you start trying to do this across clusters. Uh for for example, the moment you sort of like scale up from one cluster to many, uh the first thing that 's going to happen is what if a cluster goes down, right? When when a cluster fails, uh each each LLMD deployment that you have is running in its own you know, you you could think of it as its own bubble. So it has observability into only what replicas it has at that moment. But what you really need is observability across your clusters. You want to guarantee a certain number of replicas and a certain, you know, quality of service uh at your app layer. And at the same time, your app is now kind of like responsible for doing the routing. It's like it's supposed to detect when a cluster fails and then reroute traffic to other other replicas. And this routing problem gets when you think about KV cache awareness, because what ends up happening is if your if your app layer is simply a load balancer which is round robining or sort of doing P2C or something similar to sort of get requests to different clusters, it's not really KV cache aware. And what ends up happening is even you you sort of like end up hurting your inference performance because you are sending queries in in a classical round robin or like a classical load balancing manner instead of like KV cache aware routing. What what SkyPilot allows you to do is like it moves the endpoint from a per cluster endpoint to one global endpoint that's available to your applications and then takes the responsibilities that the application was doing in the previous example onto onto itself. So for example, that includes when a cluster goes down, right? SkyPilot can be the one responsible or this layer can be the one responsible for moving traffic to other healthy clusters and also moving replicas and scaling replicas across different clusters because it has global observability into where where capacity is available. Cool. So I I talked about the five challenges. This morning NVIDIA published a paper about Groot to how they how they trained the next big robotics foundation model. And one of the things they highlighted was they they've been using SkyPilot internally for training their models. And it follows it's it's a happy coincidence that the exact things I was talking about in the talk today is the ideas they used in their paper as well. So you can see they use PyTorch at the top level to sort of define their jobs. Ray as their like distributed orchestration system, so a distributed computing framework. And then SkyPilot takes care of the actual orchestration across 2,000 GB 300 GPUs which are spreading across different clusters. And the ideas are very similar, right? Like they run SkyPilot on top of Kubernetes. The researchers don't really think about which cluster this is running on, more of like, hey, just run this on like 2000 GB 300 nodes. Uh and what SkyPilot provides them is sort of like this unified management across across different clusters. Uh now, of course, there's a bunch of like open questions in multi-cluster management. The first one is of course like the scheduling I talked about, right? Like it's optimistic. It's based on the idea that we have some state knowledge about what different clusters have in terms of capacity and then we schedule based on that. But of course, that state information can be stale. What happens if you submit a job to a cluster, it fails to schedule? When do you decide to fail over to the next cluster? So we have some very primitive work around there, but we are now expanding into sort of like thinking about how either should we be maintaining more state in this layer or should it be more optimistic and should there be more signals from the cluster level scheduler? So all of these are very open questions for us. Data gravity is another big question. You know, often when you're doing multi-cluster, you can optionally replicate your data across different clusters, but if that's not available and you want sort of like data replication as a service, I think there's been some work from this project called Fluid, which is also a CNCF project. Very promising, very exciting that allows you to sort of like treat both compute and data as fungible across different clusters. And then finally, I talked about, you know, cache-aware routing. What we do right now is because we don't have exact KV cache awareness signals, we use sticky session routing as sort of like an approximation for KV cache-aware routing across clusters. Within a cluster, you'll always sort of get routed to a replica which has your cache. But across clusters, we do it based on session stickiness. So to to summarize, right, if you want to take one takeaway from the talk, it would be treat your clusters as a fleet, not as different clusters, right? And try to make them interchangeable, so that you sit above them instead of sort of like deploying different components onto onto each of them. And if you want five takeaways, the first one would be, you know, try to schedule your jobs globally. Don't think about scheduling as like, hey, I need to place a job in a cluster. Try to first think about I need to place this on my fleet. The second would be use intent as the driving signal from your team instead of instead of asking your team or researchers to write like pod specs specific to different clusters. And then third one would be, you know, think about observability. It becomes really important when you have a fleet of that scale and to be able to provide, you know, senior leadership about answers around like, hey, who's using how many GPUs or how are your GPUs doing is is very very valuable. And then finally about your workloads, RL is not just a training workload. It's a lot more than that. So think about the inference competence of it, the sandbox competence of it. And then finally inference, think of it as a global endpoint, not three different endpoints that you deploy [clears throat] ALB or some other load balancing on top of it. Cool. I'm going to stop here. My email is at the bottom right if you have any questions. I'll be around for any questions right now as well. Thank you. >> [applause] >> Yes. So the idea is because we maintain the global view of replicas, we also maintain the global view of metrics around like what's your request per second or token throughput and then we scale based on that across different clusters. >> Yes. So in some sense then SkyPilot sort of overrides the way it works is it declares to different clusters that hey instead of like four replicas you should now have seven replicas and the cluster then tries to scale up. But again that's opportunistic. After some time if that fails we try the next cluster. >> I like the idea of abstractions to allow same workloads to run across different environments. But like sometimes abstractions are helpful and sometimes people don't want abstractions. It's like you know and so have you ever thought or is there a construct of the workload being able to choose whether it wants those abstractions or whether it some kind of like global topology awareness so that it can schedule to specific kind of have in the rest of the world. >> Yeah. That's that's a really good question. We we also struggled with this in the start because we start with a very sort of like idealistic view of the world where we were like okay only intense everything else will be taken care of by SkyPilot. But as you sort of learned from the community right like those kind of escape hatches become really important where you are sort of like able to allow for example teams which sort of know exactly what needs to run on their cluster to sort of specify exactly you know hey this is the pod spec just you know plumb this through to my cluster. And so very recently about like one one and a half year ago we added plumbing you can call it to to SkyPilot to allow you to if you really want to sort of like bypass all the abstraction just like yeah you can set your pod spec as well. But the idea still remains that even if you submit a job with your own pod spec you're able to observe it and manage it through through SkyPilot. Uh I think we are out of time. But I'm happy to sort chat afterwards. Thank you.

metadata.title: Run One AI Model Across Multiple Clouds and GPUs (Modelplane)
metadata.author: Modelplane
metadata.shortDescription:
One model. Three clouds. Two GPU vendors. Two inference engines. One API.

The cloud native community has made the Kubernetes cluster a great place to run inference. But AI inference doesn't stop at the cluster boundary. GPU capacity is wherever you can get it, users and agents are everywhere, and sovereignty and economics decide where models can run. In this Inference Day keynote, Bassam Tabbara introduces Modelplane, the open source control plane for AI inference, and shows it running one model across a multi-cloud fleet. Recorded live at Inference Day, hosted by Modelplane and sponsored by Upbound, on November 5, 2026.

Speaker:
Bassam Tabbara, Founder and CEO, Upbound. Creator of Crossplane and Rook, and Modelplane maintainer.

What you'll see:
• Why inference, more than any other workload, is pushing teams to span clusters
• Why the fleet control plane for inference needs to be open and community driven
• An infra team provisioning clusters on AWS and CoreWeave with NVIDIA GPUs
• A model deployment that asks for the GPUs it needs without naming a cluster
• One endpoint that speaks the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs
• Scaling the fleet to Vultr with AMD GPUs and a second engine, serving the same model

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
[00:15] The cloud native waves
[00:45] Extending the stack for AI inference
[01:29] Inference doesn't stop at the cluster
[02:08] Many clusters, one fleet, one control plane
[03:02] Introducing Modelplane
[03:20] Demo: Set up the inference fleet
[03:45] Demo: Deploy a model
[04:40] Demo: Scale the fleet
[05:30] Any model, any engine, any infrastructure
[05:42] Take it for a test flight

Modelplane is v0.7, Apache 2.0 licensed and built in the open on Crossplane.

#AIInference #Kubernetes #OpenSource

metadata.title: NCP-AIO Scenario 03/5: Sharing GPUs Across Teams with Run:ai and MIG
metadata.author: Core Concept Learning
metadata.shortDescription:
Sharing GPUs Across Teams with Run:ai and MIG: a NCP-AIO exam scenario walkthrough. create Run:ai departments and projects with GPU quotas so teams can borrow idle GPUs over quota with preemption back to guaranteed quotas, use fractional GPUs for notebooks, partition inference GPUs with MIG through the GPU Operator's MIG manager with named configs, keep full GPUs for large training, and monitor per-project allocation and utilization to tune quotas.

NCP-AIO questions describe an operations task or failure on an AI cluster and ask for the right command, tool or fix. This walkthrough applies the course's checked facts to one situation, decision by decision.

What you will learn:
• The scenario: three teams, one cluster
• Projects and quotas
• Over-quota and preemption
• MIG for small workloads
• Monitoring and tuning
• Exam traps and self-check questions

CHAPTERS
00:00 Scenario 3: sharing GPUs across teams with Run:ai and MIG
00:29 Projects and quotas
00:56 Over-quota and preemption
01:26 MIG for small workloads
01:56 Monitoring and tuning
02:26 Exam traps for GPU sharing
02:55 Self-check questions

NCP-AIO scenario walkthroughs: 03 of 5. The 22 core lessons cover each topic in depth. Next: Recovering a Broken NVSwitch Node.

They buy it from a carrier, put their price on top, and hand you the result, which is fine right up until you are running real call volume, or a client asks what the telephony line actually costs, or you want to move a build from Vapi to LiveKit and find out your numbers do not come with you. This video puts your own Telnyx trunk underneath instead. The Vapi side takes three fields and no code. The LiveKit side runs through Postman so it is repeatable, and I go through the two settings that break with almost no error message to debug from.

📌 What You’ll Learn
• Connect a Telnyx phone number straight to Vapi with the native import, no code and no SIP config 
• Set the Telnyx side up once: verified account, API key, outbound voice profile, whitelisted destinations
• Build the Telnyx FQDN connection and auth credentials through Postman, so the whole thing is repeatable instead of 30 minutes of clicking
• Create the LiveKit inbound and outbound SIP trunks plus the dispatch rule, and match the agent name exactly (this one silently breaks everything)
• Fix the two failures that tell you nothing: wrong outbound destinations, and the missing X-Telnyx-Username header

✅ By the End You’ll Know
You will have a Telnyx number taking inbound calls and placing outbound calls on Vapi, and the same trunk wired into a LiveKit agent, both directions working. More usefully, you will know which layer to look at when a call connects and nothing happens, because inbound-works-outbound-dead and call-connects-no-agent have completely different causes and the errors do not tell you which one you are looking at.

metadata.shortDescription:
📞 **LiveKit + Telnyx SIP Trunking on a Self-Hosted Azure Server!**

Learn how to connect a real Telnyx phone number to your self-hosted LiveKit server on Azure and build an AI voice agent that handles real phone calls.

In this hands-on tutorial, I demonstrate **inbound and outbound SIP calls**, live call monitoring, and AI agent tracing using Arize Phoenix.

🚀 **What's covered:**
- Live demo: Phone call to an AI voice agent
- Telnyx FQDN SIP connection configuration
- Self-hosted LiveKit SIP server on Azure VM
- Docker, Redis, SIP ports, DNS and network configuration
- Inbound/outbound SIP trunks and dispatch rules
- LiveKit dashboard for monitoring active calls
- Arize Phoenix tracing and observability
- Connecting and testing your AI voice agent

Whether you're building **voice-to-voice AI applications, AI phone assistants, or real-time conversational AI systems**, this walkthrough shows how to integrate Telnyx SIP with LiveKit on your own infrastructure.

🎬 **Part 1 – Self-Host LiveKit on Azure:**  
https://youtu.be/fegGHLal_-M

📚 **Official Telnyx + LiveKit Documentation:**  
https://docs.livekit.io/telephony/start/providers/telnyx/

💡 If you're working with LiveKit Agents, Telnyx, SIP Trunking, or Voice AI, subscribe to VisionNLP for more hands-on tutorials!

#LiveKit #Telnyx #SIPTrunking

metadata.title: FCC Releases Report on the Future of the Universal Service Fund
metadata.author: ZCorum
metadata.shortDescription: The FCC released a report on the comments it received regarding how it should proceed on revamping the Universal Service Fund (USF). Currently USF is totally funded by consumers and businesses via monthly fees collected on phone bills. Initially those funds were meant to assist with service providers in providing phone service in high-cost areas. As phone service revenues have declined, and the funding of broadband service has become more prevalent, there is a need to expand funding sources for the USF program. The FCC has gathered and evaluated comments from stakeholders and has recommended that Congress clarify whether the FCC has authority to broaden the base of contributors, and to take action if needed for them to do so.

metadata.title: Consumers' Research v. FCC and the Legality of the Universal Service Fund Contribution Regime
metadata.author: The Federalist Society
metadata.shortDescription:
With billions of dollars allocated to broadband funding in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, the future of the FCC’s Universal Service Fund (USF) is a hotly debated topic. Now, with multiple lawsuits challenging the very legality of the USF contribution system, as well as new guidance from the Supreme Court on the limits of federal agencies’ power, the future of the Fund hangs in the balance. Industry experts joined us to discuss the issues raised in Consumers’ Research v. FCC and where the lawsuits stand in the aftermath of West Virginia v. EPA.

Featuring: 

Prof. Robert Frieden, Emeritus Professor of Telecommunications and Law, Penn State University

Harold Furchtgott-Roth, Senior Fellow and Director, Center for the Economics of the Internet, Hudson Institute

Michael Romano, Sr. VP of Industry Affairs and Business Development, NTCA – The Rural Broadband Association

Moderator: Arielle Roth, Legislative Counsel, U.S. Senator Roy Blunt

* * * * *

As always, the Federalist Society takes no position on particular legal or public policy issues; all expressions of opinion are those of the speaker.

metadata.title: Appeals court voids 9 billion dollar FCC telecom fund
metadata.author: LATEST NEWS UPDATE
metadata.shortDescription: The Fifth Circuit ruled the FCC had no authority to create the company collecting the nine billion dollar Universal Service Fund. Alex and Jordan explain the ruling and the risk to rural internet and phone subsidies.

segments.text: A federal appeals court just threw a
grenade into the system that keeps
millions of Americans connected, and the
fallout could be enormous.
>> This is the Universal Service Fund case,
right? The $9 billion program that
subsidizes phone and internet for rural
and low-income Americans?
>> Exactly. On Thursday, a three-judge
panel of the US Court of Appeals for the
Fifth Circuit ruled that the Federal
Communications Commission overstepped
its authority when it set up the
collection mechanism for this fund back
in the late 1990s.
>> Walk us through what this fund actually
does, because $9 billion a year is a lot
of money.
>> It's huge. It subsidizes basic
communications for rural and low-income
consumers, tribal lands, schools,
libraries, and rural health clinics.
Millions of Americans rely on it for
internet or phone service. The FCC
collects the money from carriers through
a private firm, the Universal Service
Administrative Company, which sets
contribution rates. That company was
created in 1997, and that's where the
court says the problem lies.
>> What did the judges actually rule?
>> Judge Edith Brown Clement wrote the
opinion. She said that because Congress
never specifically authorized the FCC to
create that company, the agency violated
the Government Corporation Control Act.
In plain English, the court says the FCC
built a corporate middleman it had no
legal right to build.
>> Here's the twist, though. Didn't the
Supreme Court already weigh in on this?
>> Good memory. In June of last year, the
US Supreme Court endorsed the way the
FCC funds this multi-billion dollar
program. So, this is a different legal
angle. The Supreme Court blessed the
funding model, but now the court is
attacking the entity that collects the
money. Oh, the FCC says it's considering
all its options, and the order wouldn't
take effect for at least two months.
>> So, nothing changes immediately for the
people relying on these subsidies.
>> Not immediately, no. But, think about
what's at stake. If this ruling stands
and no legislative fix comes, the
funding pipeline for rural broadband,
school connectivity, and low-income
phone service could be thrown into
chaos.
Telecom providers receive billions in
payments from this fund, and consumers
see the surcharge on their bills every
month.
>> And there's a political dimension here,
too.
Rural connectivity has been a bipartisan
priority for years, with billions more
flowing through separate broadband
programs.
A court pulling the rug out from under
the oldest and biggest subsidy program
would force Congress to act.
>> Exactly. And Congress would have to pass
a law explicitly authorizing what the
FCC has been doing for nearly 30 years.
That's not a small legislative lift in a
divided Washington, especially with
midterm elections less than 3 weeks
away.
>> So, to sum up, a nearly 30-year-old
funding mechanism is on shaky legal
ground. Millions of Americans'
connectivity could be affected, and the
clock is ticking with a 2-month window
before this order kicks in.
>> The FCC will almost certainly appeal or
seek a stay, and we'll be watching what
Congress does. This one affects real
people, from rural clinics to small-town
schools.

metadata.title: How to Peer with BGP Over the Internet Using GRE Tunnels | No ASN? No Problem!
metadata.author: Null0 Labs
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video we build a GRE tunnel across the public Internet and use it to establish a BGP peering session with a router in a remote data centre. Inspired by a @Computusio video I watched in my social feed. If you dont know he is a guy building a data centre in his basement. And I am very jealous that I dont have my own basement or space to setup some full racks of my own :(

This is a common technique used by service providers, hosting companies and organisations that want to advertise public IP space from a remote location without requiring a direct physical connection.

During the lab we cover:
Building a GRE tunnel across the Internet
Routing the tunnel endpoints correctly
Establishing BGP over the GRE tunnel
Using a Private ASN when you don’t yet own a public ASN
Repeating the configuration using a Public ASN
Receiving a default route from the data centre
Advertising your own prefixes through the tunnel

🛠️  Stuff I Use 🛠️
EVE-NG - multivendor network emulation software.
Linux, Ubuntu, Debian
OSX, Windows
Networking hardware - Multi vendor

👨🏻‍💻 About Me:
Hi I'm Matt a Senior Network Engineer with over two decades of hands-on experience architecting, securing, and optimizing high-availability networks across enterprise environments. I stream labs and create video content to help others level up their skills.


💻  Social:
Website: [null0labs.com](https://null0labs.com)
GitHub: [@null0labs](https://github.com/null0labs)
Instagram: [@null0labs](https://instagram.com/null0labs)
LinkedIn:[@mlewisonline](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mlewisonline)


🙋🏻‍♂️ Questions or ideas? Drop them in the comments.

Subscribe for protocol mastery, live labs, and routing realness.

metadata.shortDescription:
How to build a GPU mining rig in 2026, step by step: choosing cards by efficiency, the frame and motherboard, sizing the power supply, checking your circuit, cooling, software and pool setup, and power-limit tuning. Then a full worked example: a 4x RTX 4090 build with the real watts, amps and power cost.

🎁 FREE Mining ROI Calculator (spreadsheet): https://omniform1.com/forms/v1/landingPage/6a120cdfa930f52b5cd10f34/6abacc729d65c65b772404db
🧮 Live BTC and mining profit calculators: https://www.cryptominersrigs.com/calculators
▶️ Subscribe for real mining numbers: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCgkDMruoEL4xV6micLtuyBA?sub_confirmation=1

I run about 50 miners myself, so this channel is real numbers, not hype.

In this video:
- The 3 mistakes that sink most first rigs (wrong cards, PSU sized to the sticker, ignoring difficulty)
- Why efficiency (work per watt) beats raw hashrate when difficulty climbs
- PSU headroom (~80% continuous load rule) and why a normal 15 A / 120 V outlet tops out around 1,440 W
- Cooling and airflow: every watt becomes heat
- Driver, miner, pool and wallet setup (official sources only)
- Power-limit tuning: trim 10-20% power for little hashrate loss
- Worked example: 4x RTX 4090 = ~1,670 W at the wall, ~40 kWh/day, ~$4-$10/day in power

CHAPTERS
0:00 Why GPU rigs fail before they mine a coin
0:53 Mistake 1-3: wrong cards, PSU sizing, difficulty
2:10 Step 1: Choose cards by efficiency
3:14 Step 2: Frame, motherboard and risers
3:51 Step 3: Power supply and your circuit
4:40 Step 4: Cooling and airflow
5:04 Step 5: Software and pool
5:38 Step 6: Tune power limits
6:05 Worked example: 4x RTX 4090 build
7:43 Pre-build checklist

Watch next: Pearl GPU mining, RTX 4090 vs 3090 vs 3060 Ti: https://youtu.be/HiwkOoDna4Q
How to mine Pearl (PRL) step by step: https://youtu.be/KnbO8ylvzDw
Pearl mining profits, the real math after power: https://youtu.be/ea_k6NBe8nY

Sources: Pearl GPU figures are early pool-reported numbers (MiningBoard, October 2026), approximate and changing. RTX 5090 Pearl revenue decline reported by Tom's Hardware, May 2026. Always check a live calculator before buying.

Safety: have a licensed electrician check any circuit against your local code. Never daisy-chain power strips.

Not financial advice. Crypto is volatile, new coins can drop fast, difficulty can climb and mining can lose money. For taxes on mined coins, talk to a tax professional. All power-cost figures are examples; use your own wall-meter watts and your bill's rate.

AI disclosure: the script was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by a human; the narration uses an AI voice; B-roll is licensed stock footage; the music is AI-generated.

metadata.title: Confidential LLM Inference: Run Frontier Models Without Seeing Prompts
metadata.author: Duality Technologies
metadata.shortDescription:
Confidential LLM inference lets a model provider serve enterprise customers while every prompt stays sealed inside an attested enclave, even from the provider.

Enterprise customers want frontier models, but not to hand over their most sensitive prompts. In this product demo, a model provider uses Duality Technologies to offer confidential inference as a premium tier. The inference server runs on confidential GPUs in the provider's own cloud, inside a trusted execution environment (TEE), and the model weights load only after remote attestation.

What the demo shows:
- Registering an inference server as an application, with the serving image encrypted before it is stored
- The encryption key and image digest kept in the provider's own secret manager, so Duality holds no copy of either and the digest becomes the trust anchor
- Deploying a dedicated confidential service for one enterprise customer on a TEE from the provider's own GPU capacity
- The customer's own node verifying the enclave and issuing certificates to its users and apps
- Day-two operations without seeing content: CPU, GPU and memory metrics, model changes, upgrades that are attested before any weights are released, and an audit log with no prompts or responses

Who it's for: AI model providers and the platform teams that run inference for enterprise customers.

Confidential LLM inference lets a neocloud or GPU cloud serve enterprise customers while every prompt stays sealed inside an attested enclave, even from the operator.

Enterprises want to run models on your GPUs, but they won't send their most sensitive prompts to another provider. In this product demo, a GPU cloud operator uses Duality Technologies to offer confidential inference as a premium tier. The inference server runs on confidential GPUs in the operator's own data center, inside a trusted execution environment (TEE), and the model weights load only after remote attestation.

What the demo shows:
- Registering an inference server as an application, with the serving image encrypted before it is stored in the operator's own S3-compatible storage
- The encryption key and image digest kept in the operator's own secret manager, so Duality holds no copy of either and the digest becomes the trust anchor
- Deploying a dedicated confidential service for one enterprise customer on a confidential H100 from the operator's own GPU capacity
- The customer's own node verifying the enclave and issuing certificates to its users and apps
- Day-two operations without seeing content: CPU, GPU and memory metrics, model changes, upgrades that are attested before any weights are released, and an audit log with no prompts or responses

Who it's for: neoclouds and GPU cloud operators that want to win regulated enterprise inference workloads.

metadata.title: Self Hosted LLMs: Running Your Own Inference Infrastructure
metadata.author: Data Science Festival
metadata.shortDescription:
A talk by Daniel Burkhardt Cerigo from datavaluepeople

When does it make sense to run your own LLM inference infrastructure instead of paying per-token to third-party APIs like OpenAI or Anthropic? This session gives you a practical framework for that decision and the technical foundations to execute it. We'll ground everything in three concrete use cases - interactive chat, batch document processing, and high-volume stream classification - showing how different requirements around latency, throughput, and data sovereignty lead to different answers. You'll leave with a clear understanding of the tools that make self-hosting tractable (vLLM, open-weight models), the critical inference-server performance metrics, and an honest view of the cost trade-offs involved.

Technical Level: Introductory level/students (some technical knowledge needed)

This session was part of the Data Science Festival Big Birthday Bash event 2026. Find out more at https://datasciencefestival.com/event/big-birthday-bash-2026/

The Data Science Festival is the place for data-driven people to come together, share cutting-edge ideas, and solve real-world problems. We run monthly events, meet-ups, and the biggest free-to-attend data festivals in the UK. Join the community at https://datasciencefestival.com/

Would you like to learn how your organisation could partner with and support DSF events? Click the link below! 
https://datasciencefestival.com/become-a-sponsor/

metadata.title: Claude Architect Professional (CCAR-P) Part 11: Compliance, HIPAA, FedRAMP and Ethical AI
metadata.author: CodeFlow Daily
metadata.shortDescription:
Claude compliance and ethical AI for the Professional exam: GDPR roles, zero data retention, Covered Models, HIPAA readiness and BAA, Claude Code coverage, data residency and inference geo, FedRAMP platforms, audit evidence, bias testing, fairness, transparency and human accountability for high-risk decisions. Domain 5, objectives 4 and 5. Unofficial study material, not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

Chapters:
0:00 Cold open
1:18 Scope and sources
3:16 Who is responsible
6:00 Retention and ZDR
9:26 Covered Models
11:48 HIPAA readiness
15:26 HIPAA and Claude Code
18:01 Data residency
21:10 FedRAMP
23:53 Evidence and audit
26:45 A compliance design
29:54 Decision procedure
32:32 Bias
35:53 Fairness in practice
39:18 Transparency
42:18 High-risk accountability
45:41 An ethics review
48:39 Decision records
51:11 Walkthroughs
53:00 Anti-patterns and recap

What you will learn:
- Choose retention, HIPAA readiness, data residency and platform settings, and know which features each arrangement does and does not cover
- Collect audit evidence with the Compliance API, Access Transparency and your own logs, and write a control, owner and evidence for every requirement
- Test for bias with counterfactual pairs and slice metrics, disclose AI use, and place a qualified human before delivery in high-risk areas

Official sources:
- https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/api-and-data-retention
- https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency
- https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/access-transparency
- https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance
- https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup

Narration is an AI-generated voice; all visuals are drawn by code.

#CCARP #ClaudeCertification #Anthropic #AIArchitect

The API checks every request from a HIPAA enabled organization against that list and rejects the ones outside it, so nobody can step outside the agreement by accident. The fix is not to ask for an exception. The fix is to remove the feature or to do the calculation in your own code. That one picture holds the lesson of this part. Compliance is not a label on the model. It is a set of choices, which agreement, which features, which region, which retention, which platform, and who is accountable. This is unofficial study material, not affiliated with Anthropic. This is part 11 of the Claude Certified Architect Professional Series. This part finishes domain five, governance, safety, and risk management. The domain is 14% of the exam. Part 10 covered guard rails, failure modes, and human review. Today we cover the last two objectives. Ensure compliance with regulations, for example, GDPR, HIPAA, and FedRAMP, and address ethical AI considerations, namely bias, fairness, and transparency. Anthropic's privacy center articles on retention, processor roles, certifications, and server locations. Anthropic's acceptable use policy. Anthropic's posts on FedRAMP and Bedrock and on evaluating discrimination and political bias. All were read on November 10th, 2026. One, honest limit. The exam guide names three regulations. Anthropic documentation describes its own controls, not the text of those laws. So when I describe what GDPR requires, I am giving general knowledge and I will say so. Under a zero data retention arrangement, Anthropic does not store customer prompts or responses at rest after the API response is returned. You request it from sales. The workload that needs the most capable model runs in a workspace that accepts retention. Different API keys, different workspaces, different guarantees. And an audit can show which key goes where. The business consequence is a tradeoff to put in front of the stakeholder. A covered model might give a better result and carry a retention requirement. Whether that is acceptable depends on the data and on the commitments you have made to your own customers. That is a conversation, not a default. Scenario. A bank's contract promises no retention of customer messages. Its fraud analysts want the strongest model for investigation notes that contain no customer messages, only internal analysis. The bank puts the analysts in a separate workspace with standard retention, keeps the customer facing workload in the zero data retention workspace and documents the split. The trap. Turning off zero data retention for the whole organization to unblock one workload. Takeaway. Scope retention exceptions to a workspace, not to the organization. Now HIPAA. General knowledge first. HIPAA is a United States law about protected health information, often called PHI. A covered entity such as a clinic or insurer and a business associate, a vendor that handles PHI for it, must protect PHI. A vendor handling PHI signs a business associate agreement, a BAA. You download the agreement and the implementation guide, then accept as an authorized legal representative. A negotiated BAA goes through sales. Four facts to hold. One, it is enforced at the organization level and once enabled, it is permanent. An administrator cannot switch it off. So if you need both HIPAA-ready and general-purpose access, use separate organizations. Two, the API enforces the feature list. A HIPAA-enabled organization that sends a non-eligible feature gets an HTTP 400 invalid request error naming the feature. Client-side tools that the eligibility table marks as not blocked are accepted, but still sit outside HIPAA readiness. Three, your signed BAA is the official source of truth for what is covered. Four, HIPAA readiness is designed as an alternative to zero data retention for PHI, not an addition. With it, data can be retained with safeguards such as encryption, access controls, and audit logging. Zero data retention means not stored at rest. They cover different feature sets. What is not covered? Console usage for PHI. >> Claude platform on Amazon Web Service. >> Claude code under the API arrangement. Beta features, unless the table lists them as eligible. And the Privacy Center adds that a BAA covers only the organization that accepted it. Feature details the table spells out. Inline PDFs through the messages API are eligible. PDFs through the files API are not. The web search tool is eligible. The web fetch tool is not. And a [snorts] subtle one. When you use structured outputs or strict tool use, the API compiles your JSON schema into a grammar that is cached separately from message content. Those cached schemas do not get the same PHI protection. So never put PHI in schema definitions. Put patient names in the message, not in an enum. Scenario. A telehealth company wants a triage assistant. It signs the BAA, enables readiness in a dedicated organization, sends inline text, avoids the code execution tool, and keeps its schema generic. When a developer adds the files API for lab reports, the API rejects it, and the team moves the PDFs in line. The trap. Treating the BAA as a switch that makes every product HIPAA compliant. Takeaway. HIPAA readiness is an organization setting plus an eligible feature list, and the API enforces the list. The most common exam confusion is Claude Code. Two pages seem to disagree, and they do not. The API retention page says Claude Code is not covered under API HIPAA readiness. The Claude Code Legal and Compliance page says that if a customer has a BAA, it extends to Claude Code in two configurations. One, the HIPAA configuration. The command line interface or the code tab in Claude Desktop used with a Claude Enterprise account. where the organization has HIPAA enabled and the HIPAA configuration is applied to Claude Code in local mode. Two, Claude Code with zero data retention enabled for the organization, which is not available for all organizations. Under the HIPAA configuration, cloud sessions, remote control, Claude Code in the mobile app, and Claude Code routed through a third-party provider or gateway are not covered. So the same product has covered and uncovered modes depending on the surface and the plan. The privacy center's BAA article adds two items. Skills are available but not covered and they are off by default in HIPAA organizations. Connectors, which include NCP servers, are also not covered when they send data to third parties. Administrators who enable them are responsible for compliant use. The BAA excludes the console, co-work in the cloud, and beta features. What do you do with that as an architect? A hospital engineering team wants Claude code for its developers. Developers will sometimes read logs that contain patient identifiers. You set the parameter inference geo on a request to the value S or the value global or you set a workspace default. It is chosen when you create a workspace and cannot be changed afterward. The documentation says that currently the only available workspace geo is us. Mechanics to remember. Inference geo is supported on Claude 4.6 and later models. Sending it to an older model returns a 400 error. The response usage object reports where inference actually ran. A workspace can set allowed inference geos which restricts what requests may ask for and a default inference geo which applies when a request omits the field. So an administrator can enforce a policy across every key in the workspace rather than trusting each developer. The batch API accepts it per request. Managed agents pin it in the agent's model configuration and it is eligible for zero data retention and HIPAA readiness. The price. For Claude 4.6 and later models, us only inference is 1.1 times the standard rate across input, output, cash rights, and cash reads. Global routing is standard price. If you have a priority tier commitment, each token used with us only inference draws down 1.1 tokens from your committed capacity. Now the architect's reading. That data is stored in the United States and that some internal processing occurs where Anthropic or its affiliates operate. So an EU only promise cannot be met by settings alone. The team sets allowed inference geos to us only at the workspace level, sets the default to us, and budgets an extra 10% on token costs. It then checks the usage field on responses in its monitoring. The trap. Believing the data residency feature lets you choose any country. Takeaway. Two settings, inference and storage. Know the values that exist, the price, and what is enforced at the workspace. FedRAMP now. General knowledge. The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program is the United States government's approach to assessing cloud services for federal use. Authorizations are given at impact levels, low, moderate, and high. And an authorization belongs to a specific service offering with a defined boundary. It is not a property of a company or of a model. What Anthropic's pages say? A post from June 2025 announced that cloud models were approved for use in FedRAMP high and Department of Defense impact level four and five workloads through Amazon Bedrock in the AWS GovCloud US regions. At that time, two older models were available there, and the post said more might be added. This same post says government customers can use Google Cloud's Vertex AI for FedRAMP high and impact level two and Amazon Bedrock for FedRAMP moderate and high and impact levels two, four, and five. And Anthropic's government page says Cloud for Government is delivered through a FedRAMP high authorized environment with Cloud also available through Bedrock and Vertex.
